The subject of this book is the kind of
economic interaction and interdependence
that has arisen amongst nations in the con-
temporary world economy, the nature and
significance of the pattern of trade balances
that have resulted from them, and the ~ Js-
tion of what, if anything, shor!” Jc done by
national governments about that pattern. The
need for international coordination of eco-
nomic policies is also investigated.
The book opens with an article by Edmund S.
Phelps who introduces the theme and
presents, in summary, the most relevant
conclusions that can be assumed from the
works as a whole. This is followed by an
important essay by Robert Mundell who
presents the historical and theoretical per-
spectives for the entire volume. The essays
that follow are then organized into three
specific sections.
The first concentrates on single countries’
economic policies and their effects, in terms
of balances and imbalances in their foreign
accounts. In the second section, various
contributions regarding economic interde-
pendence are reviewed both in terms of
techniques for measuring interdependence
levels and of applied analysis, of their
impact on the various countries’ balance of
payments. Finally, relations between markets,
monetary and fiscal policies on one hand, and
the problem of interdependence and the ever-
growing need for international coordination
of economic policy on the other, are ana-
lysed.

General Editor: Mario Baldassarri, Professor of Economics, University of
Rome, ‘La Sapienza’, Italy
This new series is a joint initiative between Macmillan and SIPI, the
publishing company of Confindustria (the Confederation of Italian In-
dustry), based on the book collection MONOGRAFIE RPE, published by
SIPlI and originated from the new editorial programme of one of the oldest
Italian journals of economics, the Rivista di Politica Economica, founded in
1911. This series is intended to become an arena in which the most topical
economic problems are freely debated and confronted with different
scientific orientations and/or political theories.
The 1990s clearly represent a transition period in which the world
economy will establish new international relationships and in this con-
text, new challenges and new risks will have to be faced within each
economic system. Fundamental issues on which economic theory and
policy have long based their reasoning over the last two or three decades
have to be critically reviewed in order to pursue new frontiers for
theoretical development and economic policy implementation. In this
sense, this new series aims at being a “place of debate” between profes-
sional economists, an updated learning tool for students and a specific
reference for a wider readership aiming at understanding economic
theory and policy evolution even from a non-specialist point of view.

Preface
In this volume the theme of interdependence and integration in interna-
tional economics is pursued in relation to heavy disequilibria in trade
balances and in balances of payments over the last ten years and to the
problem of international coordination in economic policies.
Theessays presented deal with the themes mentioned both fromthe point
of view of economic theory and relative to more or less recent empirical
experience. These works were presented at the First International Eco-
nomic Conference at Villa Mondragone in Rome, and organized by the
University of Rome (Tor Vergata) under the supervision of Luigi Paganetto
and Edmund S. Phelps.
The text opens with an article by Edmund S. Phelps who introduces the
theme and presents, in summary, the most relevant conclusions that can
be assumed from the works as a whole.
This is followed by an important essay by Robert Mundell who presents
the historical and theoretical perspective for the entire volume.
The essays which follow are organized into three specific sections.
In the first section, the relationships of individual countries’ economic
policies are analized and the effects of these policies in terms of balances
and imbalances in their foreign accounts are assessed.
In the second section, various contributions concerning economic inter-
dependence are reviewed in terms of both the techniques for measuring
the degree of interdependence and applied analysis, with related impacts
on the balance of payments in various countries.
Finally, in the third section, always within a theoretical and empirical
context, essays have been included which concern, on one hand,
relationships between markets and monetary and fiscal policies and,
on the other hand, the problem of interdependence and the growing
need for the international coordination of economic policies.

on participation by nationals in that market and already has taken

Take an increase in a country’s budgetary deficit — say 20 billion
expressed in US dollars — from some combination of expenditure
increase and tax rate reduction. If the prospect of increased future
taxes that present citizens or their heirs must pay together with the
present tax cut stimulate a lesser increase in private saving — say 5
billion dollars — there is a net contraction in the world supply of
saving to the world capital market, a 15 billion dollar contraction in
my example. The impact of that, given the (new) path of consumption
that an unchanged path of employment makes possible, is an increase
in the rate of interest required by savers, at least over the near term.
In a world of non-monetary economies, which I find a potentially
useful abstraction, particularly one with non-shiftable capital and
either real wage rigidity or real wage stickiness, the result of the
reduced supply of saving and consequent rise of real interest rates is a
co-determined fall of world investment. Further, the world-aggregate
increase in households’ desire for consumption cannot be satisfied
sufficiently to take up the labor slack this created if capital cannot at
once be re-outfitted to make consumers goods instead of capital goods
and workers will accept lower real wages, if at all, only insofar as total
employment falls. Hence there is a decline of world employment. (It is
possible that in the home country,where the fiscal stimulus originates,
employment will fall least or actually rise as the real appreciation of
home assets relative to assets abroad induces an increase in interna-
tional competitiveness of the home country and thus increased sales
to foreign customers; but such a gain, if it occures, comes at a further
expense to employment in the rest of the world.
The effects of a country’s fiscal stimulus on employment abroad
in a world of monetary economies — particularly the effects prior to
completion of the adjustment of nominal wages and prices to the
shock — have long been a standard subject in international macro-
economics. In the Keynesian world of inertia or wrongway behavior
by nominal wages and prices, the internation] repercussions of fiscal
stimulus in a country are rather different. The rise in the world
demand for consumption is not frustrated by real wage rigidity or
stickiness.

4 Edmund S. Phelps
cases demand for consumer goods or goods produced by that sector,
were accompanied by a seemingly spontaneous decline of time prefer-
ence as evidenced by a decline of private thrift as a ratio to disposa-
ables incomes, especially but not only in the United States. The early
paper by Lal and vanWijnbergen ranges widely and eloquently on this
1980s phenomenon. From all of the theoretical pespectives cited
above, therefore, it is not a coincidence that the 1980s must be seen as
the decade of high expected real rates of interest, although they have
come down to an important degree — as has world fiscal stimulus in
relation to world consumption, if I am not mistaken — in the past
three years. According to the non-monetary perspective I discussed at
the beginning, and according to the monetary models in the Fitoussi
and Phelps monograph, it is also not a coincidence that the 1980s
have been a decade of depression from which most economies are
only now decisely emerging — a decade of depressed real prices of
capital goods, depressed relative prices of primary metals and other
primary materials, and swollen mark-ups of prices over costs.
In his essays Clark Reynolds has pointed to a further dimension of
this problem of fiscal impact abroad. The rise of real interest rates
dealt a double blow to Latin America: a higher debt service on their
recently acquired indebtedness to the commercial banks of the North
on top of the depressed real prices of the primary products that many
of them export. The increased overseas interest burden set in motion a
tidal wave through the Latin American economies: a flight of capital
from the “tax man” and from the risk of economic collapse, and the
consequent drying up of capital goods expenditure and much capital
goods output in those countries.
Robert Mundell has widened the perspective some more, as he
has done so often. If the world finds that the real and financial assets .
produced by the United States now possess an enhanced non-pecuni-
ary attractiveness, that fact will also plunge the United States balance
of trade into an increased deficit. The implication of the model is that
the real rate of interest falls in the United States and rises in the rest of
the world. So far as I can see, the repercussions of that rise of real
interest rates abroad are like the ones I discussed above when the
source was fiscal stimulus. Of course, the 1980s have not been a
decade of reduced real interest rates in the United States nor even a

Introduction and Major Conclusions 5
decade of a reduced differential, but one only needs to bring in the
American fiscal stimulus occurring alongside the newfound appeal of
American assets to wriggle loose from that implication.
I might mention two other papers at this juncture. In all theories
of the esternal effects of fiscal stimulus in a country, an auxillary
argument is that a stimulus causes a real appreciation in the home
country. The paper by Juergen Schroeder takes the further step of
recognizing, however, that as the public debt in the home country
piles up the country loses credit worthiness. He shows that the effect
of that prospect is to moderate the initial effect of the fiscal shocks on
the exchange rate and on the balance of trade. The interesting paper
by Masaru Yoshitomi bears on the effects of the comcomitant depreci-
ation of the currency on overseas countries, in this case Japan. This
paper is particularly concerned with the effects of the exchange rate
on the balance of trade, Through such studies we also learn something
about the effects of the value of the yen on employment in export and
import-competing industries in Japan and in the rest of the world. We
will have to look forward to some future paper, though, for an
examination of the general-equilibrium effect of the exchange rate on
total employment levels.
It is natural to ask whether these international effects I have been
discussing, effects which are external diseconomies on some definition
or other, can be moderated or blocked by the adoption of a suitable
monetary regime. The answer, I think, is “maybe yes” for some near
term; but not after nominal prices and wages have time to make a full
adjustment to the altered monetary situation, provided that money is
neutral. The paper by Emil Claassen indicates that an economy will
suffer the same real appreciation (or depreciation) following a real
shock no matter whether the country adopts a fixed real exchange
rate regime or a floating rate regime.
Yet in the near term, before full nominal adjustment, a country
facing a currency depreciation but wanting a fixed rate will need to
tighten money, and that will temporarily worsen the contraction of
employment that, according to the non-monetary model and the
Fitoussi-Phelps models, will result from fiscal stimulus abroad. That
suggests that Europe would have suffered a sharper contraction than
the one it actually experienced if it had been operating on a fixed-ex-

6 Edmund S. Phelps
change-rate system. Yet it is plausible, at least ot me, that the choice
of regime would not have had any appreciable lingering effect by the
late 1980s.
In this connection I very much admired the point made by
Stephen Marris in his paper that the swimg seen in so much of the
world toward a fixed-rate or stabilized-rate system may have the
unwelcome effect of encouraging countries to persist in their deficits.
There is a New England saying of which some American poets and
presidents have been fond: don’t tear down a fence until you find out
why someone put it up. An apparent corollary is: don’t rebuild a fence
until you have found why it fell down or was torn down. Before we
reconstruct the world along the lines of some sort of fixed-exchange
rate system we should consider whether the Bretton Woods system
collapsed because of its invitation to members of the stabilization club
to run large and indefinite budgetary deficits.
What should we hope to see develop in the fiscal area over the
1990s? Reduced deficits, of course. There is nothing the United States
and Italy, for example, could do for Latin American within the feasible
wish-lists that would be better than to bring down to zero their
inflation-adjusted budgetary deficits. If there is fear of the employ-
ment effects at home, this could be done in provisional steps, and
monetary policy could be deployed to make the Keynesian adjust-
ments, of course, so as to make unnecessary a possible one-time
downward adjustment of money wages relative to trend.
Could such a move really be good for much or all of the rest of
the world? I realize that that most economists were brought up on the
locomotive theory: If spending anywhere falls, nominal interest rates
rates will have to fall everywhere, causing a general slowdown of the
velocity of money and hence a general downturn in employment. But
my analysis suggests that ridding ourselves completely, not just
partially as has already been done, of the high real interest rates of the
1980s will usher in a new posperity in most or all of those areas of the
world that have fallen on hard times, or even desperate times, in this
past decade. I was pleased and fortified when Jeffrey Sachs, reporting
on some work by him and his associate for a recent issue of the
Brookings Papers, used the Fitoussi-Phelps framework in some simul-
ations of their MSG model and found that a policy move toward a

Introduction and Major Conclusions 7
reduced budgetary deficit in the United States would not be contrac-
tionary for Europe; it would after a short while be expansionary.
There seems to be a sea-change developing-developing so slowly that it
is not always possible to be sure that it is ‘actually occurring in the
way the economics profession looks at fiscal stimulus, both in a
closed- economy and, more especially, in a world-economy setting.
The decade of the 1980s gave us one observation, hardly more than
that, with which to test that theory; one might even say that the
observation inspired the theory rather than providing an opportunity
to test it. With a bit of luck, the 1990s will witness further shrinkages
in fiscal stimulus, accompanied by further declines in real rates of
interest, and thus provide us with a fresh opportunity to test the new
paradigm.

and fell prey to a former cook, who robbed him, set fire to his house, and murdered

until Jevons’ article in 1881. Cantillon had read most of the early writings of

developed the importance of the distinction between open and closed economies, the
vital difference between the effects of an (exogenous) increase in the supply of money
from, say, gold mines and an increase in money arising from a surplus of exports over
imports; whereas the former would lead to an increase in prices the effects of the latter
are more complicated. The prices of traded goods could not rise by much (beyond the
cost of transport) because they must be equal to foreign prices; whereas the prices of
domestic goods could rise. Although SEKINE (op. cit.) and HUMPHREY-KELEHER (loc. cit.
p. 128) argue that Cantillon does not define the conditions of monetary equilibrium, the
fact that the theory of the distribution of specie was evident in many early mercantilist
writings (e.g. Petty and North), and can be inferred from Locke’s work, makes it
plausible to attribute that concept to Cantillon as well. JosePH SPENGLER has called
Cantillon the “first of the moderns”, in his Essays in Economic Thought, edited by
Spengler and Allen (New York, Rand McNally, 1960).

would raise prices in an isolated economy, but objecting to his implication that it would
do so in a country trading with the rest of the world, where prices of goods that are
transportable could not diverge much (in the same currency unit) from world prices.
Hume willingly conceded the point to Oswald and promised to amend his draft
accordingly. On this important point see the reference there to James M. Lowe, An
Eighteenth Century Controversy in the Theory of Progress (The Manchester School,
September 1952): 314-16, on which Humphrey and Keleher rely.

approach”. Gervaise’s work suffered from an (even then) obsolete

had an advanced concept of the global equilibrium, the distribution of
money around the world, the real balance effect, and the distinction
between domestic and traded goods, and had an early general-equilib-
rium approach to the balance of payments. Hume, on the other hand,
stressed the immediate effect of changes in the money supply on the
balance of trade, the law of one price, and the short-run effect on the
balance of trade of the introduction of credit or convertible paper; in
this respect Hume was an explicit forerunner (if not an originator) of
the monetary approach to the balance of payments. Hume also, it
should be noted, recognized the time interval between changes in the
money supply and the consequent increase in prices during which real
effects on trade and employment could take place, yet he correctly
shrank from advocating an expansive monetary policy based on credit
because he recognized that it would not successfully increase the
money supply but only replace gold (5). The three writers were
pioneers of distinct approaches to international monetary theory (6).

1. - The “Marshall-Lerner Condition”
Whether Hume was the originator of the price-specie-flow
mechanism, and thus the precursor of the “elasticity approach to the
balance of payments”, is a subject worthy of detailed inquiry—but not
here. The conventional interpretation of Hume is that the increases in
the money supply originating from an export surplus would raise
prices in the surplus country (and correspondingly lower prices in the
deficit country). The basis for this interpretation is the following
passage: «Suppose four-fifths of the money in Great Britain to be
annihilated in one night... Must not the price of labour and all
commodities sink in proportion...?»
Recent evidence and interpretations suggests a quite different
meaning. On the basis of James Oswald’s letter to Hume, referred to
in the preceding footnote and the Humphrey-Keleher interpretation of
it, it is possible to conclude that Hume was engaging in a hypothetical
experiment, the object of which was to show that the price level in
Great Britain could not go down by four-fifths. He purposly exagger-
ated in order to show that it could not happen. He explicitly asserted
that (in an open economy) the domestic price level could not diverge
was an equilibrium amount of money, proportionate to “trade”, that could be retained
within a single country because the commodities must have an equal, or at least near
the price of the same species of commodities in the neighboring countries. However, he
failed to develop explicitly the mechanism by which too much or too little money in a
country was disposed of. He did, however, have a great influence on subsequent
writers, especially Richard Cantillon who acknowledged his indebtedness.
When this paper was presented at the Mondragone conference, Giuseppe Tullio
called my attention to the work of Antonio Serra, which was published in translated
form in Monroe’s Early Economic Thought. Tullio argues, if I have interpreted him
correctly, that Serra deserves credit for his discovery of the international adjustment
mechanism based on the expenditure-income relation. Born at Cosenza, Serra had
applied himself to the task of discovering how to keep money in a kingdom, specifically,
the Kingdom of Naples. His Brief Treatise on the Causes which Can Make Gold and
Silver Plentiful in Kingdoms Where There are No Mines, was written while Serra was
imprisoned on a charge of counterfeiting (coining), and published in Naples in 1613.
Serra’s treatise apparently had influence neither on the government nor on his
contemporaries. When it was rediscovered around 1780 he was acknowledged to be
one of the most outstanding of the 17th century, arriving at conclusions in advance of
the English mercantilists, Malynes, Misselden and Mun, obsessed with the same
problem in keeping money in England during the depression of the 1620s. I have not
had the opportunity to reread Serra’s work or to examine Tullio’s article on the subject.
I had, however, been under the impression that Serra’s work did not contain the
quantity theory of money.

Trade Balance Patterns as Global ete. 13
much from the world price level; this is therefore the only interpreta-
tion of Hume that makes his different essays consistent with one
another. Additional support for the Humphrey-Keleher interpretation
is that neither Thornton (7), Wheatley, Torrens nor Ricardo inter-
preted Hume to imply changes in price levels as the mechanism of
adjustment. His experiment was designed to show that the price level
in an open economy cannot diverge much from the price level in the
rest of the world.
If Hume is not the father of the price-specie-flow mechanism,
then who is? That dubious honor goes to John Stuart Mill (8). Mill’s
contributions to international trade theory are enormous. It was Mill
who completed the analysis of real equilibrium in international trade
by completing the Torrens-Ricardo theory of comparative advantage
to explain the mechanism by which the equilibrium terms of trade is
determined; Mill also was the first to recognize the problem of stability
(although mixing its solution up in execution with the even more
complicated problem of existence). Nevertheless Mill shunted the
theory of international adjustment off in the wrong direction by his
(7) See HENRY THORNTON (1760-1815) published his The Paper Credit of Great
Britain in 1802, a seminal work that, among other contributions, distinguished between
drains arising from expansion of country banks and those arising from external drains;
he was the first to note that short-term funds are responsive to the rate of interest; he
recognized the difference between nominal and real interest rates; and that output
could rise along with prices when the quantity of money was increased. His main
contribution to the theory of the international adjustment mechanism is his refinement
of Hume’s idea that a country could replace gold with convertible paper without
causing inflation; Thornton noted that the export of gold would tend to raise prices
abroad and hence also at home. The effect would be negligible in a small open
economy, but not in a large country.
(8) See JoHN Stuart MILL: Principles of Political Economy, London, Ashley
Edition, 1909, p. 627. «...The result is that a country which makes regular payments to
foreign countries, besides losing what it pays, loses something more, by the less
advantageous terms on which it is forced to exchange its productions for foreign
commodities». This was his conclusion under conditions of barter; he then argues that
the same holds under conditions of exchange under money. This notion was contrary to
that held by a number of the bullionist writers including Wheatley and Ricardo, and it
was explicitly refuted by Ohlin and Rueff in 1929.
While Mill erred in his neglect of income effects in his transfer analysis he is not
guilty of the “Marshall-Lerner Criterion Fallacy”. He explicitly introduced the notion of
the real exchange (rate), but said that devaluation had no effect on it: «When, therefore
the real exchange is at par, there will be a nominal exchange against the country, of as
much per cent as the amount of the depreciation” (loc. cit., p. 635). He concluded that
“the depreciation of the currency does not affect the foreign trade of a country: this is
carried on precisely as if the currency maintained its value» (ibidem).

Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc. 15
It was sad that Keynes never incorporated Ohlin’s expenditure
effects in his models either in the Treatise or the General Theory,
leaving a legacy of error. The error was serious enough in the
closed-economy macroeconomic model, for it led his followers to
ignore the implications of the financing counterpart to spending
decisions, including the method of financing budget deficits. But our
interest here is in the international ramifications of his neglect. He
perpetrated the idea that the trade balance had a separate existence
from the process by which it is financed. Whereas classical economics
— Ricardo, James Mill, John Stuart Mill and Marshall — held that
devaluation changed the price level and left the real exchange rate,
the terms of trade and the balance of trade unchanged, the new
question was how much did devaluation or some other policy improve
the balance of payments. One answer, already developed by Bicker-
dike, endorsed by Joan Robinson and Lloyd Metzler, was that it
depended on a specific set of partial-equilibrium elasticities. Marshall
had already formulated an elasticity criterion based on changes in the
terms of trade, but Abba Lerner developed a look-alike partial-equilib-
rium elasticity criterion based on the assumption that all elasticities of
supply are infinite. The literature then spawned a terminological
atrocity, due, I believe, to Professor Kindleberger, known as the
‘“Marshall-Lerner” Condition. Marshall must have turned over more
than once in his grave at having his stability condition, which was
based entirely on real phenomena, transmogrified into a criterion for
devaluation to alter the balance of trade, a relationship he explicitly
stated should not be made. Marshall explicitly denied the proposition
that exchange rate changes alter the terms of trade or the balance of
trade.
The international adjustment mechanism was discussed at the
end of World War I in the report of the Cunliffe Committee (9), which
described the gold standard mechanism in terms of interest rate
changes (which would suffice only for reversible changes in the
balance of trade) and then relative price changes: “... When the
balance of trade was unfavourable and the exchanges were adverse, it
(9) See Committee on Currency and Foreign Exchanges After the War, First
Interim Report, 1918.

16 Robert Mundell
became profitable to export gold... The result was a decline in general
prices in the home market which, by checking imports and stimu-
lating exports, corrected the adverse trade balance which was the
primary cause of the difficulty”.
This description of the adjustment process ignores the effect of
changes in money on expenditure and income independent of any
changes in prices, and it should have been subjected to severe
criticism. But it was in line with the Mill-Taussig position, later
adopted by Keynes. Unfortunately it was taken to be a fair description
of the adjustment process under the gold standard, and even used as
“evidence” for attacking any system of fixed exchange rates. What
country would want to be on an international standard that required
price inflation in surplus countries and price deflation in deficit
countries? Prevention of those ills was just becoming a prime object of
policy in the 1920s.
It was with this perception of the adjustment mechanism under
the gold standard that Keynes wrote his famous Tract attacking the
sacrifice of internal stability for external stability. The choice posed
was internal instability under fixed exchange rates or internal stability
with flexible exchange rates (10).
It is no wonder that the gold standard — and in fact any fixed
exchange rate mechanism — became the bete-noire of economists,
granted this perception of the adjustment mechanism under fixed
exchange rates. They were led to believe by economists of the stature
of Taussig and Keynes that adjustment of the balance of payments
required changes in relative prices and wages between countries.
When in the 1920s the recognition grew that downward rigidity of
wages, enforced by increasingly strong trade unions, it was realized
that attempts at deflation would instead cause unemployment. This
view was reinforced when Britain returned to the gold standard at the
prewar rate, overvaluing the pound and British labor, leading to labor
riots, the great strike of 1926 and a prerevolutionary atmosphere. It
was the model of the late 1920s that Keynes used for his theory of
unemployment in the General Theory. The problem in the 1920s was

not the adjustment mechanism under fixed exchange rates; it was the
problem of deliberately overvaluing the pound (for, it must be
admitted, important reasons) and joining a gold exchange standard
that could collapse whenever countries chose to convert their foreign
exchange balances.
2. - Plato vs. Aristotle
Necessity, one of the mothers of theories, stimulates action.
Economic problems have stimulated search for theories to understand
them and in the process science progresses. It was probably no
accident that Socrates emphasized the importance of the authority of
the state after democratic Athens had succumbed to totalitarian
Sparta; his pupil, Plato, followed him in this authoritarian disposition
and he extended it to the monetary system of the ideal state. Plato’s
ideal was a fiat money internally, and controlled use of gold and silver
for international trade and travellers. But Aristotle, perceiving the
inequities and dislocations of state-produced inflation, advocated the
use of the same convertible money like gold and silver internally as
well as externally. These two philosophies of monetary practice have
demarcated divisions in the monetary history of the world that survive
virtually in the same form to this day.
When a country uses a metal of intrinsic worth for money, it
cannot use money for the purposes of balancing deficits. Over time
countries oscillate from fiat money to hard money and back to fiat
money. The temptations of inflationary finance are strong during
emergencies because it appears at first that the inflationary finance
can be achieved at little cost to inflation. But excess money creation
always leads to inflation, and eventualy the public rankles under the
terrible burden of inflation and supports a new hard currency. The
history of money is a history of periods of stability, interrupted by
debasements and devaluations. Britain early on established a sound
money principle when it gave William the Conqueror tax revenues in
lieu of sequential devaluations. Britain learned early that it was better
to let the monarch levy taxes than use the inflation tax.
Until 1666 any person in England was permitted to bring bullion

| 18  |     | Robert Mundell  |     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --------------- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
(both silver  and  gold) to the mint,  and receive  it back  in the form  of
coin,  less  a  certain  deduction  called  seigniorage.  But  in  that  year,
during  the  reign  of Charles  II, free  coinage  was  introduced.  It was
introduced  as  a measure  to ameliorate  the great  scarcity  of currency
in  those  decades  (preceding  the  Great  Recoinage  of  1694).  The
measure  was  renewed  at seven-year  intervals  and then  in 1768  made
permanent.  But the free coinage  of silver was  suspended  in 1798  and
abolished  in 1816. The British practice was widely imitated in the later
nineteenth  century,  although  many  governments  retained  small  seig-
niorage  charges.  This practice  took the profits out  of money  creation
and  ensured  Britain  a  silver  or  gold  standard  from  1666  to  1931,
barring  the  special  periods  1797-1819  and  1915-1925.  But  after  the
dollar  had  become  the  most  important  stable  currency  in  1915  the
terminal  point,  ending the great era of Aristotelian  money,  was  1934.
Aristotelian  money  came  to an end in the United  States when in 1934
the  US  dollar  was  no  longer  redeemable  in  gold  or  silver  by  US
citizens.  The  age  of inconvertible  currencies  and  exchange  controls
since  1934,  and especially  since  1971,  when  the dollar was  no  longer
convertible  into  gold  for  foreign  central  banks,  has  attained  the
Platonic  ideal  money  more  closely  than  any  earlier  period.
With  respect  to the future,  if history  has anything  to say  on  the
subject at all, it is that the world’s monetary systems oscillate between
hard and soft currencies,  from inflationary  to stable money,  and from

in the Mediterranean

Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc. 19
world, the new gold supplies in Thrace that inspired the stater of
Philip II of Macedon, the plunder of the Persian Empire by Alexander
with its great influx of money to Europe, the silver mines of Iberia that
fed Rome, and the gold mines of the Caucasus and Crimea that
enabled Byzantium to maintain a stable (but overvalued) gold cur-
rency for eight hundred years, and Venice to benefit from the plunder
of Constantinople and the capture of its Crimean mines to make the
sequin an international currency; and later the Portuguese conquests
in, and trade with, West Africa that lowered the value of gold relative
to silver and increased gold coinage in the 15th century. It must not be
supposed that the managers of finance in the nations and empires of
the Ancient World and the Middle Ages were ignorant of appropriate
monetary and fiscal policies even if the cold lips of history have little to
say on the subject.
4. - The Renaissance Inflation and Its Aftermath
It was in the late Renaissance that we find the firm records for the
development of an economic science of money that did not disappear
from the pages of later history. The economists of the late Renais-
sance, confronted with the influx of gold and silver from the Western
Hemisphere, gave birth to the Renaissance version of the quantity
theory of money, first by Copernicus in the 1520s (“money usually
depreciates when it becomes too abundant”); then (independently) at
Salamanca in 1556 by Navarrus who noted the effects of the influx of
specie; and then (probably not independently) by Jean Bodin
(1530-1596) in 1568. The event takes some credit for the theory that
explained it.
A concomitant event was the formulation of the school of
economic thought that become known, in a partly pejorative sense, as
“mercantilism”. They were looked upon unsympathetically by Adam
Smith and the classical economists and derided for their fetish with
increasing the quantity of gold or silver in their countries. It was easy
for early classical economists, faced with the inflationary problems of
the Napoleonic Wars, to deride the mistakes of inflationists. But the
situation that gave birth to mercantilism was specific to their era and

20 Robert Mundell
plagued the hapless Stuarts for most of their tenure on the throne of
England. The Stuarts fell victims to Gresham's Law.
It can be seen, in retrospect, that the early English mercantilists
were confronted by two problems. One was the fall in the world price
of silver relative to gold which, with a fixed bimetallic ratio at the
mint, was driving out gold as only silver was being brought to the mint
and gold was disappearing in hoards or for exports. The second
problem was the drain of currency of any kind for reasons that were
little understood at the time and came to a head in the great
depression of the 1620s.
To understand the problem fully we would have to begin over a
century earlier, at the time the great influx of specie from the New
World began. In the early decades of the 16th century, the specie
flow was about equally divided between gold and silver. But the
situation changed spectacularly after discovery of silver in Potosi, the
first of the three great silver mountains to be opened in Spanish
Peru. Opened in 1545, only ten years after Pizarro founded Lima,
silver from Potosi began to fill the Spanish galleons and to pass to
Spain and thence to Holland and the rest of Europe. After its
opening the mine yielded an annual average of more than five
million ounces, and during the period 1581-1600 an average of more
than 8 million ounces per annum, and it was still, in 1601-1620,
yielding on average over six million ounces. Total world production
of silver rose from 1.5 million ounces in the first three decades after
Columbus, to about 3 million before 1544, to about 10 million from
1545-1580, 13 million from 1580 to 1520, after which production
stabilizes and tapers off. These phases in the influx of money from
the “Indies” have different economic effects that the economic writ-
ers at the time were trying to elucidate; a direction of causation valid
at one time might not have applied at another time in the day when
general theories had not yet developed. The lack of continuity in
development of the theory stems partly from the fact that the world
environment was changing.
The silver influx began to overwhelm the bi-metallic systems in
Europe. The price of silver fell below the mint ratio, and gold began to
disappear from circulation, or to be clipped. The Stuarts had to bear
most of the legacy of the adjustment. But even before James assumed

Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc. 21
the throne Elizabeth, who had, after 1559, stabilized the English
currency for most of her reign, succumbed to a remarkable mistake.
Almost on her deathbed, confronted with a falling silver price that was
forfeiting the gold currency, she lowered the ratio of silver to gold.
This created enormous confusion for her successor, who was ‘able to
reverse Elizabeth’s edict and restore the original ratio.
James I put the back to its original position, but the problem
remained; only gradually was the mint price of silver lowered (the
ratio increased), a fact which occupied the minds of Sir Walter
Raleigh and Sir Francis Bacon: Raleigh found the solution to the
exchange rate problem, an increase in the ratio of silver to gold;
Bacon in 1616 was perhaps the first to apply the term “balance of
trade” to the national accounts (See Viner’s: Studies, p. 8). But the
problems did not abate. For as the ratio was corrected, Britain fell into
a depression in the 1620s, imported from Germany, where the Thirty
Year’s War had shut off much trade. The mercantilists noted the
correlation between industry and trade and the dearth of money —
but got the direction of causation wrong. It was this depression that
caused the drain of specie, not the drain of specie that caused the
depression. But we owe to the bullionist controversy caused by the
depression that important flowering of economic opinion that was
stimulated by the bullionist controversy in that decade. Malynes and
Misselden engaged in a dispute over the theory of the exchanges, and
suggested remedies for retaining the stock of money; Mun defended
the outflow of specie occasioned by the transactions of the East India
Company and argued that the raw materials imported would raise
English manufactures to the point where the country would end up
with more total specie. The depression, like a harvest failure, leads to
an outflow of money; the only solution is to raise the demand for
money and some of the measures that were suggested, like tariffs and
devaluation, might be short-run palliatives. Devaluation, a temporary
solution, might work if the depression ended before domestic prices
had increased by the full amount of the devaluation.
The flowering of monetary discoveries featuring Malynes, Anto-
nio Serra, Misselden and Mun was provoked by the disturbances
created first by the accelerated influx of silver and its impact on the
bi-metallic ratio, and then by the stabilizing and decrease of the rate of

2D Robert Mundell
production at the time when growth required more money. What
united the mercantilists, who disagreed with one another, was the
common belief in the need to stop the drain of money and later to
increase it as the needs of trade expanded. The classical economists,
following Adam Smith, failed to see the problems of the mercantilists
in the light of the situation applicable to their countries at the time
they wrote.
5. - The Introduction of Credit and Paper Money
Another monetary innovation that enriched economic theory was
the use of credit, the development of banking and the introduction of
paper money. Hume was the first to show how the introduction of
credit displaces specie as the circulating medium without augmenting
the total quantity of money and so not creating inflation as long as
convertibility of the credit money is convertible into specie. Both
specie and paper could circulate side by side as long as confidence in
the credit money were retained. Adam Smith learned this idea from
Hume and generalized it to convertible paper currency; he argued
that the whole of convertible paper money can never exceed the value
of the gold and silver it displaces, commerce remaining the same. The
monetary innovation would create a temporary balance of trade
deficit, its accumulated value equal to the stock of specie displaced. It
might be noted in passing that the reduction in the gold-currency ratio
enables a country to increase its capital stock, lowering the real rate of
interest and increasing national output; see Mundell (11).
Thornton made an important development and qualification of
the Hume-Smith theory by taking account of the export of gold to the
rest of the world which, he argued, would raise world prices and thus,
by implication, domestic prices. It cannot therefore be said that the
substitution of specie by credit or paper would have no inflationary
effects; but it could be argued that they are likely to be small. Hume

Inflation and Growth in the World Economy, Goodyear, 1971.

Trade Balance Patterns as Global ete. 25
growth. The stock of monetary silver was reduced when the market
price of silver in the world as a whole rose relative to gold, and this
offset part of the increase in monetary gold. The mechanism works
through the operation of bimetallic standards, the United States and
France adhering at the time to bi-metallism. In France, the major
country on a bimetallic standard, gold rather than silver was brought
to the mint and silver was rapidly exported to the Far East, to the
extent that France lost most of her silver coinage. The French silver
supply acted as the shock-absorber that temporarily cushioned the
impact of the new gold supplies on prices. It is this cushioning feature
of bimetallic systems that won adherents to it and prompted Sir Roy
Harrod (The Dollar, 1952) to dub it the “high-brow” standard.
For two decades after the Californian and Australian discoveries
gold predominated in new coinage. But the tide turned early in the
1870s. Forces of both supply and demand played a part. On the one
hand there was a reduced rate of increase in the supply of gold (not so
much because of diminished production but because of an increased
stock) outstanding; contemporaneously there was an excess supply of
silver arising from both the supply and the demand side. There was an
increased supply of silver because of improvements in technique and
the exploitation of the rich mines of Colorado and Nevada. But the
factors on the side of demand were more critical: countries were
going onto the gold standard and off the silver standard. The newly-
formed German Empire had shifted from a silver standard to a gold
standard in 1872; between 1872 and 1878 about 20 million ounces of
gold were coined in Germany; the Scandinavian countries (not Fin-
land) followed suit the year after. France, faced with a falling price of
silver and the threat of having to replace her gold coinage by silver,
closed its mints to the coining of silver in 1873, adopting a kind of gold
standard in 1874; silver coins, however, remained legal tender. In the
same year France’s partners in the Latin Monetary Union, Belgium,
Switzerland, Italy and Greece, moved to gold. The United States
stopped coining silver in 1873 — the “crime of ’73 — and went onto
gold de facto in 1879, coining nearly 25 million ounces between 1873
and 1881 (The US formally adopted the gold standard in 1900). All
these changes worked to lower the value of silver and raise the value
of gold. The countries that shifted away from a silver standard caused

26 Robert Mundell
inflation in the silver countries, while those that shifted onto a gold
standard created deflation in the gold countries.
The changes in the demand for gold on the part of those new
entrants to the gold standard made gold appreciate for almost over
two decades. By contrast those countries like Russia, Austria Hun-
gary, India and many less-developed countries, that adhered to silver
until much later, suffered inflation from two sources: the greatly
enhanced output; and the dumping of silver by those countries that
left the silver standard. Austria-Hungary moved to gold in 1892, Japan
in 1897; Russia also moved to gold in the 1890s in measures that,
however, stopped just short of a full gold standard. Many of the less
developed countries, including China, remained on silver.
From 1870 to 1896 gold was a deflationary standard. But already,
in 1886, with the discovery of phenomenal gold reefs in the Witwaters-
rand, signals of a coming change in monetary relations were on the
horizon. The gold discoveries in South Africa were to eclipse, by many
times over, all preceding gold ever produced. Walras, the father of
mathematical general equilibrium theory, correctly predicted that the
South African discoveries would cause inflation in the gold standard
countries (12). Gold arrived from South Africa in mounting volumes,
overtaking gold production in the United States by the turn of the
century, and then breaking all records, exceeding by many times over
any other source of gold.
The new gold production threatened to turn the deflationary gold
standard into an inflationary one. However there was a long lag. A
mitigating factor was the greater demand for gold with the adoption
of the gold standard by, as already noted, Austria-Hungary and Russia
and Japan in the 1890s. As a consequence of the increases in the
demand for gold emanating from these sources, the inflation was very
moderate up until the outbreak of war in 1914, of an amount that was
close to Walras’ prediction. It is probable also that the rapid develop-
ment of joint stock banks in this period contributed to the mild
upsurge of prices from 1896 to 1914.

Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc. Daf
These examples of countries shifting from one standard to
another demonstrate the interdependence of national monetary sys-
tems, how one country’s choice of metallic standards has an impor-
tant effect on the rest of the world. But the story does not stop in
1914.
The Great War of 1914-1918 set in motion a chain of monetary
events from which the world has not yet recovered. Only Japan and
the United States, among the great Powers, remained on the gold
standard during the war. It was a puzzle for many economists and
officials in the early years of the war why the United States — which
unlike the belligerents — had obediently remained on the gold
standard, should be caught up in inflation. Treasury officials vehe-
mently denied that the US had engaged in inflation because the price
of gold had been constant and convertibility maintained. This view is
interesting because it was the view of those accustomed to believing
that gold convertibility would always be a safeguard against inflation.
The facts were nevertheless clear: the dollar price level had doubled
and the value of gold had fallen in half. What the analysts at the
Treasury and many others had overlooked was that gold had become
unstable when Europe went off gold. The Hume-Smith-Thornton
mechanism of replacing specie with paper money or credit was at
work here. Thornton’s idea that the flight of gold from a group of
countries that replaced gold by paper would cause inflation in the rest
of the world had a fitting application during World War I. The exodus
of gold from Europe was an influx of gold to the United States,
bearing in mind the continuing and rapid production of new gold from
South Africa. There had been a decline in the demand for gold in the
world as a whole and its value fell with the US dollar.
World War I and its aftermath inaugurated the monetary in-
stability and inflation of the twentieth century. We have not yet
escaped from it. Certainly no previous century has been more unsta-
ble monetarily than the 20th. By whatever rough measure we rate the
inflations of Greece and Syracuse; the dislocations of the Roman
Empire in the reign of Diocletian; the inflation of the 14th century
after the Black Death; the inflation of the 16th century; they are
outshadowed by our own. The total record of inflation in our century
is appalling. But it has been concentrated in specific periods inter-

28 Robert Mundell
mixed with periods of stability. There was stability in the dozen or so
years before the First World War; again during the brief interlude of
the 1920s gold exchange standard; yet again during the gold-based
dollar standard of the Bretton Woods era. The cumulative inflation of
our century has been due to war-time inflation that has not been
reversed; changes in the monetary standard; and the utter breakdown
of the standard. The monetary standards broke down because of
credit inflations and the absence of a monetary standard has allowed
the monetary instability to be tolerated and accon:modated.
It was only a few years after the great War that, and with some
justice, Keynes could argue that gold was an untrustworthy standard.
Europe’s abandonment of gold made gold unstable during the war
years. The question after the war, therefore, was whether it would be
better to resurrect the gold standard or to scrap it. Keynes, a visceral
chrysophobe, wanted to scrap it; indeed even before the war he had
advocated widening the gold margins to permit more exchange
flexibility. Irving Fisher had since 1912 been an ardent opponent of
the gold standard, and in 1925 suggested that the US should seek
stability of the dollar in terms of commodities and the rest of the
world stability of their currencies in terms of the dollar, a system that
has a very modern ring. The British establishment, however, including
especially Montagu Norman, Governor of the Bank of England, and
Winston Churchill, Chancellor of the Exchequer, favored a restoration
of the gold standard at the old parity.
The argument in favor of the official view was that the gold
standard had worked in Britain for a century, that it had served as an
instrument of peace, that officials still knew how to run it, and
restoration of the pre-war parity would keep faith with bond holders.
The real argument (not sufficiently heard at the time) against going
back to the gold standard was that there was, at existing dollar prices,
a gold shortage. The gold shortage had been temporarily suppressed
by the use of sterling and dollars to supplement gold reserves, a plan
which the Gold Delegation of the League of Nations had recom-
mended in their Genoa meeting in 1922. But to build a system on the
basis of an unstable component of reserves created a time-bomb that
would explode at the least disturbance to confidence.
Had the monetary officials and economists in the 1920s under-

Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc. 29
stood clearly that the world gold base was too small at the high
post-war price level — ample gold for the US but inadequate for the
world — they would not have urged a reformation of the international
gold standard at the existing parities of the pound and the dollar. The
system from 1914 to 1924 had been too inflationary. The German and
Austrian hyperinflations had made stabilization of their currencies,
and their neighbors’ currencies, imperative. Thus it was that Austria,
Germany, Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Soviet Union, Latvia,
Lithuania, Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and Holland all stabilized at
least de facto their currencies in terms of gold before Britain. Britain
rejoined the gold standard on April 28, 1925, and that set the stage for
the rest of the countries to follow. France stabilized the franc in 1927
and formally devalued it in June 1928 at a level that wisely recognized
fully the depreciation that had taken place. The franc was valued
more correctly in terms of gold than either the pound or the dollar,
and was accordingly seriously undervalued against those two cur-
rencies. The Poincare-Rist stabilization put France in the driver’s seat
of the gold buggy, able to accumulate a huge stock of gold and foreign
exchange. By the end of 1928 most countries had rejoined the
precarious gold exchange standard.
In retrospect we can conclude that the gold standard that was
reformed after 1924 had an inherent instability. The existing stock of
monetary gold could not be stretched to form an adequate reserve
behind the credit component of the money supplies of the countries
that returned to gold and the new countries that joined gold for the
first time. This gold shortage was not due to the failure of the gold
mines, which continued to disgorge unprecedented quantities of gold,
nearly all from South Africa. Much more gold was needed in 1925
than in 1914, not only because of population and economic growth
but because of the weakened confidence caused by the recent history
of currency instability. In the nineteenth century the Bank of England
had been able to survive on a comparatively slender gold reserve, but
gold coins were in circulation at that time and there had been almost a
century of stability. The gold shortfall would have to come eventually
from the reserve center.
Had the gold shortage not been temporarily finessed by the use of
pounds and dollars in lieu of gold, deflation would have unfolded at

30 Robert Mundell
once. The deflationary catastrophe was postponed for a few years
because of the temporary respite of using sterling and dollars as
substitutes for gold. Because it had been postponed the crash was
more sudden and deeper.
Several alternative events might have ruptured the fragile stabi-
lity. After the 1929 Wall Street Crash, the Smoot-Hawley tariff (and
the retaliation against it), the curtailment of US lending, reparations
problems and budgetary difficulties, confidence was undermined and
the international climate had soured. France and other countries had
started converting foreign exchange even before 1929 and these
conversions accelerated, squeezing the gold reserves of other major
countries. Britain was the weak country on the margin and after a
rather lackadaisical defense Parliament authorized the suspension of
gold payments by the Bank of England on September 21, 1931.
After Britain suspended convertibility the pound depreciated
drastically. The United States then became the weak country on the
margin. The US economy had been imploding and the commercial
banking system was under a state of siege. From 1929 to 1932
industrial production had fallen by 47% and national income by 52%.
The Federal Reserve could save the economy and the banks or save
the gold standard; they made the bureaucratic choice to save the gold
standard and in its defense tripled the rediscount rate. The economy
continued to deteriorate and the banking system was on the verge of
collapse. Since the gold standard was scheduled for collapse anyway it
would have been better to follow Britain’s lead and abandon conver-
tibility at the same time.
In the elections of 1932 both Hoover and Roosevelt campaigned
for a balanced budget and sound finance. At the time of the inaugu-
ration there were 14 million unemployed. President Roosevelt declar-
ed a nationwide bank holiday and froze the gold stocks of the banks.
On April 20 the US suspended the gold standard by putting an
embargo on gold exports. Less than a year later, after arbitrary
intervention in the gold market to depreciate the dollar, the Gold
Reserve Act was signed at the end of January 1934, providing for a
devaluation of the dollar by about 40% and a new price of gold at $35
an ounce.
The new arrangements were a far cry from the old gold standard.

Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc. 31
Gold controls and prohibitions severely restricted monetary freedom.
The US public was required, upon strict penalties, to turn in all the
gold in its possession to the government in exchange for paper
currency. US citizens were forbidden to hold gold in the United States
(except for legitimate industrial or artistic uses); and were prohibited
from buying gold abroad (13). The system that was created in the US
in 1934 was a system closer to the authoritarian monetary system
espoused by Plato than the democratic and free system advocated by
Aristotle.
The devaluation of the dollar in 1934 now put pressure on the
other gold currencies mainly France and associated countries. Ger-
many had remained on the gold standard after Britain devalued
because in the public’s mind, devaluation was regarded as equivalent
to inflation; apparently the German hyperinflation had washed all
money illusion out of Germany and when von Papen considered
devaluing the Reichmark, the labor unions threatened to raise wages
by an equivalent amount. Germany instead adopted the mantle of
foreign exchange controls in the summer and fall of 1931, and after a
further abortive attempt at deflation at the end of the year, adopted
the policies that were to make the name of Hjalmar Schact, the
President of the Reichsbank from 1933 to 1939, and Minister of
Economics from 1934 to 1937, an infamous adjective. Meanwhile
France became the country on the margin after devaluation of the
Anglo-Saxon currencies. France’s policy in the 1920s had made the
franc the strongest of the currencies before the breakdown, but after
the other devaluations it was among the weakest. Before devaluing
France suffered severe deflation, only succumbing to the inevitable on
October 1, 1936; this was quickly followed by the abandonment of the
gold standard and the introduction of flexible exchange rates on June
30, 1937. The round of devaluations had now completed the circle,
and it was as if all countries had simultaneously raised the price of
gold. Had there been a mechanism for arranging a universal increase
in the price of gold at anytime before 1932 the course of history would
have been entirely altered. But recognition of that fact had an
(13) These prohibitions were reaffirmed and tightened in the Kennedy administra-
tion and remained until 1975, when, during the Ford Administration, the prohibition of
gold was lifted.

32 Robert Mundell
important influence on the Articles of Agreement of the IMF which
contained a provision for a universal change in par values (change in
the price of gold).
The Tripartite Agreement of 1936 among the United States, Great
Britain and France — an arrangement that anticipated essential points
of the IMF system eight years later — arranged for advance notifi-
cation of and agreement on any changes in gold parities (what
became, in the IMF, “par values”). There was no longer an excess
demand for gold, and at one stage a gold scare developed when there
was speculation that the US might lower the price of gold. Given the
internal gold prohibition and the elimination of gold coinage, coupled
with the dismantling of the gold standard around the world, there was
now an excess supply of gold. The US again — playing the role of
buffer stock holder and the residual holder — was faced with
purchasing huge quantities of gold at the price of $ 35 an ounce. This
tendency was aggravated by capital flight from Europe as war clouds
gathered. By 1940 the US had acquired over three-quarters of the
world stock of monetary gold. Even before the war the world had
entered into a situation not unlike that which prevailed in the decade
after 1914.
The US was the only country to stay on gold (albeit in its funny
way) during World War II and an international gold standard was not
restored after the war. The salient features of the post-war system had
already emerged as early as 1938. Because only one country was
using gold for monetary purposes there was an overhang of excess
gold. Despite full employment, interest rates were maintained at very
low levels and real interest rates were negative as wartime and
post-war inflation proceeded. But the inflation put an end to the
overvaluation of gold and to its excess supply, even for the United
States. As a result of wartime and post-war inflation the price level in
the United States had more than doubled and the real value of the
gold stock had fallen in half. To release more gold for external
purposes the Federal Reserve System’s required gold cover behind its
liabilities (currency and member bank reserves) was lowered from
40% (in effect since 1934) to 25%. Twenty years later, in 1965, the
gold reserve requirement was partially eliminated and in 1968
completely abolished.

Trade Balance Patterns as Global ete. 33
History now repeated itself. The shortage of gold after World War
I at existing prices was repeated after World War II, after the war and
post-war inflation. But like the earlier period the shortage of gold was
not recognized. In the early years of the post-war, period economists
and officials complained of a “dollar shortage” not a gold shortage. As
long as other countries were certain that dollars were convertible into
gold, they preferred dollars, and that was the sense in which there was
a dollar shortage rather than a gold shortage. From the US point of
view there was a surplus of gold. The US had, after all, almost three
quarters of the world’s stock of monetary gold. Few people at the time
thought in terms of a global monetary model that would have made
the potential gold shortage obvious.
Only a few voices noticed that the increasing dollar liabilities
were becoming weaker claims on a dwindling gold stock. Charles
Rist, Jacques Rueff and Sir Roy Harrod were among the select few
that were concerned about a potential gold shortage. When in 1954
the London gold market opened (to non-US citizens) US gold could
be drained by gold sales in London converted at the US Treasury.
The drain accelerated after European (external) convertibility in
1958.
In the late 1950s and early 1960s European central banks conver-
ted hundreds of billions of ounces into gold at the undervalued US
gold price of $ 35 per ounce. In 1953 the US had 653 million ounces of
gold; fifteen years later it had only 276 million ounces, a reduction of
377 million ounces sold at the price of $35 an ounce. In the same
period the combined gold stocks of Germany, France, Italy, Nether-
lands, Belgium and Switzerland increased from 199 million ounces to
477 million ounces. Obviously a continued loss at this rate was
unsustainable and recognition of the problem in the 1960s slowed the
gold losses to a trickle. The major countries had become aware of the
oligopolistic interdependence of the system and that the US would
close the gold window if threatened with excessive conversions. Not
until 1971, after open talk of devaluation had taken place, were
requests for gold renewed, giving the government an excuse for
dismantling an apparatus that had outlived its usefulness.
The gold exchange standard constructed after the Second World
War broke down for reasons not completely dissimilar from those

34 Robert Mundell
which destroyed the gold standard after the First World War. In both
cases there was insufficient gold, at post-war prices, to manage an
efficient international gold standard. The US was the major holder of
gold with adequate gold reserves for its own purpose. But it turned
out to be insufficient to redistribute gold to the rest of the world to
build an adequate reserve base for a full gold standard in other
countries. The gold-based dollar standard — a la Bretton Woods —
would have worked only if the Common Market countries on the
Continental Europe had been willing to accommodate their policies to
the US needs as a reserve center. For political reasons Europe was not
willing to accept the degree of monetary leadership acquiescence to a
gold-based dollar standard would have implied.
There were several options open to the Deputies of the G-10,
charged with finding a way out of the dilemma, raised by Professor
Triffin, that the system, if it were not reformed, risked collapse either
because of a shortage of liquidity or because the US would run out of
gold. The deputies of the G-10, assigned to study the problem, had
four basic choices: 1) raise the dollar price of gold and continue the
system for another two decades or so; 2) accept as a fait accompli the
dollar standard and accept US leadership as the pilot country; 3)
create a new reserve asset and/or a world central bank that would
replace the dollar and gold; or 4) move to a system of flexible
exchange rates. The G-10 took the politically-viable alternative at the
time to paper over the cracks in the system by creating the SDR,
initially a form of paper gold with a gold-weight guaranteed asset that
would be a substitute for gold in central bank holdings.
For various reason the SDR did not solve the basic problem and
the system broke up. But it must be said that the countries adopted
the better alternative in the breakup of the Bretton Woods system,
compared to the breakup of the inter-war system. Restoring the gold
standard in the inter-war period at too low a price was a major cause
of the depression; blame for the depression rests on the willingness of
the authorities to sacrifice their economies and banking systems
rather than leave the gold standard. By contrast the Bretton Woods
system had a friendly divorce from gold. The Bretton Woods system
itself was sacrificed to avoid the monetary tightness that adherence to
it would have required. After 1965 countries stopped gold conversions

Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc. 35
short of forcing monetary tightness on the US because the US would
simply have suspended gold conversions.
The Bretton Woods system did not create deflation; it was argued
on the contrary that it had become an engine for too much inflation. A
later echo of the view that the gold standard caused the depression is
the view, advanced by Dr. Otmar Emminger (Chairman of the
Deputies of the G-10 and later president of the Bundesbank) and
Gottfried Haberler, that the gold-based dollar standard of the Bretton
Woods era broke down because it was too inflationary. The reserve
countries (i.e., the US) were following a too-inflationary monetary
policy. The surplus countries, especially France and Germany, vexed
under the burden of inflation that the dollar system placed on them.
Because the world economy was suffering from inflation — rising to
3% in the late 1960’s — the burden of adjustment should have been
placed on the deficit countries, not the surplus countries; adjustment
should always take place first in the “erring” country.
Before the creation of the SDR the European countries wanted
the US to adjust its balance of payments before international mone-
tary reform; whereas the United States wanted reform as part of the
adjustment, on the new argument that the deficit could not be
corrected by the US alone because it was endemic to the system itself.
Countries acquired dollar reserves voluntarily, and earned interest on
them to the extent they were invested in treasury bills or savings
deposits. After the disbanding of the gold pool and the Gold
Communique in March 1968, European gold reserves had become
suddenly immobilized: no central bank was willing to sacrifice gold at
the official price when the market price was already higher.
The big upsurge of dollar holdings after 1968 was partly a result
of the increased demand for dollar balances to add to their reserves to
replace the now unusable (except at great cost) gold reserves. But if
Europe was following policies to accumulate more reserves in dollars,
and the dollar accumulations represent the US balance-of-payments
deficit, by what policies could the US correct its deficit?
The crisis of 1971 was a crisis of miscalculation. There were some
very distinguished economists who believed that a little jiggle of the
exchange rate, by say 10 or 15%, would correct the balance of
payments deficit. This influential view was based on the partial-

Would  the  Bretton  Woods  crisis  have  unfolded  as  it did  in the

1971? The mark crisis in April  1971, in which eurodollars  flooded into

is that the system  could  have been prolonged  for several  years with  a
