Why did the much  heralded  creation  of the SDR’s  not  prevent  a
breakdown  of the  Bretton  Woods  system?  One  answer  is that  they
came  too little and too late; another is that they were  poorly designed.
Because they were  not backed by any tangible assets they were looked
upon  with  suspicion,  not equivalent  to  gold  or  even  dollars.  I have

Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc. By,
discussed some technical implications of this issue in considering the
optimum structure of a world central bank (14). Pure fiat money
depends on its acceptability, which depends on trust; and trust will
prevail only if there is a central force, such as a strong government, or
by unbreakable international agreements among friendly nations. The
creation of the unbacked SDR could hardly have come at a worse time
when France and Germany, irked under the “burden” of accumu-
lating US assets and implicitly helping to finance a war they deplored.
It is true that the SDR’s did have a gold-weight guarantee, but there
was no way in which these pseudo-convertibility pledges could be
effectively honored. When the price of gold skyrocketed the gold
guarantee was ripped away from the SDR.
In retrospect, it has to be said that the Bretton Woods System
performed far better than either its predecessors, the chaotically
variable fluctuating exchange rate system in the 1930’s and the gold |
exchange standard of the 1920’s; or its successors, at least up until the
Louvre “system” was agreed upon. In December 1971, an agreement
was reached at the Smithsonian Institution to devalue the dollar
against gold by 6% and to appreciate some of the other currencies by a
like amount, giving the US the magic exchange rate adjustment it was
supposed to need. But this flimsy exercise did not stand in the way of
the foreign accumulations of dollars. Only two years later the ex-
change rates agreed at the Smithsonian had to be changed. In
February 1973, the US devalued again. The second devaluation of the
dollar had no more salutary effect than the first. The following month
the Committee of Ministers of the Economic Community formulated
plans for a joint float of the European currencies against the dollar,
but cohesiveness was then lacking and the joint float was unsuc-
cessful. This paved the way for the final breakup of the international
monetary system. In the following June, the Committee of Twenty
gave up on international monetary reform until, as they said, in-
dividual countries could bring their national inflations under control.
It apparently did not occur to them that the major function of an
(14) See MUNDELL R.A.: Monetary Theory: Interest, Inflation and Growth in the
World Economy, op. cit. See the last chapter, The Optimum Structure of a World
Central Bank.

38 Robert Mundell
international monetary system was to create a stable international
currency system anchored in some way to prevent inflation. —
The international monetary system since the breakdown of the
Bretton Woods system has been the most unstable system, from the
standpoint of preventing inflation, in history. The world price level has
risen more than three-fold, and by some measures four-fold, since
1968, when gold ceased to play a major role in the system. Once the
Golden Anchor was lifted the purchasing power of the currencies of
the major countries went the way of most inconvertible paper cur-
rencies. For the United States the inflation was greater than in the two
world wars put together, more inflation than in the prior history of the
US Republic.
With no currency in the world anchored to the commodity world,
the global money supply became elastic. It became a hostage to OPEC
whose actions were ratified by credit expansion in the Eurodollar
market and US monetary expansion. Inflation and growth created the
oil scarcity that made it possible to engineer artificial shortages that
allowed the price of oil to rise in 1974 and 1979 far beyond its
competitive equilibrium. When the US finally took monetary actions
in the early 1980s to arrest the great inflation the price of oil fell in
half, to a more sustainable price. The payments deficits in Europe and
Japan occasioned by the oil price increases were financed through an
explosion of liquidity in the unregulated Eurodollar market. The
money supply became elastic and ratified the cost-push inflation
engendered by the oil price changes. The blame for the great inflation
experienced over the past two decades and that we are still in today,
rests with the failure of our international monetary system, and of our
own failure to understand it.

Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc. 39
PART TWO
The purpose of this part is to utilize the information from the
preceding discussion of doctrine and history in order to prepare the
groundwork for a more formalized approach to the analysis of
balance of payments issues. There is no field in economics where it is
more important to develop a general equilibrium approach to policy
analysis than the balance of payments. Specifically lacking in the
traditional formulations of general equilibrium theory in international
trade has been the theory of international-reserve-creation. An
analysis of the global mechanism that provides reserves to the coun-
tries in the international system has been lacking.
For didactic purposes it is convenient to discuss the theory of
international economics in three separate parts, or models. One is the
model of the small open economy. The second is the model of
interacting economies that takes into account all the repercussions of
one country on another and also the degree of oligopoly based on
differential sizes. The third part, which has been missing from a great
deal of international trade theory, is the global analysis, which treats
the world as a closed economy. It is this third part that has been
lacking in the formalized analysis of general international equilibrium.
Until now we have not been able to avoid discussing the global
mechanism in our review of the evolution of the international mon-
etary system over past centuries, and the development of key parts of
the theory. Some of the earlier economists of ‘the cosmopolitan
century, the eighteenth, seemed to have understood the global
mechanism better than economists in the twentieth century. What has
not been properly dealt with in a comprehensive way is the relation
between the general theory of national balances of payments and the
global mechanism for creating reserves, a problem we have alluded to
in our earlier discussion of the reserve centers.
Under the gold standard there is an excess of surpluses over deficits
equal to the increase in monetary gold. This arises because the gold-
producing countries treat gold exports differently from other countries.
Gold exports are treated as ordinary commodity exports, whereas cen-
tral banks regard inflows of gold, not as any commodity import, but as
changes in international reserves. There is no commodity import

40 Robert Mundell
counterpart to the commodity gold export, so that there is an excess of
commodity exports over imports in the world as a whole equal to the
purchases of gold by the monetary authorities for monetary purposes.
In a growing world every country can attain the mercantilist nirvana of
a balance-of-trade surplus if precious metals are being produced, over
and above commercial use, in the world as a whole.
When a national currency is used as an international money there
is an analogous asymmetry. The money producer does not look upon
an increase in foreign holdings of domestic money balances in the same
way as it would look upon an outflow of its own reserves and it might
ignore it entirely. During the war Britain did not worry (much) about
the accumulation of sterling balances by members of the sterling area,
and after the war it was able to whittle the real value of these balances
down by inflation and devaluation. Similarly the rest of the world accu-
mulated huge foreign balances in US currency but the United States
worried mainly about gold losses; since 1971 the US pays very little
attention to dollar balances of foreign countries which have multiplied
several times since the advent of floating exchange rates.
What is the appropriate definition of the balance of payments of a
reserve center? The balance of payments deficit or surplus is usually
regarded as a symptom of disequilibrium and should therefore be
defined to reflect that fact. If the rest of the world is acquiring, and
wants to acquire, dollar reserves, there is no disequilibrium. If
non-zero balances are to be regarded as a disequilibrium and an error
signal, a new definition of the balance of payments is needed.
Some years ago (15) I suggested that the balance of payments of a
reserve center be defined as the involuntary component of reserve
accumulation. According to my definition the balance of payments of a
reserve center should be defined not as the total increase in home-cur-
rency balances held by the rest of the world, but only as that component
of it they accumulated unwillingly. To calculate this means dividing
actual reserve accumulations into one component which represents
secular demand and another component that is “involuntary” in the
sense that it is required to achieve a country’s exchange rate goals.
Every country has reserve goals and there is no disequilibrium if these
(15) See MUNDELL R.A.: “The International Monetary System: Conflict and Re-
form”, Private Planning Association of Canada, Montreal, 1965.

Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc. 41
are being attained and the world price level is increasing at the desired
rate. This definition allows for the fact that countries under the Bretton
Woods system wanted to increase their dollar holdings each year to in-
crease their international liquidity more or less in proportion to other
assets. Adopting this definition, the reserve center would take no action
as long as other countries want to increase their dollar reserves by the
amount they are actually increasing them. Only if there are excess dol-
lar accumulations should the reserve provider undertake deflationary
steps; and if there are insufficient dollar accumulations the reserve
center should take expansionary action.
To make the definition operational it is necessary to find an
explicit method of distinguishing between desired and undesired
reserve acquisitions. A signalling mechanism is needed. Under a
smoothly-working gold exchange standard, that unlike the Bretton
Woods system did not start out with undervalued gold, the partici-
pating countries can signal their preferences by dollar conversions
into, or from, gold. Thus if a country has too large a balance of
payments surplus (larger than needed to accumulate the desired level
of reserves) it can signal its discomfort to the reserve center by
converting dollars into gold. If, on the other hand, a country wants to
acquire a larger balance-of-payments surplus — perhaps to accumu-
late reserves at a faster rate — it should sell gold and buy dollars. The
first action puts pressure on the reserve center to contract, the second
to expand. The end result will not depend upon any individual country
but on the actions of all countries combined. The US would react as a
result of the total change in its gold stocks. I have discussed elsewhere
(16) the formal dynamics and stability properties of such a system.
In the 1960s this mechanism could not work because gold was
undervalued at $35 an ounce, and gold was converted for speculative
profit rather than for adjustment requirements. The disequilibrium of
the 1960s was compounded by the Euro-American power struggle.
Although France was critical of the United States for its exploitation of
an “exorbitant privilege” and its “deficit without tears”, that country
was itself the reserve-provider to the CFA franc area, having the same
(16) See MUNDELL R.A.; International Economics, New York, MacMillan, 1968,
ch. 20, «The Crisis Problem».

42 Robert Mundell
reserve-currency advantages on a regional scale that the US was
“enjoying” on a global scale.
Such a system works best within a family of nations, rather than
the world as a whole. For the first ten years the Bretton Woods system
operated more of less under family principles, when Marshal Plan aid
and Nato had underwritten European recovery and the dollar was
looked upon as good as gold. The urgency of this family relationship
diminished after the Sino-Soviet split, which enabled the inherent
desire for a resumption of European sovereignty in the monetary
sphere to be addressed.
From an international political standpoint it rankles other countries
to use a national currency as an international reserve asset. The three
main problems are 1) prestige; 2) the seigniorage income; and 3) effective
control over the rate of inflation. After World War IJ the US had almost
unlimited prestige, it was giving away with Marshall Plan more than the
seigniorage, and the gold exchange standard was supposed to keep in
check US monetary policy. If other countries vexed under their dollar-
convertibility discipline, the US had its own gold contraint. There was
therefore a parity of considerations that neutralized the gains and losses.
Those considerations altered in the later 1960s as US prestige declined
(relatively), as the US gained more seigniorage with inflation; and US
control over the inflationary spigot came into question. The European
currency movement of the 1970s was a tentative attempt to replace the
dollar with an alternative currency for Europe, a movement that has re-
cently, toward the end of the 1980s, accelerated.
It is doubtful whether it is possible to construct an asset that
could replace the major currency. There have been numerous plans
for reform that have considered the use of an international currency,
but none that have achieved sufficient support to be negotiable. The
major difficulty thus far has been that the more “international” the
projected world currency gets, the more removed it is from the
sources of power that endow it with confidence. National reserve
currencies are backed by national productive power and export
capacity; the basis for international currencies rest on the more flimsy
reed of international agreement. The one experiment thus far tried —
the SDR — has not been a happy precedent.
We conclude this section by noting that analysis of the pattern of
balances of payments requires study of the international monetary

Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc. 43
system, and in particular those characteristics that determine the
relations between the balance of payments and the mechanism for
reserve creation. Theories of the balance of payments should specify
the characteristics of the reserve-generation mechanism.
Growing countries normally want, and should have, a balance of
payments surplus in order to generate the required increase in non-infl-
ationary external liquidity. The gold standard enabled all countries to
run balance of trade surpluses at the same time. Under reserve cur-
rency standards the rest of the world can have a balance of trade sur-
plus equal to the increase in the reserve center’s money it accumulates.
But it is inevitable that a country whose currency is used as foreign ex-
change reserves will over time have a déficit in its balance of payments.
The balance of payments deficit of the reserve center will be a function,
not only of policies in the reserve center itself, but also of policies in the
rest of the world. The explanation for a reserve-center’s balance of pay-
ments deficit must be found in the growth rate of the rest of the world.
1. - The Demand for Dollar Assets in General
The “deficit without tears” of the reserve center applies to the
accumulation of liquid assets in the money markets of the reserve
center. The share of national income attributable to the right to
provide the world’s reserve money is equal to the product of the
outstanding dollar (or whatever alternative money) liabilities and the
rate of interest, divided by national income.
Many advocates of flexible exchange rates thought that balance-
of-payments deficits would disappear once fixed exchange rates were
given up. Nothing could be further from the truth. The subject
received some debate in the twilight of the Bretton Woods system. In
a speech printed in the Congressional Record (17) in 1968 I argued

that the dollar would become more important as a reserve asset in the
future, whatever happened: «... Even if General de Gaulle has his way
...and the price of gold is changed, or gold is demonetized, the dollar
will emerge even more powerfully as the world’s currency... If you
follow the advice of my colleague, Milton Friedman, who says get out
of the gold market, then the dollar will become more important than
it is now. If you don’t follow his advice and simply do nothing, then
the dollar will become more important than it is now. You cannot
fight the basic evolutionary forces that have been at work in the
international system for a decade and that are simply reflections of the
fact that it is the dollar and not gold that is the determining factor».
Sir Roy Harrod also pointed out, to the befuddlement of his
critics, that under flexible exchange rates the need for foreign ex-
change reserves, far from abating, would increase. This has turned
out to be the case. Foreign exchange holdings (mainly dollars) were
$ 13.5 billion in 1951 and only $ 32.6 billion in 1968. But they were
almost ten times this amount, $ 293 billion, in 1980, and $514.5
billion in 1989. Over the two decades of fluctuating exchange rates
foreign exchange reserves, which advocates had thought would dis-
appear, have multiplied by fifteen times. Balance-of-payments deficits
have been augmented, rather than reduced, by the introduction of
flexible exchange rates. This shows clearly that the advocates of
flexible exchange rates failed to understand the important global
mechanism by which reserves were demanded and supplied.
Countries hold liquid international reserves to intervene in the
exchange market, alter the money supply or achieve exchange rate
goals. Under fixed exchange rates this intervention is explicit and
automatic. When exchange rates are fixed, speculation is reduced to
speculation about possible changes in the peg. But speculation is
insidious under flexible rates. The foreign exchange market now
amounts to over $ 400 billion per day (!), most of it useless specul-
ation. More reserves are needed under flexible exchange rates than
under fixed rates because of the great increase in uncertainty about
future monetary policy. Under fixed exchange rates there is an
automatic target for monetary policy. But under flexible exchange
rates there is no set target for either the rate of inflation, interest rates
or the money supply. Everything depends upon the personality of the

Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc. 45
central banker. Because the foreign exchange market is a stock
market, not a flow market, abrupt changes in the perceived states of
the world can provoke sudden changes in confidence and dramatic
movements of the exchanges. No monetary authority can afford to be
caught without adequate reserves to defend its currency when faced
with a speculative attack.
The currencies of Great Powers throughout history have occu-
pied a special place in the international monetary system. There is a
world demand for the currency of the largest powers not only for
liquidity but for investment purposes when their economy is sound
and their currency is stable. In a growing world there is a steady
demand for additional assets from the dominant country. This de-
mand for capital assets of the dominant country must be financed by
an excess of savings over investment in the rest of the world. On the
other hand, equilibrium requires that the dominant country, be
willing and able to run a balance of payments deficit. Equilibrium
exists when voluntary net borrowing of the dominant country equals
voluntary net lending of the rest of the world.
When the US pursued an inflationary policy that led to a steep
depreciation of the dollar in the late 1970s, money and capital fled
the United States, nominal interest rates rose and real interest rates
became zero or negative. This capital flight prevented the already
substantial balance-of-trade deficit from worsening. But when Chair-
man Paul Volcker of the Federal Reserve (finally) tightened, interest
rates rose to unprecedented heights and dollars ‘became suddenly
scarce. Confidence was restored to the US dollar and the capital
flight of the preceding administration was reversed. Restored confi-
dence in the dollar, tight money and an appreciating currency
brought huge sums of capital to the United States, much of which
came from Japan and Europe, meeting the excess demand for
capital partly supplied by the financing of the US budget deficit; at
the same time US lending abroad dried up. The capital inflow and
the net accumulation of dollars imposed a corresponding balance-of-
trade deficit in the US.
The US trade deficit was attributed by many academics and
officials to the appreciating dollar, rather than to the capital inflow
that financed the excess of expenditure over income. As a result, after

46 Robert Mundell
the Plaza Agreement to devalue the dollar, it was widely believed that
the depreciation of the dollar would correct the trade deficit.
Perhaps no theory was more quickly disproved than the view that
depreciation of the dollar would correct or reverse the US trade
balance. The appreciation of the dollar in the first half of the eighties
did not create the deficit, and the even greater depreciation of the
dollar in the last half of the same decade has not corrected the deficit.
The deficit is a consequence of the net influx of capital into the United
States and the use of the dollar as an international reserve asset. Until
the US renews its net outward lending the current account will remain
in deficit.
2. - Sixteen Approaches to the Balance of Trade
A correct analysis of the balance of trade of a country must take
into account all the factors that enter into the balance of trade. The
literature has given the bulk of its attention to three approaches to the
balance of payments or trade: a) the elasticities approach; b) the
absorption approach; and c) the monetary approach. The usual
assumption made in the literature is that the capital account is either
zero or exogenous, unchanged by the effects of exchange rates so that
the analysis applies indifferently to the balance of trade or the balance
of payments. But in a complete analysis where capital flows are
allowed for, the elasticity and absorption approaches are ways of
analyzing the balance of trade, and only the monetary approach is a
way of analyzing the balance of payments.
The standard literature discusses only three of the many
approaches to the balance of payments or trade. In fact there are
exactly sixteen approaches to the balance of trade (or balance of
payments). The next few paragraphs draw on and summarize the
analysis of my paper with the above title delivered at the Caracas
Conference on Financial Markets in January 1979 and published in
Spanish in the Conference volume.
General equilibrium requires analysis of the conditions of equilib-
rium in three broad aggregates: goods, securities and money. Each
sector should be broken down into domestic and foreign components,

Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc. 47
and subdivided into the innumerable categories relevant in the real
world. However, to illustrate the sixteen approaches to the balance of
trade or payments, it will be convenient to maintain the degree of
aggregation as if there were only three things being traded, with no
change in the basic ideas advanced. For the sake of simplicity, I shall
bypass the difference between GDP and GNP, and the corresponding
difference between the trade balance and the current account. But a
big warning is in order: this difference cannot be ignored when we
deal with the eight intertemporal approaches to the balance of
payments!
The first equation we write down is the identity utilized by
practitioners of the elasticity approach, namely that the balance of
trade is equal to exports minus imports, B = X — M. By specifying
supplies of exports and demands for imports we arrive at approach 1)
to the balance of payments. Approach 2) in the same family results
from specifying the supply of exports and the demand for imports in
the foreign country. From “Cournot’s Law”, the trade surplus of one
country is the trade deficit of the rest of the world, due allowance
being made for asymmetries in the treatment of reserve suppliers and
gold producers. Analysis of these factors owe much to Bickerdike,
Robinson, Lerner, Haberler, Meade, Machlup and Metzler. A more
sophisticated development of this approach would incorporate into
the demand functions for exports and imports not just exchange rates,
prices and output, but domestic expenditure, capital movements and
wealth; it should then not be called the elasticity approach (why not
income propensities approach?) but rather the “direct approach”
because it examines directly the forces determining exports and
imports. The direct approach is no more and no less valid than the
other seven pairs.
The next pair of approaches makes use of the absorption rela-
tions’. B = Y — E where Y is income and E is expenditure (absorp-
tion). This relationship can be subdivided into separate sectors to yield
the equation S — [| + T — G = B, where S, I, T and G, refer,
respectively, to savings, investment, tax revenues and government
spending. There are two equations of this type, of course, one for the
country under analysis and the other for aggregate of economies in the
rest of the world. These approaches owe much to Gervaise, Metzler,

48 Robert Mundell
Viner, Machlup, Chipman, Meade, Alexander and Harry Johnson.
Alexander called “absorption” what Meade had called “domestic ex-
penditure”, and this inspired the name usually given to the approach.
The next pair relies on the balance-of-payments identity. The
balance of payments identity is just the external counterpart of
Walras’ Law. The current account surplus is equal to net capital
exports plus the balance of payments deficit. Put another way, the
current account surplus finances an import of securities (which is a
capital export) or an inflow of money (balance-of payments surplus).
We can write B = K + P, where K is the net capital outward flow and
P is the balance of payments surplus. The lesson from this approach is
to look at the means by which deficits are financed and surpluses are
disposed of.
There has been in international economics a long-standing
dispute about the direction of causation, if any, in the balance-of-pay-
ments identity. First it should be emphasized that the identity itself
says nothing about causation. It cannot be inferred from the balance
of payments identity whether the financial transfer determines the
trade balance or the trade balance determines the financial transfer.
The classical school, up until Mill, put the capital flow in the driver’s
seat. It emphasized the fact that the mere act of making a financial
transfer automatically implies the additional saving to finance it, so
that the mere existence of an outward capital flow implies an excess
of income over expenditure. But the Mill-Taussig-Keynes neglect of
expenditure effects opened the way for Keynes’s idiosyncratic view of
the trade balance as a entity independent of financial transfers.
Although this involves a false dichotomy — independence of spending
from finance — Keynes’ view has influenced the modern literature to
its detriment. It is easy to see why economists who write down
equations specifying exports as a function of output and prices fall
prey to the single-entry book-keeping approach that ignores the
mechanism though which expenditures are financed.
Causation can in principle go in either direction. But it is
inconceivable that fundamental and enduring changes in the balance
of trade can be motivated other than by basic financial transfers. It is
true that a shift of domestic expenditure from home to foreign goods
will worsen the balance of trade and immediately force accommo-

|     |     | Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc.  |     |     | 49  |
| --- | --- | -------------------------------------- | --- | --- | --- |
dating finance,  a loss of reserves  er a change in the exchange rate.  But
accommodating  finance  is  purely  temporary  and  short-run.  Major
trade  deficits  and  surpluses  are  nearly  always  not  only accompanied
by but induced by voluntary financial transfers of one kind of another.
Because  there  are  two  equations  of  this  type,  one  for  each
country,  we  now  have  six approaches  to the balance  of trade;  there
| are  only ten  | remaining.  |     |     |     | :   |

Approaches  7) and 8) make use of Walras’  Law directly. The sum
of  all  excess  demands  is  zero,  so  that  any  excess  supply  of
commodities  must  be  matched  by an  equivalent  excess  demand  for
securities  and money.  Because the trade balance is equal to the excess
supply  of  goods  it  must  also  be  equal  to  the  excess  demand  for
securities  and  money.  It is possible  to  see  this  result  in  a  slightly
different  way.  The  excess  supply  of goods is equal to the sum  of the
budget  surplus and the excess  of saving over  investment.  Any budget
surplus must be expended on money or securities;  it implies an excess
demand  for money  or  government  bonds  on  the part  of the  govern-
ment.  Similarly,  an  excess  of saving over  investment  equals an excess
demand  for  securities  and/or  money.  We  can  therefore  deduce  the
current  account  deficit  solely by examining  the markets  for securities
and  money.  This  approach  applies to both  countries  so  that we  now
have  eight  approaches  to the  analysis  of the balance  of trade.

Now for the’ inter-temporal dimension, the other eight
approaches. We often say that deficits — whether trade or budget —
are unsustainable. If a deficit is insustainable the worry is not that it
will endure but that it will disappear in an unpleasant way. The above
equations do not reflect this fact because they have not as yet taken
into account the inter-temporal version of Walras’ Law. Trade deficits
integrated over time yield net debt; and debt has to be paid back. We
owe to David Hume the theorem which Charles Kindleberger called
Hume’s Law that exports equal imports. Hume meant by this that the
balance-of-payments adjustment mechanism would eventually bring
imports into equality with exports. This is emphatically not true in the
short run; the US has had a trade deficit for a generation. But Hume is
right that exports pay for imports in the long run. A country’s net
indebtedness is limited by its perceived export capacity. The US can
sustain a trade deficit because it is believed to have the productive
power to finance it. But no country can pile up debts indefinitely
unless they are at the same time increasing the means for repaying
them. At some point diminishing returns will set in and the net
indebtedness will have to be reduced and perhaps eliminated. Higher
debts require larger interest payments and eventually untenable trade
surpluses to maintain a given current account. At current rates the US
is increasing its debt at the rate of 3% of GNP a year; at some point the
capital inflow will cease and the US trade balance will have to become
positive just to maintain a zero current account.
The LDC’s borrowed excessively in the negative real interest days
of the late seventies and early eighties. When their future export
capacity seemed insufficient to service their debts and real interest
rates rose, the flow of capital dried up and they were left with a
painful adjustment process that has hardly abated. In the long run no
country can feasibly borrow indefinitely because every country,
sooner or later, comes up against diminishing returns and an inability
to continue growth fast enough to keep up with needed repayments.
And so we come, finally to the additional eight approaches to the

52 Robert Mundell
balance of trade, that each one of the above-mentioned eight
approaches has its reverse counterpart in the inter-temporal dimen-
sion when surpluses and deficits have to be reversed. It would not be
out of place to analyze the implications of today’s policies by looking
into the future condition when the problems are reversed.
In the long run, therefore, we need to pay special attention to the
difference between the GDP and GNP, and to the equivalent differen-
ce between the trade balance and the current account balance. When
we construct models of current behavior we commit a serious error if
we fail to take into account the expected future net outpayments or
inpayments of debt service on disposable income and expenditure. We
must also take account of the pall that heavy indebtedness casts over
expectations about the exchange rate and rising interest rates that
indicate decreased credit-worthiness. In the long, long run, we should
take account of debts as a subtraction from wealth that should affect
our current propensities to save. We do that with our personal debts,
but the condition of rationality is that we calculate our share of the
public debt, after adjusting for the differential burden arising from the
age distribution of the population, and let that affect our saving
behavior and our ability to repay debt once incurred. Ricardian
equivalence applies in the long run to the indebted countries.
3. - Applications of the Analysis
The sixteen approaches to the balance of trade apply equally well,
mutatis mutandis, to the balance of payments. The methodology is
applicable to any of the sixteen categories in the interdependent
tableau. Ex post all sixteen approaches are equivalent. The issue is not
therefore whether one approach or another is correct. It is rather a
matter of research strategy. Which approach is most efficient, in view
of the availability of data and analysis of it? We should use those
approaches that best exploit the available data and then verify the
results by ensuring its compatibility with known elements from the
fifteen alternative approaches.
Analysis of the very large trade deficits and surpluses of the 1980s

Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc. 53
can be elucidated by attention to the sixteen approaches. The policy of
the US government, from 1985 to 1988, was to lower the value of the
dollar against the currencies of the major surplus countries. From
February 1985 to 1988, the values of the mark (and many other
European currencies) and the yen doubled against the dollar. Despite
this some economists have argued that the US trade deficit will only
be corrected if the dollar falls to the magic figures of 100 yen and 1.5
marks.
Nothing in the above analysis encourages the view that manipula-
tions of exchange rates alter the balance of trade. The usual analysis
applies partial equilibrium theory to a general equilibrium problem. In
order to change the exchange rate it is necessary to alter relative
monetary and fiscal policies. Monetary expansion in 1985 and mon-
etary contraction in Japan and much of Europe were responsible for
the depreciation of the dollar (although the fall in the price of oil
played a role). The elasticity criterion takes into account only ex-
change rates and prices and ignores the monetary and expenditure
changes necessary to bring about the exchange rate changes; the shift
in the demand and supply curves induced by changes in macro-
economic policy are not taken into account.
The sixteen-approaches analysis also forces attention on the
capital account of the balance-of-payments equations. The US current-
account deficit is matched by an influx of capital or increases in dollar
holdings abroad. If a depreciation of the dollar were to have an effect
on the trade balance it must also have an effect on the capital account.
But a depreciation of the dollar that increases competitiveness
(because money wages change by less than prices) must shift the
distribution of income along the factor-price frontier, raising the
return to capital. This attracts capital from abroad financing an even
larger deficit (measured in domestic currency). In a large country like
the United States, the prices of fixed capital assets, land and labor lag
behind the prices of tradable goods which increases, at least tem-
porarily, their rates of return. The old argument that the rate of return
to capital is unaffected by devaluation because product prices change
in the same proportion as factor prices is true only in the case where
devaluation does not change relative prices, including the real ex-
change rate, in which case it does not then alter competitiveness or

54 Robert Mundell
the balance of trade. There is some evidence that since 1985 devalu-
ation has lowered the relative prices of land, hotels and factories,
creating the fire-sale phenomena that has attracted capital and in-
duced US trade deficits.
Another feature that is illuminating in the sixteen approaches is
the importance of saving. The absorption approach already indicated
the importance of an excess of saving over investment and the budget
deficit in creating a trade balance. But saving and investment, as well
as budget deficits, have counterparts in the securities markets. An
improvement in the trade balance can only materialize if there is an
increase in lending abroad (or reserve accumulation). This would arise
as a result of an increase in saving, or a decrease in a budget deficit,
because the increase in saving would create an excess demand for
securities (or money), and a decrease in the budget deficit would have
the same effect.
What is the outcome of our lesson in taxonomy? Do we as yet
have a theory of deficits that will explain the persistent balance-of-pay-
ments problems of the United States, at least since the 1950s? The
answer is, not yet. The persistent problems are empirical and em-
pirical generalizations do not come from pure deduction. The basic
lesson of the tableau is to guard against single entry book-keeping in
the study of trade or payments balances. Nothing occurs in one sector
of the economy without an equal and opposite accompaniment in
another sector of the economy. If that lesson is learned it will be
difficult to make a mistake in the formulation of models seeking to
illuminate empirical phenomena.
4. - The “Seventeenth” Approach
It is necessary now to take into account explicitly features of the
international monetary system. The demand for and supply of interna-
tional reserve assets is a necessary component of a general theory of
the global monetary mechanism. Now all the countries in the world
make up the global demand, and it would therefore be possible to
incorporate the demand for and supply of reserve assets into the

Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc. 55
tableau of the sixteen approaches. If for example, there were a world
government it would be possible to analyze the situation of that
government as a separate «country» or to allocate its demands and
supplies among the actual countries. To keep the new features of the
global analysis distinct and because it will be conducive to organi-
zational clarity, we shall develop the global analysis as a “seventeenth”
approach to the balance of payments. ;
It has been mentioned before that under a metallic standard there
is in the world as a whole an excess of surpluses over deficits in the
balance of payments equal to the increase in monetary gold reserves.
We know also that under a reserve currency system there is an excess
of surpluses over deficits in the balance of payments equal to the
increase in foreign exchange and gold reserves. We know also that
under a reserve currency system there is an excess of surpluses over
deficits in the balance of payments (conventionally defined) if the rest
of the world increases its balances in the reserve currency and if the
reserve center does not count its increasing foreign liquid liabilities as
part of a balance of payments deficit. These possibilities suggest that
our monetary equations, which suggest a zero-sum game of payments
deficits, is overly simplified, and that we should instead allow for a
global balance-of-payments surplus equal to the increase in the de-
mand-supply of global reserves.
Consider the situation alluded to earlier of the so-called US
balance of payments deficits when the rest of the world was accumu-
lating dollar reserves in the 1950s and 1960s. Following the devalu-
ation of sterling in November 1967 the US balance-of-payments deficit
mounted alarmingly, leading to the Gold Communique in March and
the two-tier “system” in which the price of gold on the free market
was allowed to rise relative to the official price; the Bank of England
would no longer feed the London gold market because the US was
reluctant to convert the dollars acquired into gold. The price of gold
then rose above its official parity of $35 and was generally forecast to
go much higher. No central bank was then willing to sell gold to other
countries at the official price yet they committed themselves not to
trade in gold at higher prices. As a result European countries were
suddenly short of usable reserves. With gold suddenly immobilized
and unattainable countries wanted larger dollar reserves to compen-

56 Robert Mundell
sate for their immobilized gold stocks. Recognition of the reserve
demand for dollars and gold led to the creation of the SDR, agreed
upon in 1967, ratified in 1968, and implemented in 1970. But the
creation of the SDR’s came too little and too late to avert the crisis of
the gold-dollar standard in 1971 and the demand for dollars did not
abate even after the fixed exchange system had collapsed in August
1971.
The seventeenth approach takes into account the secular demand
for international reserves. It is necessary to formalize the explanation
of the US deficit in terms of this approach. The undervaluation of gold
made the dollar-exchange standard untenable. But even if the price of
gold had been higher, the US balance of payments deficit would have
remained. The US balance-of-payments deficit in the 1950s and 1960s
can be explained by the steady secular demand on the part of the rest
of the world for US dollar liquid assets to serve as foreign exchange
reserves. It is convenient to make an economic model of this approach
to the balance of payments of a reserve center. Let R = k* Y* be the
demand for reserves on the part of the rest of the world (outside the
US), where Y* is the nominal Gross Product of the rest of the world
and k* is the fraction of Gross Product that the rest of the world
wants to hold in the form of dollar balances. Under a pure dollar
standard the US payments deficit, P, is equal to the increase in
reserves, dR/dt, so that, by differentiation, we find that
P= ks ny
where 7 is the rate of growth of nominal Gross Product in the rest of
the world. If in, say 1970, n = .06, Y* = $4 trillion, and k* = .01,
then P would equal $2.4 billion, not far from the annual magnitude of
the persistent US balance-of-payments deficit. This excess flow de-
mand for dollars on the part of the rest of the world must be matched
with the annual flow supply of dollars from the United States, which
must in turn be equal to an excess demand for goods or securities. The
exigencies of defense and social problems, however, have made the
US a generous supplier of dollars and other liquid assets to the rest of
the world. Only during the dollar shortage, say between 1938 and

Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc. 57
1950, was foreign demand not satisfied by dollar assets. From that
time the supply side has not provided any barrier to the US satisfac-
tion of the rest-of-the-world’s demand for reserves.
When in 1981 confidence in the dollar was restored by tight
money the secular demand for dollars resumed and still continues.
But a new dimension to the problem of the reserve center has been
added since the recovery of the American economy from the recession
of 1982 and the new efficiency stimulated by the 25% tax cut starting
in 1981 and the Tax Reform Act of 1986 both of which lowered
Federal income taxes from a maximum rate of 70% in 1981 to a
qualified maximum of 23% in 1987. Lower taxes and a booming
economy have raised the marginal efficiency of capital and attracted it
to the United States. But the attractiveness of US assets is not a
monopoly of the current decade. There is a long run component to the
demand for US assets based on the size of the US economy, its
comparative political and economic stability, and the extremely high
marketability of all dollar assets and investments in the US. The same
characteristics of the US that make the dollar the major international
currency make it the major producer of long-term securities, an
attractive residence for flight capital, a safe haven in a troubled world.
The globalization phenomenon that was expedited by the fall in
the price of oil in 1985-86 and the enormous transfer of wealth to
Japan, creates an automatic demand for identifiable prime stocks and
bonds. The US government is the only one in the world that produces
marketable long-term bonds with maturities of thirty years. This a
reflection of the debt-carrying capacity of the United States, only now
being exploited in the global market. Whereas foreign lending to the
United States accelerated, US lending abroad dried up (partly because
of the LDC debt crisis), creating a net capital import to the United
States. There is no indication that the US will abdicate its role as a
major supplier of long-term debt. US assets have moved into the
“trophy” category in the globalization phenomenon that has increas-
ingly integrated international securities markets in the 1980s.
To model the role of the supplier of long-term earning assets, it is
convenient to assume that demand in the rest of the world for US
earning assets is a given proportion, c*, of the Gross Product in the
rest of the world. Let A = c* Y* relate total assets desired to Gross

= c*dY*/dt. Then, assuming that the United States continues to

financing on the part of the rest of the world for the US current
account deficit will have to be:

this hypothetical calculation the rest of the world would, other things
constant, voluntarily finance a US trade deficit of $120 billion!
Analysis of the demand for and supply of international assets
cannot be ignored when dealing with a country that produces reserve
assets and other securities and ownership claims for the rest of the
world. We have looked at the subject mainly from the demand side. It
would be possible to extend the analysis to the supply side taking into
account the factors that create the supply of desirable reserve and
capital assets, leading to an eighteenth approach to the balance of
payments, involving all those factors that make a country like the
United States a reserve center.
But time does not stand still. The factors that make the US a
reserve center and a provider of long-term debts change over time. To
take account of the effect of time on the longevity of a reserve and
capital center, it is necessary to analyze the future supply and demand
for the center’s assets, which leads to the nineteenth and twentieth
approaches to the balance of payments. An analysis of the supply side
would show the characteristics necessary for a country to be a reserve
center and indicate the most likely candidated for an alternative to the
use of the dollar and US claims. Analysis of the demand side will show
that a country that builds up its international indebtedness will sooner
or later run into a situation of diminishing credit-worthiness, higher
debt service, budget deficits, and speculation against the reserve

Trade Balance Patterns as Global etc. 59
currency. Thus has fared the great world currencies of the past, from
the stater and the drachma to the besant and the pound (18). It is not
likely that the dollar will resist the inevitable. In the long run the
creation of a reserve center is an act of creative destruction.
5. - Conclusion
The main purpose of this paper has been to examine the develop-
ment of principles of international monetary economics in the light of
historical changes in the international monetary system and the
contributions of particular individuals from the past. The theoretical
purpose is to explore the anatomy of trade disequilibrium in the light
of the sixteen approaches to the balance of payments (or trade). It is
further to emphasize that the balance of payments of a reserve-cre-
ating country is best treated as a special case outside the ordinary
framework of the sixteen approaches. The demand for liquid reserves
harks back to the gold-exchange standard of Bretton Woods days. But
as countries mature their demands for international assets, especially
the assets of the supereconomy, go beyond purely liquid financial
assets. The demand for financial assets, backed by the economy with
the greatest debt-carrying capacity, complementary to the demand for
the liquid balances of the reserve center, suggest the appropriateness
of a seventeenth approach to the balance of payments providing for
(18) The “stater” was a Greek gold coin, meaning “standard”, but it was the
Macedonian kings Philip II and his son Alexander the Great who established it as an
international currency.
The “drachma”, meaning “handful”, was a silver coin used throughout Greece and
the Mediterranean area before its domination by the Romans. The “besant”, or
“bezant”, was the Byzantine version, established by Constantine, of the Roman gold
coin, the “solidus” or “aureus”, established by Julius Caesar’s in 46 B.C. Caesar’s
“solidus” was 125 grains of gold, but the “besant” was kept unchanged for almost nine
hundreds years at about 70 grains of gold (about 1/7 of an ounce).
The pound, and likewise the pounds-shillings-pence-system, is derived from the
Roman system; the libra of account was always equated to 5 “aurei”.
The Franks first adopted, then rejected, this Roman system, but readopted it under
Pepin the Short and Charlemagne, from whence it travelled to England, and Alfred the
Great’s coinage system, and after an “interregnum” of Danish money, arrived in
England again through William the Conquerer.

The Real Exchange Rate
Under Alternative Nominal Exchange
Rate Regimes
Emil-Maria Claassen
University of Paris-Dauphine and Freie Universitat Berlin
1. - Introduction
The real exchange rate measures the relative price of goods while
the nominal exchange rate stands for the relative price of currencies.
The most comprehensive definition of the real exchange rate is
represented by the ratio of the foreign to the domestic price level,
both expressed in terms of the domestic currency. If each price index
contains nontradable, exportable and importable goods, a change in
the real exchange rate can account for changes in the relative price of
nontradables in the two countries and for changes in the terms of
trade.
In the literature, two types of models are used for the analysis of
real exchange rate determination (Camen/Genberg [1]). On the one
hand, there are “purely real models” in which markets clear in-
stantanously and where changes in the pattern of production and
expenditure give rise to modifications in the equilibrium value of
relative prices and of the real exchange rate. On the other hand, there
are monetary (or macro-oriented) models in which only asset markets
continuously clear while there is some stickiness of prices in the goods
markets. Consequently, monetary disturbances have also real effects
producing changes in the real exchange rate as an outcome of the
asymmetry in the speed of adjustment of goods and asset markets.

Since we  restrict  ourselves  to a one-country  view,  the concerned
economy  must  be to the small-open  kind of a economy  for which  the
terms  of trade  are  given  exogenously.  Consequently,  the  relevant
measure  of the real  exchange  rate  comprises  exclusively  the  relative
price of nontradables  of the domestic  country.  Since,  furthermore,  we
are concerned with the long-run movements  in the real exchange rate,
only  real  disturbances  will  affect  them  resulting  from  differential
productivity  growth  rates  between  tradables  and  montradables  or
from divergent income  elasticities  of the demand  for each category  of
goods.  Under  this aspect,  the appropriate  model  of the real exchange
rate  determination  should  be based  on  the  Balassa-Samuelson  refor-
mulation  of the  purchasing  power  parity  theorem  (PPP).  A recent
support  of  this  model  has  been  provided  by  Kravis  [7]  and  his  |

In  order  to  simplify  the  analysis,  we  assume  a  non-growing
economy.  Real  shocks  arise  only  from  the  demand  side.  We  have
chosen  expenditure-switching  fiscal  policies  as  an  example  for  a
demand  shock  in  the  goods  markets.  The  aim  of  the  analytical
exercize  is to show  that  the subsequent  change  in the  real exchange
rate  takes  place  independently  on  the  underlying  nominal  exchange
rate  regime.  The  nominal  exchange  rate  regimes  are  neutral  with
respect  to  the  real  variables  including  the  real  exchange  rate.  The
difference  between  fixed  and  flexible  nominal  exchange  rates  con-
cerns  only the proper  mix  of flexibility  of the absolute  price levels  of
tradables  and  nontradables.  The  neutrality  properties  already  have
been  elaborated  by  Stockman  [12],  [13].  His  methodological
approach  is in terms  of general  equilibrium  analysis  within  a  two-
period  and  two-country  framework.  Our  one-country  model  repre-
sentes  a macroeconomic  simplification  of the  Stockman  approach.
In  Section  2,  the  real  side  of the  macro-model  is  developed.
Section  3 treats  the effects  of various  switching  fiscal  policies  on  the
real  exchange  rate.  In  Section  4,  the  nominal  variables  are
determined.  For  the  case  of  nominal  flexible  exchange  rates,  the
money  market  fixes  the  equilibrium  values  for  the  price  levels  of
tradables  and  nontradables.  Under  the  hypothesis  of fixed  nominal
exchange  rates,  the money  market  determines  the  equilibrium  value

3. - Switching Fiscal Policies
By definition, real disturbances emerge in the goods market
either on the supply side or on the demand side. To the extent that
they create a disequilibrium in the market for nontradables, a change
in the equilibrium value of the real exchange rate must necessarily

government  expenditures  either  in favor of nontradables  (creating  an

second  type of fiscal policy deals with tax-financed  increases  of public

la. The initial equilibrium is again at point Q. The increase in public

effects: the substitution effect of the relative price change reducing the

ondly, the wealth-value effect of the real appreciation (F °de) rein-
forces the decline of private expenditures for nontradables. As far as
the domestic demand and supply of tradables are concerned, there is
an excess supply of tradables at point R. The excess supply arises from
the assumed decrease of public expenditures on tradables being partly
offset by the substitution effect of the real appreciation on the demand
and supply side of tradables but reinforced by the wealth-value and
operating on the demand side of tradables. At point R, a current
account surplus emerges creating now the wealth-volume cffect (e

market of nontradables, private consumption rises and the clearing of
the market necessitates a further real appreciation. The adjustment
process moves over time from R towards U. At U, the wealth level is
slightly higher than the former real wealth at Q. The ultimate rate of
real appreciation reflects the new expenditure pattern provoked by
government action and consequently also the new production pattern
in terms of a higher production of nontradables and a lower produc-
tion of tradables (3).

The Real Exchange Rate etc. 79
5. - Concluding Remarks
The equilibrium approach for the determination of the real
exchange rate has shown that the behavior of real exchange rates is
invariant to the underlying nominal exchange rate regime. At first
sight, this statement is in full contradiction with reality. By regarding
the evolution of the level as well as the periodical percent changes of
the real exchange rate, we know that the variability of the real
exchange rate has increased considerably during the floating period
compared to the pre-1972 period of fixed nominal exchange rates (see
Dornbusch [2], pp. 26-8). From our model one would except that the
real exchange rates variability would have remained rather unchan-
ged during both periods. However, there are two important explan-
ations for the increased variability under floating rates which are not
necessarily in contradiction with our model.
On the one hand, by using the generally accepted proposition of
the sluggishness in the adjustment mechanism of goods prices, Mussa
[8] comes to the widely held conclusion that the substitution of
flexible for fixed nominal exchange rates involved an increased vari-
ability of the real exchange rate caused mainly (according to Mussa)
by nominal disturbances. Our model was of the equilibrium type and
we assumed full flexibility of goods prices such that nominal shocks
would not produce changes in the real exchange rate. We operated
with such an assumption in order to underline another cause of real
exchange rate changes which are represented by real shocks.
Within the framework of our model one could derive a higher real
exchange rate variability under floating nominal rates for two other
reasons as they have been suggested also by Stockman [13]. First, dur-
ing the 1970s and 1980s, a greater number of real shocks emerged in
various parts of the world economy and they would have also occurred
under the hypothesis of having maintained the fixed nominal exchange
rate regime. Second, the exchange rate regime itself may have condi-
tioned specific economic policies. Under fixed exchange rates,
economic policies are under the pressure of balance of payments con-
straints which are less pronunced under floating rates. Or, in other ter-
ms, the flexible nominal exchange rate regime may have modified the
constraints as they were perceived by policy makers, giving rise to more
policy action. These two advanced reasons still require testing.

The Economic Effects
of Expected Fiscal Policy
in Small Open Economies
Jiirgen Schroder
University of Mannheim
In this article, the short run and the long run effects of an
expected increase in credit financed government expenditure will be
investigated (1). It will be shown that in open economies these effects
crucially depend on the impact of the expected fiscal expansion on the
country’s international creditworthiness (2). Therefore, two — ex-
treme — cases will be discussed.
In case one it will be assumed that an expected fiscal expansion
does not effect the country’s long run international creditworthiness,
(1) This question has been addressed recently by McKinnon [6] with regard to
monetary policy. He shows that an expected increase in money supply leads, if
expectations are fulfilled, to a proportional increase in the price level as well as in the
exchange rate in the long run. There are no long run real effects. The short run effects
of the expected expansionary monetary policy are very different however. Assuming
that the exchange rate is a forward looking variable, then the current exchange rate will
jump immediately to the long run expected higher level. This depreciation of the home
currency has — via several channels — a positive short run impact on real private
absorption and real income whereas the short run effect on the real balance of trade is
indeterminate.
Advise: the numbers in square brackets refer to the Bibliography in the appendix.
(2) We make no distinction between the country’s international creditworthiness
and the governments national and international creditworthiness. Although an expected
— and actual — increase in government expenditure usually implies a huge long run
increase in government debt, it is here assumed that at any point in time the
government is as creditworthy as private domestic borrowers in both domestic and the
international financial markets.

84 Jiirgen Schroder
regardless of the long run impact on the trade account. People expect
that any long run deficit in the trade account can easily be financed by
international borrowing and that the corresponding growing interna-
tional debt has no impact on the international creditworthiness (3). It
will be shown, that in this case, there is a negative effect on the price
level and the exchange rate in the long run, but that real income and
real private absorption will increase, causing a deficit in the real trade
account. In the short run there will be deflationary pressure and —
contrary to the long run situation — there will be a negative impact on
real income and real private absorption, while the impact on the real
balance of trade is indeterminate.
In case two, the assumption of constant international
creditworthiness is abandoned. Instead, it is assumed that there is a
positive causal relation between a country’s net foreign position
and its international creditworthiness. It will be shown that, under
this assumption, an expected fiscal expansion leads to an increase
in the interest rate, the price level, and the exchange rate in the
long run while there is no impact on real income and the real trade
account because private absorption is crowded out by the amount
of the increase in government expenditure. In the short run there
will be inflationary preasure and — despite the interest rate in-
crease — a positive impact on real income whereas the impact on
real private absorption and on the real balance of trade is indeter-
minate (4).
In investigating these two extreme cases a model developed by
McKinnon and Ohno [5] is used, in which particular emphasis is put
(3) It is clear that such a situation and therefore such expectations can not last
forever. Nevertheless, for a limited time people can expect such a development. See
more on this point in footnote four.
(4) In reality there is no clear distinction between these two extreme cases. In fact,
the general case will very probably be that in the first place an expected credit financed
government expenditure has no negative effects on the international creditworthiness of
a country which is otherwise well known for economic and political stability. This is the
more likely the more it is expected that expenditures are, or the smaller they are in
relation to income. However, the larger and the more persistant the actual government
deficit already is, and therefore the faster the government debt and thus the country’s
international debt grow, the more likely it becomes that the country’s international
creditworthiness suffers and a transition from case one to case two takes place.

The Economic Effects etc. 87
being a forward looking variable, the domestic interest rate in a small
open economy is determined by the world market interest rate plus a
possible risk premium as described in (6). It is further assumed here
that commodity prices are sticky in the short run. This implies that
any ‘news’ which immediately affects the nominal exchange rate has
the same effect on the real exchange rate in the short run. Volatility in
the real exchange rate, and with it short run deviations from pur-
chasing power parity, have several undesirable effects in very ‘open
economies. A real depreciation leads to an exppected inflationary
pressure, as described in (5), because of demand pull and cost push
effects originating in the export and import sectors. The expected
price increase lowers the real interest rate, which has a positive effect
on real private absorption. In addition to this real interest rate effect,
an undervalued currency causes competitive advantages for the ex-
port and import competing sectors and increases thereby the
profitability of investment in these sectors (6). These two effects are
considered in the private absorption function (2) by assuming

These short run effects as well as the adjustment process to the
expected — and actual — new long run equilibrium, are presented in
Graph 1. The initial equilibrium values of the endogenous variables
are indicated by the subscript “1”, whereas the subscript “2” shows
the expected — and actual — long run equilibrium values. In time t,,
news about the future fiscal expansion arrives. This leads to an
immediate appreciation of the home currency to its long run expected
value, e decreases from e; to e2. This appreciation causes deflationary
preasure, 1.e. p becomes negative, which implies an increase in the
real interest rate. Both the real appreciation and the rise in the real
interest rate cause a reduction in private absorption (investment) and
thus a decrease in real income. The short run impact on the real
balance of trade is ambiguous because of the two opposing impacts
stemming from the change in real income and in the real exchange
rate. In the medium run, p begins to fall and initiates the adjustment
process. The fall in p reduces the initial real appreciation of the home
currency and the expected deflationary pressure. Therefore, private
absorption begins to increase and so too does real income. The
increase in real income causes a deterioration in the real balance of
trade. The new steady state equilibrium is reached when p has fallen
over time by the same proportion as e has jumped downwards in ft; as
a result of the news, because then the pre-news real exchange rate is
restored and p is zero.
It is now interesting to investigate briefly the short and long run
effects of an expected increase in government expenditure under the
assumption that fiscal policy has no lasting effect, i.e. no long run
impact, on real income. A plausible reason for this assumption is that
it is not possible to lower the long run natural rate of unemployment
by demand side fiscal stimuli.
From (/) and (2) it is clear that, with a constant real income,
private absorption and/or the balance of trade have to decrease by the
amount of fiscal expansion. However, (2) shows that, with Y constant
in the long run, private absorption in constant in the long run as long
as it is assumed that the expected fiscal policy has no impact on the

2. - Case Two:
Variable International Creditworthiness
One important result of the investigation in case one was that an
expansionary fiscal policy causes a deterioration in the trade account
in the long run regardless of whether it generates a positive long run
effect on real income or not. Therefore such a policy has a negative
impact on the net foreign position and sooner or later the country will
become a debtor in the world capital market. Because of the small
country assumption, the accumulation of foreign debt will have no
impact on the world interest rate. However, international investors
will become reluctant to provide additional loans because the continu-
ous increase in the country’s negative foreign position increases the
possibility that the interest payments and the reapayments of the loans
may become difficult in the future. Therefore, it will be assumed that
the risk premium that international investors demand depends posi-
tively on the country’s foreign debt position — once a critical size is
reached. Assuming this relation, then the risk premium, and thus the
domestic interest rate, increases as long as the country experiences a
trade account deficit. However, the increase in the domestic interest
rate has, via negative effects on domestic absorption, a positive impact
on the trade account. Therefore, with an increasing risk premium
and, pari passu, an increasing domestic interest rate, the deficit in the
trade account shrinks and the increase in the negative net foreign
position diminishes. Risk premium and domestic interest rate are in
long run equilibrium when the trade account is equilibrated and

3. - Summary and Conclusions
Under the assumption that asset prices, i.e. the interest rate and
the exchange rate, are forward looking variables, the short run effects
of an expected fiscal expansion depend on its long run effects. The
long run effects, in turn, are determined by the impact of the expected
fiscal expansion on the country’s international creditworthiness.
If people expect that the international creditworthiness does not
suffer then there is no long run impact on the interest rate and
therefore a positive long run impact on real income and a negative
long run impact on the price level and on the exchange rate.
However, this long run positive real effect causes a contraction in real
income in the short run, because the long run expected appreciation
of the home currency will immediately be telescoped into the current
exchange rate, causing deflationary pressure and a demand decrease
in the real sector.
However, if the expected fiscal expansion reduces the country’s
international creditworthiness, the risk premium and also the dom-
estic interest rate will increase in the long run, causing a long run
increase in the price level and the exchange rate and a crowding out
of private absorption to the extent of the fiscal expansion, so that real
income does not change. As the long run expected increase in the

The Pass-Through Puzzle:
The Missing Prince from Hamlet (*)
Jagdish N. Bhagwati
Columbia University
1. - Introduction
Much has been made of the “puzzle” that the past appreciation
and recent depreciation of the dollar have not resulted in an equal
pass-through in dollar prices of imports within the US as in earlier
periods (1). The media see Robert Kuttner [15] in the New York
Times a yeart ago, reporting on a 1987 Brandeis Conference of local
experts on international macroeconomics) have presented this with
some fanfare and, presumably encouraged by economists in the field,
(*) I briefly state a hypothesis to explain the “pass-through” puzzle that macroeco-
nomists have been concerned with recently. I have advanced orally this explanation
over the last two years to many macroeconomists, past students and present colleagues
among them, after reading MANN [18], and especially after noting Paul Krugman’s
omission of the explanation in a talk on the pass-through problem in early 1987 at the
World Bank. I felt that the explanation needed to be written down for a wider audience
since the main body of macroeconomists continues to be puzzled by the pass-through
phenomenon. The hypothesis advanced here fits the broad facts on an eye-scan. Thanks
are due to Mike Gavin and Paul de Grauwe, whose favourable response to the proposed
explanation encourage me to explore it systematically here. I am also grateful to
CATHERINE MANN for pointing out her more recent work where the role of trade barriers
is noted in the context of examinning the influences on import prices. Douglas Irwin
has been enormously helpful with insightful comments, as usual. Guillermo Calvo and
Avinash Dixit also provided useful suggestions.
(1) The phrase “pass-through”, to my knowledge, was first used by my former
student, STEVE MAGEE [17], in a classic article on the subject. It is not clear to me that
the pass-through is, or should be, particularly stable, anyway: MANN [18], pp. 369-70)
herself notes several studies of pre-1980 experience which show pass-through varying
from 50 to 80% but this problem is ignored in the present note.
Advise: the numbers in square brackets refer to the Bibliography in appendix.

104 Jagdish N. Bhagwati
as a major crisis in international economic theory. And it has led to a
search for explanations, including a revival of the Samuelson-Kemp-
Wan type of hysterisis theories in the important work by Richard
Baldwin [1] and by Baldwin and Krugman [2].
But a major and indeed obvious explanation has simply been
missed. It lies, of course, in the fact that the early 1980s (when the US
dollar was overvalued) saw a significant rise in non-tariff barriers
(NTB), e.g., in the form of high-track protection such as YERs
(Voluntary Export Restriction). In lieu of depreciation to correct for
the overvaluation, imports were therefore restricted, leading to sub-
stantial premia in a number of therefore restricted, leading to substan-
tial premia in a number of sectors such as autos, steel and textiles (2).
It is well-known to those such as myself who worked on exchange
rate and trade policies for developing countries in the 1970s that a
devaluation with such import restrains will not result in a comparable
pass-through as a devaluation without such restraints. The devalu-
ation will generally cut into the premium, which will “absorb” the
devaluation’s impact.
In Bhagwati [3] therefore, I argued in India, while working on
the economics of the forthcoming June 1966 devaluation, that it was
inappropriate to assume that a devaluation would necessarily increase
domestic prices as commonly assumed: import restrictions already
had led to import premium in the range of 50 to 70% on many import.
I also argued that, given the excess of impports over exports,
reflecting substantial aid-absorption, a devaluation would be defla-
tionary (again, contrary to traditional presunptions) and that this
implied, ceteris paribus, that the price-level could even fall, following
the devaluation (3). I might add that I also advanced at the time,
therefore, the distinction between “gross” and “net” devaluation: the
latter, on the import side, was the parity change minus the tariffs that
frequently had been imposed in lieu of devaluation and often were
removed once devaluation was undertaken. This distinction has also

(3) See RICHARD CoopER [8], subsequently developed the same idea independently.
A later article by KRUGMANN and TayLor [14) also has examined more intensively the

become commonplace to international theorists who are familiar with
developing countries (4).
2. - The Main Fact and Proposed Explanation
The principal facts that have created the puzzle are best seen
through the important work of Catherine Mann [18]. She used the
weighted average exchange value of the US dollar to calculate the
“estimated” unit value of US non-oil imports, assuming a conventional
60% pass-through based on pre-1980 experience.
Plotted against the actual behavior of the unit value of non-oil
imports, based on the trade-weighted consumer price index, the
estimated series naturally mimics beautifully the actual until 1980.
But thereafter, there is a remarkable divergence (Graph 1).
Why? Let me then propose that the main explanation is to be
found in the fact that the 1980s showed a progressive increase in the
share of US imports covered by voluntary export restrictions (VERs)
and other nontariff barriers (NTBs). Thus, Table 1 shows a significant
increase in NTBs to US imports over the early 1980s. Their index
shows a 23% increase from 1981 to 1986. Nogues, Olechowski and
Winters [19], document that by 1983 over 40% of US imports were
covered by some sort of explicit NTB or monitoring measure. Table 2
shows a similar increase in a subset of “hard-core” NTBs in the US
Laird [16] finds that VERs constituited the single most important
category of NTBs (excluding the MFA-Multifibers Agreement) in the
US and that between 1981 and 1986 the percentage of trade affected
by VERs nearly doubled. In 1986, 14.5% of all US trade was affected
by VERs (including MFA). In that same year, according to Laird, 37%
of imports from Japan were affected by VERs (not including other

Graph  3 then  shows  how  this  analysis  must  be modified  in the

The Pass-Through Puzzle etc. 111
If the quality restraint is varied up from OQ to OQ’, the pass-through
will also rise correspondingly (8).
If, instead of import restraints, we had export restraints by Japan
— through VERs, OMAs (Orderly Market Agreements), et. al. — then
Graph 3 must be reinterpreted a little. The import premium AC in the
zero-pass-through case will now accrue to the Japanese; the pass-
through will of course remain unchanged (9).
4. - Rxplaining the Pass-Through in the 1980s:
A Recapitulation
Consider anew the unfolding scenario in the 1980s. The dollar
appreciates through the 1980s but NTBs are imposed on an increasing
basis to offset the import effects of the appreciation. The actual price
is more or less left unchanged: the historical pass-through relationship
is broken, and the divergence of the estimated conventional-pass-
through-based price level from the actual price level increases with
increasing dollar appreciation. With the Plaza Agreement, the dollar
begins to fall sharply, with the conventional-pass-through-based esti-
mated price level moving up rapidly towards the actual price-level,
but, with the premium on scarce imports absorbing the dollar devalu-
ation, there would be little impact on the actual price-level itself. An
eye-scan of Catherine Mann’s [18], chart, Graph 1, confirms this
broad scenario.
5. - Further Observations
If my explanation of the “pass-through” failure is reasonable,
then important implications follow.
(8) I should add the caveat that the analysis here is in partial equilibrium, like the
small group imperfect-competition-in-product-markets analysis of trade today. The
passthrough can vary, even given the supply and demand curves. But it can vary also if
these curves shift over time, as may be relevant in they are embodied in general-equili-
brium models where the consequences of exchange rate changes with and without
trade barriers are compared.
(9) On the other hand, because VERs are in practice discriminatory, there will be
differential effects arising from the porosity of such protection, as noted earlier.

112 Jagdish N. Bhagwati
First, the view is occasionally advanced that exchange rates no
longer work: the evidence cited is precisely for the exchange rates in
the 1980s. Thus, for instance, Paul Krugman ([{13], p. 40) has recently
argued that exchange rates “seem to matter so little’ import prices do
not adjust quicky to them any longer, while altogether forgetting from
his brief excursion into empirics the fact of trade barriers. If exchange
rates did not matter much during the dollar’s appreciation, and they
mattered as little during the dollar’s depreciation, a major (possibly
the critical) reason was surely the growth of trade barriers (as
explained in this note). In consequence, exchange rate changes could
not be expected to have the desired impact: if prices faced by the
economic agents are not allowed to change, the expenditure-swit-
ching that must occur for a favourable impact on the balance of trade
will simply not follow.
Second, we can the wind up in a catch-22 (10) situation: trade
barriers will make the exhange rate changes ineffective, and the
inefficacy of exchange rate changes will prompt the imposition of
more trade barriers. Failure to diagnose the key role of trade barriers
in the “pass-through” phenomenon may then have costly conse-
quences even though it may be good for the development of economic
science!
(10) Famous paradox one to the essay an the Second World War by S. Heller:
Catch 22.
