118 Luigi Paganetto
The question becomes all the more important when one bears in
mind that 1989 sees the world economy enter its sixth consecutive
year of expansion and that there is now growing concern regarding a
forthcoming turn in the business cycle and, above all, that the
adjustment of the present imbalances at the international level, given
the lack of any appropriate corrective interventions, may take the
form of a hard landing. The persistence of the US trade deficit shows
that even though the marked devaluation of the dollar has led to a
considerable recovery of US exports, it does not provide a sufficient
stimulus for the necessary rebalancing. To this, one has to add that
even if the trade deficit were to be cut back at a more rapid pace in the
near future than is the case today, there would still remain the
problem of the current deficit, which now also has to sustain the
burden of the foreign debt. Morgan Guaranty Trust evaluations
suggest that the near future may bring the problem of financing the
US deficit: even if the external debt could be kept below 1000 billion
dollars, it would still be necessary to find at least 500 billion dollars to
finance the accumulated current deficit. This, quite obviously, places
even greater emphasis on the problem of the proper level of the dollar
exchange rate that would create confidence in the tendential stability
of the US currency and thus make it possible to finance the deficit and
to achieve international adjustment with a soft landing. In this
connection it has to be recalled that, according to the same source, if
priority between now and 1995 were to be given to stabilizing the
value of the dollar, maintaining the growth rate of the economy
around 2.4%, the current deficit would increase to 435 billion dollars
and the foreign debt to 2500 billion; but if — given the same growth
rate of GNP — the dollar were to depreciate by 14% in real terms, the
deficit would reduce to 75 billion dollars and the foreign debt to 1200.
Since the first hypothesis seems highly improbable, not least because
2500 billion dollars represent one third of the US gross product and
would therefore raise a problem of debt sustainability long before this
point is actually reached, there remains the other hypothesis, or
others of a similar kind, though all of these necessarily presuppose
that Japan and Europe would be prepared to accept the appreciation
of their currencies and to adopt vigorous measures to sustain their
home demand.

International Economic Interdependence etc. 119
2. - The US Deficit
and International Economic Adjustment
When the phenomenon first presented itself, the magnitude and the
speed of the changes in the exchange rates had caused a great deal of
concern regarding a possible Japanese recession as inflation in the
United States accelerated. Though these problems did not arise in actual
practice, there can be no doubt that the trading imbalance between
Japan and the United States increased in nominal terms in 1986 and
1987 and diminished only slightly in 1988. The phenomenon is explained
in many different ways: there are those who hold that even though the
system of flexible exchange rates has absolved many important tasks in
the adjustment process, it has thereby revealed its limited effectiveness,
while others say that the markets bring about appropriate adjustments in
time and do not need any specific measures to correct their natural
evolution. On the other hand, it has been pointed out that depreciation
of the dollar can reduce the external deficit only if the US were to adopt
restrictive policies designed to cut down domestic expenditure. Unfor-
tunately, the 1987 reduction of the fiscal deficit, which amounted to
about 70 billion dollars, was almost wholly compensated by the greater
consumption propensity that occurred during this period. World trade
grew by 9% in 1988, following an 8% increase achieved in 1987. This
particularly favourable trend was not utilized by the US economy,
probably because home demand was so strong as to absorb its entire
productive capacity. If this is true, one would hardly be justified in
complaining that changes in the exchange rate are insufficiently
effective. At the same time, however, one must bear in mind that the
situation of full capacity exploitation attained by the US economy
induced a restrictive monetary policy from the beginning of 1988
onwards in order to forestall a possible acceleration in the inflation.rate.
This policy was undoubtedly effective in containing inflationary tensions,
but it certainly also contributed to increasing the dollar exchange rate via
the upturn in the short-term interest rates that accompanies it.
There can be no doubt that a strong dollar is hardly the medicine
required to adjust the present imbalances. According to some recent
calculations (Dornbusch [4]), the dollar would have to undergo a
further 30% devaluation in order to permit an adjustment of the US

120 Luigi Paganetto
trade balance and a soft landing of the international economy on its
way to a new balance. Ever since the Plaza Hotel agreements, indeed,
the principal features of economic policy have been to accompany the
devaluation of the dollar with an expansion of domestic demand in the
economies enjoying a surplus and a reduction of the budget deficit in
the United States.
Japan’s external surplus is often seen as a cause of trade conflicts
and requests for protectionist measures. According to the data of the
Japanese planning agency, total Japanese imports during the first
three months of 1989 were as much as 51% above the average for
1985, while exports had increased only by 10%.
Bearing in mind that in real terms Japanese exports diminished
by 3.9% of GNP between 1985 and 1988, Japan would clearly seem to
have changed its growth model, passing from growth based on
exports to growth stimulated by home demand. In nominal terms, of
course, the trade surplus remains of the order of 80 billion dollars
because the dollar price of Japanese exports increased by as much as
52% between 1985 and 1989. This phenomenon represents the conse-
quence of the revaluation of the yen vis-a-vis the dollar, which
amounted to 100% in the period under consideration.
If we now look at this phenomenon from point of view of the
apparent incapacity of dollar devaluation to throttle imports to the
United States, one can readily find some important explanatory
features. Data are now available (Bhagwati [1]) in support of the idea
that a gradually increasing share of US imports has been covered by
voluntary export restriction (VER) and other non-tariff barriers
(NTB). Bhagwati’s data show that, in 1986, 37% of the imports from
Japan, 20% of the trade with Greece and Spain and 17% of the
imports from Korea were affected by VER practices. If these figures
are correct, we are here concerned with an important phenomenon
that is not to be ignored. :
The downturn in US domestic prices has been compensated by
the scarcity effect imposed by practices bound up with the non tariff
barriers, thus avoiding the price change that would have been
required for adjustment. When the dollar began to appreciate in the
eighties, these non tariff practices compensated the effects that the
exchange rate should have had on US imports. Following the Plaza

the world, there can be no doubt that the expansion has led to a

by a high growth rate and substantial profit margins, and the slow-
growth sectors with only marginal productivity increases. This has
had repercussions also in the export flows, creating lines of strength
and weakness that have not always been in line with the ups and

dollar has produced highly diversified adjustments in the US trade

3. - Fiscal Policies and Trade Balance Trends
The underlying theoretical question is whether and to what
extent the national fiscal policies exert an influence on the interna-
tional capital market. According to one interpretation of the economic
events of the eighties (Feldstein [5]), the origin of the imbalances is to
be sought in the US budget deficit.
This view is based on the idea that the fiscal expansion that
occurred in the USA during the eighties has led to an upturn in the
growth rate of the US economy, an increase in the long-term real
interest rates, and an appreciation of the dollar; the latter, in its turn,
has brought about a worsening in the current part of the balance of
payments.
The macroeconomic logic of this line of argument lies in the fact
that if a budget deficit is not balanced by an increase in private
savings, there must necessarily be an excess of investments over
savings and this, in turn, provokes an upturn in the real interest rate.
The increase in the real interest rate attracts capital from abroad and,
consequently, tends to push up the real exchange rate. In the presence
of a growth rate of the US economy above that of the rest of the
world, therefore, imports will tend to increase and exports will
diminish, thus creating a deficit in the current balance of payments
that is balanced by the inflow of capital attracted'by the high rates of
interest. What causes one to cast doubt on this interpretation is the
fact that even though the dollar exchange rate has been diminishing

accompanied the steep appreciation of the dollar in the years pre-
ceding 1985. The authors further claim that two thirds of the effects
on the external deficit of the excessive GNP growth and the revalu-
ation of the dollar are explained by the mix of expansive fiscal policy
and restrictive monetary policy adopted by the United States, which
has to be seen in combination with the fiscal contraction that occurred
in the other industrialized countries during the same period. The
remaining effects are said to be attributable to the problem of the
foreign debt of the developing countries and the agricultural policy
adopted in the United States. The persistence of the deficit almost four
years after the commencement of the dollar’s decline from its pre-
vious peak finds an explanation — at the microeconomic level — in
the previously mentioned change in the behaviour of exporters in
fixing their prices for the US market.
If one further bears in mind that the persistence of the deficit may
also be due to normal adjustment lags (including J-curve effects), that
US export prices have not yet felt the full effects of recent exchange
rate movements and that the capacity of foreign exporters to
compress their profit margins seems close to its limit, at least in some
sectors, one will incline to agree with the prevalent opinion that
deems the process of balancing the US budget deficit to have already
been got under way.
It is an equally widespread conviction that, even though the
external deficit of the United States will diminish during the next year
or two, it will certainly not disappear completely; indeed, it is likely to
remain at a rather high level between now and 1991 (Bryant [3]).
In this general perspective, then, the problem becomes that of
asking oneself whether the external debt can coexist with the present
exchange rate and yet ensure an acceptable growth rate for the US
economy. Rather than from a valuation of the various available
forecasting scenarios, an answer to this question may be provided by a
reflection about the adjustment mechanisms and, more particularly,
about the interaction of the variables that come into play in these
mechanisms.
The most important point to be examined concerns the impact of
fiscal policy on the current part of the balance of payments. According
to a rather widespread view, the budget deficit plays a direct part in

International Economic Interdependence etc. 127
prices of consumer goods will increase relative to the prices of
investment goods and this will lead to a demand for higher negotiated
wage rates, which — in their turn — will exert a negative effect on
output and employment.
In parallel with this, the firms operating in the customer markets
will take competitive advantage of the depreciation of the exchange
rate to obtain higher earnings than before, but to this end they will
increase their mark-ups rather than their market shares. And this,
again, will reduce both output and employment in Europe.
If one now thinks of the effects of a fiscal stimulus in this
situation, one can find some theoretical justification for the reluctance
shown by the European countries as regards the adoption of a an
expansive tax policy.
As the model shows, .in fact, only if this fiscal stimulus were to
become transformed into increased expenditure in the investment
goods sector, and this both through government subsidies for private
investments and the direct purchase of investment goods by the
public, would there be a positive effect in Europe in terms of income
and employment.
Moreover, the magnitude of the fiscal expansion asked of Europe
would not seem to be compatible with an increase of expenditure
aimed exclusively at the capital goods sector and it cannot therefore
be taken for granted that the interests of Europe coincide with those
of the rest of the world.
This difference of interest also comes to the fore in other
approaches that consider further aspects of the interdependence of
the various world areas. For example, if one assumes that a substan-
tial element of asymmetry to be constituted by the tendential rigidity
of nominal wages in the USA and the rigidity of real wages in Europe,
one can indeed highlight the advantages of coordinating economic
policies, but the analysis will also show that these advantages are
bound up with the adoption of an expansive monetary policy in the
USA to accompany the fiscal expansion in Europe (Van der Ploeg
[10]).
In fact, an expansive monetary policy will tend to increase
nominal interest rates, diminish real money demand, push up the US
price level, and erode real wages in the United States, thus increasing

| and  Capital              | Movement  |       |        |     |
A very  general  proposition  of the  pure  theory  of trade  concerns
the potential  gains that international  trade by itself,  merely extending
the  possibilities  of transformation  of commodities  into  one  another,
causes  to the welfare of any single country as well as of the world as a
whole.
It has been  demonstrated,  in particular,  partially  in two  classical
articles by Samuelson  [21],  [22] and in a complete way in a paper by
Kemp and Wan  [12], that free trade  is a status  that imposes,  broadly
speaking,  less  restrictive  constraints  on  the  world  welfare  maximi-
zation  process.  It  is,  therefore,  the  authors  claim,  by  a  simple
application  of the  LeChatelier  principle,  potentially  more  beneficial
| than  the  more  | constrained  | situation  | of no  trade.  |     |
| ---------------- | ------------ | ---------- | -------------- | --- |
If we  introduce  distortions  like  tariffs,  taxes,  subsidies,  etc.,  the
solution  is not simple anymore  and presents second best connotations.
Besides,  since the effects of distortions  on the economy  depend on the
characteristics  of the economy  itself,  it is necessary  to make  explicit
assumptions  about  the technology,  the taste  structure,  the behavioral
functions,  etc.,  of the  countries  involved  in the  trade  relationship.
The model which is used mostly in the pure theory of trade and in
many  of its  empirical  applications  is the  so  called  Heckscher-Ohlin
model.  This  model,  based  on  drastic,  but  not  rejectable,  simplifi-

132 Pasquale Lucio Scandizzo
cations, translates the idea of comparative advantage into a simple
mathematical structure and provides a theoretical framework suitable
for analyzing relatively complicated problems of international trade.
In particular the model has proved to be manageable and fruitful
for welfare analysis of alternative trade situations with respect to
second best conditions and for the analysis of the implications of these
for the distribution of the gains from the trade.
Certain hypotheses of the model, however, were formulated in
the very early stages of development of trade theory and proved to be
not only unrealistic but unnecessary to the basic structure and
simplicity of the model. One of these assumptions, probably the most
important, has been the assumption of complete and strict factor
immobility. That this assumption has been so firmly held approaches
paradox in that Ohlin himself stresses the importance of factor
movements: «the mobility of goods to some extent compensates for
the lack of interregional mobility of the factors (1). ... International
trade theory cannot be understood except in relation to and as a part
of general location theory, to which the lack of mobility of goods and
factors has equal relevance (2). The movement of goods to some
extent takes the place of factor movements (3)».
On the other hand, many descriptive, historical and empirical
treatments can be found which examine the implications of interna-
tional capital movements with regard to welfare consequences of
international trade. Many of these studies are based on unfashionable
Marxian ideas and stress the importance of unbalanced trade-invest-
ment relationships and unequal distribution of the gains from trade.
For example, Singer [26] claims that underdeveloped nations have
been secularly disadvantaged in their trading-cum investment rela-
tions with industrialized countries. The studies by Levin [14] on the
Peruvian economy, Frank [6] on Chile and Brazil, and the Magdoff
[16] and O’Connor [18] analyses of economic imperialism also
support the contention put forward by Singer.
The position of the pure theory of trade in this regard seems to

Other rationalizations  which  are  mainly found in the Marxist  and
neo-Marxist  literature  suggest  that  economic  growth  of  industrial
the
countries  is the  cause  of their  expansion  abroad.  The  first  and

134 Pasquale Lucio Scandizzo
main representative of these ideas is Rosa Luxembourg [15]: «The
capitalist nations are surrounded by primitive economies, each in-
sulated from others like a nut within its shell, waiting to be cracked.
The capitalists break open a primitive economy and enter into trade
with it, whether by enticing its inhabitants with commodities they
have never seen before, by political cunning or by brute force. Now
exports to primitives provide an outlet for the product of the last batch
of capital goods created at home. After a little while another nut is
broken, a use for more capital is thereby found, and so on, as long as
the supply of untouched primitive economies lasts...».
The idea of an exploitative relationship between lending and
borrowing countries has also received attention from some theorists
more in the neo-classical tradition, like Kindleberger [13]: «In discuss-
ing the performance of the Iraq Petroleum Company in Iraq, Edith
Penrose held that the Company had “exploited” the country because
it had earned a return higher than the minimum it would have been
willing to enter the industry for. But the use of so pejorative a word
runs the risk of confusing the analysis. The Iraq Petroleum Company,
like any direct investor, has an advantage to exploit-whether tech-
nology, outlets for oil, or access to large amounts of capital. Initially,
Iraq’s advantages are limited merely to sovereignty over oilbearing
sands. But this is a bilateral monopoly situation-the confrontation of a
monopolist with a monopolist, for which there is no determinant
solution...».
The discussion by Kindleberger is interesting in that it provides an
hypothesis for relating international investment-cum exploitation to a
concept of international market power stronger and richer in impli-
cation than the usual tariff and/or tax imposing monopoly of the pure
theory of trade.
In the following parts of this paper a particular specification of
this concept of monopolistic power will be used to try to incorporate
some of the arguments 1) and 4) into the measurement of the degree
of protectionism. The paper is divided into three further parts: (i) the
examination of a simple model of unequal partnership with monopoly
power and capital movement; (ii) the analysis of some measures that
might be adopted to capture the effects of both trade protection and
factor movement; (iii) some empirical results.

A Framework to Develop Measures etc. 135
2. - A Simple Model of Trade
and Capital Movement
Assume a two country, two good, two factor international trade
model with the usual assumption of identical production functions
which are homogeneous of degree one. The two countries each
produce goods X and Y, where Yi s labor intensive relative to X at any
relative factor price, and factor endowments are such as to éxclude
specialization.
In Graph 1 the curve Ty To is the production possibility frontier of
country A, the country which is well endowed with labour but poorly
endowed with capital relative to country B. Wo, W; and W, are
indifference curves of a well behaved index of social welfare. With
international factor mobility ruled out, the no-trade point is P while
with free trade country A exports PR of good Y and imports RS of
good X.
Assume that a tariff is imposed by country A and that capital is
allowed to move internationally. Then, as Mundell [17] has shown,
capital will flow from B to A, at least up to the point at which country
A can produce enough X and Y with the capital from country B to
consume the same bundle of goods consumed under free trade and at
the same time make the required payment on the capital from country
B.
This point in Graph 1 is represented by P’; S is the consumption
point under trade, T* T* is the equilibrium expanded production
possibility frontier; and Y° X° and Y* X* represent the identically
sloped price lines (4) of the free trade and the no trade situations with
capital movement (5). SP’ is equal in value to the marginal product of
the capital inflow. In fact, PP’ is the change in output associated with
the increase in capital; the output of X increases by RS, but the output
of Y decreases by PR’. The marginal product of the capital inflow is
equal in value to RS minus PR’ which, in terms of Y, is P’S. P’Sis a
form of economic surplus: it corresponds, mutatis mutandis, to the

L’INTERNATIONAL TRADE AND CAPITAL MOVEMENTS
(6) Since the prices before and after the expansion stay constant, the compensating

A Framework to Develop Measures etc. 137
Consider now the segment S* V. This segment is also a form of
economic surplus and corresponds to the distance betwen the free
trade and the no trade indifference curves under the assumption
that the country is constrained to buy the free trade quantity of
good X. SV is, in the Hicksian terminology, an equivalent variation
and is a measure (one of the four possible) of the gain from trade
of country A.
Two of the crucial assumptions needed to obtain the results that
international factor movement and product trade are perfect sub-
stitutes are that: (i)) country A is “small” both before and after the
growth induced by foreign capital, so that no adverse effects occur on
its terms of trade and, (ii) the domestic capital markets are undistor-
ted, so that the imported capital is efficiently used.
Because most of the LDC’s, who borrowed heavily in the 70s are
exporters of primary commodities, condition (i) is likely not to hold in
many of the recent more relevant cases. Condition (ii), on the other
hand also appears unlikely in practice due to the general conditions of
the LDC: factor markets. With conditions (i) and (ii) failing we may
thus witness a peculiar case of immiserizing trade.
Since country A borrows against the promise of future returns,
the ex ante loan proceeds are fixed at the ex ante value of marginal
product of capital. As these proceeds have to be paid by expanding
sales of A’s export goods, however, terms of trade will turn against A.
Furthermore, because of the inefficiencies encountered in the market,
growth will be lower than expected. In this case, therefore proceeds
due on the loan will be larger than the ex post value of marginal
product of capital.
A strategy of import substitution may thus appear very attrac-
tive to a developing country, since by restricting trade it seems to
achieve three desirable results at once: (i) protect infant industries,
(ii) improve the country’s terms of trade on the market of primary
exports and, (iii) attract foreign capital into the country. As many
LDC’s are experiencing today, however, this policy may carry the
sting of time inconsistency. In time, the borrower may find the very
effort to repay the loan self-defeating, as terms of trade (and
interest rates) may respond in a way that greatly increases its
burden.

138 Pasquale Lucio Scandizzo
3. - Measure of Protectionism
In spite of their importance for the current debate on interna-
tional economics, empirical measurements of protectionism are not
abundant, mostly out of date and with very limited practical coverage.
In addition to the data problem, the reason for this is to be seen in the
elusive nature of the concept of protection and the difficulty to
maintain naive forms of measurement in the face of the development
of trade and global markets for goods and factors.
The theoretical foundation of the concept of protectionism lies in
the pure theory of trade, and specially in its two-good version. In this
simple paradigm, in fact a domestic industry producing an importable
is said to be protected if the importation of the competing foreign
good is penalized by an import duty or restricted by a quota.
Conversely, a domestic industry producing an exportable is said to be
taxed if its proceeds are curtailed and its sales discouraged by an
export tax or restricted by licencing or other types of administrative
controls and constraints. Because exchange rates are assumed to be
constant and money absent, in such a model an import tariff is
equivalent to an export tax, to an overvalued exchange rate or to a
combination of the two. It follows that if trade is restricted in any
way, the domestic production of importables is protected and the
domestic production of exportables is necessarily, and symmetrically
“anti-protected”’.
The simplicity of this conclusion, however, is lost as soon as one
tries to cast the problem in a more realistic manner. In the first place,
in fact, importables are more that one, so that a restriction placed
upon the trade of one of them may in fact harm the domestic
industries producing the other. Second, non-tradeable goods, while
favored coeteris paribus, may be favored or disfavored by trade
restrictions depending on the relationships of substitution or comple-
mentarity with importables. Third, factor prices may change and
factors may move, internationally in response to trade impediments.
Fourth, if exchange rates are allowed to float, a devaluation may also
result. Finally, any attempt at creating privileges through market
intervention will inevitably result in a sequence of efforts to extent
these privileges to other sectors, to remove them or to counterbalance

A Framework to Develop Measures etc. 139
them with subsidies, taxes or transfers of various sorts. Thus, the end
result of any market intervention cannot be predicted on a priori
grounds and can only be measured on the basis of what has effectively
taken place after the economic system has reacted to the intervention
from outside.
As explained in the previous section of this paper, an additional
complicating circumstance has been created by the integration of
international capital markets and the increasing interdependence
created by economic growth and diversified trade. Because of such
interdependence, which is especially spurred by the drive to global
markets for capital and labor, protectionism is becoming an increas-
ingly hazy concept. If factor markets are integrated, in fact, and
progressively out of reach of domestic policies, protectionist measures
are liable to generate effects both within and outside the national
boundaries even in the absence of retaliation. Also, monopolistic
power in the factor markets is likely to be the key condition to
interfere succesfully with market forces, since all other efforts are
likely to be at least partially frustrated by countervailing factor
movements.
The indicators currently used to measure the degree of commer-
cial protection may thus be severely biased, because they do not take
into account two concurrent phenomena: (i) the substitution of
product trade with factor trade in presence of trade distortions and,
(ii) the increased interdependence that (i) causes between the trading
countries. In this context, the so called “globalization” of markets is
also a phenomenon that concerns primarily factor movement, which
in itself is much more capable than product trade to unify the markets
of different countries and create multiple reciprocal obligations.
How can we take into account these phenomena? Indicators of
protection can be classified according to whether they measures “ex
ante” specific commercial interventions (tariffs, taxes, etc.) or “ex
post” differences between prices, output and real incomes induced by
the interventions. Focusing on these “ex post” measures, the general
definition of the degree of protection is:

Table  1 shows how the most common  measures  of protectionism
rely generally on the mechanism  of expression  (/) and do not take into
account  at  all  either  interdependence  or  factor  movement.  Even

|     | A Framework  | to Develop Measures  |     | etc.  | 141  |
| --- | ------------ | -------------------- | --- | ----- | ---- |
“overall”  measures  of divergence  between  prices  with  and  without
protection,  such  as  the  SCF and  the  CCF,  do not  consider  at all the
possibility  that  countervailing  capital  and/or  labor  movements  may
make  a difference.
The  key problem  that  factor  movement  poses  to the  concept  of
protection is that the country responsible for the trade restriction finds
itself “extended”  over  the rest  of the world because  of the relocation
outside  of its boundaries  of some  of its factors.  Alternatively,  it may
find that parts of its economy  are  being “taken  over”  by factors  that
have  moved  in from  the rest  of the world.  From  the point of view  of
the individual  country,  therefore,  it is no longer sufficient  to compare
economic  statistics with and without the trade restriction,  unless these
statistics  are  made  inclusive  of the effects on  factor relocation  abroad
and purged  of the effects  of the location  of foreign  factors  at home.
In order  to deal  with  these  problems,  we  can  still  apply  expres-
sion  (/), but we  find that we  cannot  use  any of the measures  in Table
1, since  none  of them  takes into account  the change in the economic
availability  of factors  of production  that  occurs  as  a consequence  of
their  relocation  at  home  and  abroad.  However,  if the  factors  of
production  are traded,  they can be considered  tantamount  to interme-
diate  inputs  and as  such  included  in the calculation  of the protection
index.
Because  of  international  factor  movement,  therefore,  we  can
define  a  protection  index  as  the  ratio  of two  magnitudes  that  will
progressively  converge  to two proper cost-benefit  concepts (Scandizzo
and  Bruce,  [23]):  (i) net  private  benefit  (NPB)  and,  (ii) net  social
benefit  (NSB):

problems and they will therefore seek to obtain loans to meet payment
commitments. Trade imbalances, therefore, may be seen as the other
side of the coin of international financial relations.
In an international economy the ultimate source of finance is
represented by exports. Insofar as the growth process produces
negative net exports international credit will be demanded. A country
will — in general — be willing to pursue a debt financed expansionary
policy if today’s negative net exports will be financed by positive net
exports tomorrow. If the development mechanism is successful and
well monitored loans will be transformed into profitable activities
(investments) which will generate enough profits (met exports) to
repay initial debt. Given the terms of trade and the degree of
protection, we may assume that exports depend on foreign demand
and domestic capacity (and hence on domestic investment) while
payment commitments depend — for a given outstanding debt — on
the level of the interest rate. For our purposes it is sufficient to
consider that, for the system as a whole, the level of world demand
depends on the policies pursued in the North, i.e. we can assume
away the hypothesis that the South can take up the role of the engine
of growth for the system. In order to describe the build-up of financial
fragility in the North-South system we will assume, for the moment,
that the level of world demand is exogenously given.
For a given level of world demand and of the world interest rate
each country in the South will set a rate of growth of investment (3)
which will eventually lead to a balance of trade deficit. For a given
rate of world demand the rate of growth of exports will increase with
domestic accumulation which relaxes supply constraints. If the
country is successful in its export growth process it will be easier for it
to obtain international credit as its creditworthiness will increase.
Credit availability will enhance the country’s investment opportunities
and export capacity starting a virtuous circle.
This situation may change the attitude of countries and banks in
the sense of increasing the euphoria of both. The success of the
growth process will encourage countries to borrow more and banks to

model.

152 Pier Carlo Padoan
lend more (4). Countries will borrow to finance trade deficits and
interest payments while banks will de facto finance medium and long
term investment while having to face short term deposit servicing on
the liability side. An orderly development of such a process i.e. a
situation in which the system neither slips into recession nor explodes
into uncontrolled euphoria — rests on the fulfillment of two crucial
conditions: the existence of a high and stable effective demand to
provide outlets for the indebted countries and what may be called a
source of “ultimate liquidity” to prevent the system from slipping into
situations of financial distress (5). In this respect these two macro-
economic conditions represent the public goods which are necessary
for an orderly functioning of the system (6). In a closed economy such
public goods are provided by the national government and monetary
authorities. In an international system, where no supranational
government exists, the production of these public goods depends on
the interaction of national policies, that is, on the organization of
international regimes (Kindleberger [28]).
International regimes have been defined as the set of norms rules
and institutions wich govern the behaviour of an international system
(Krasner [29]). Regimes are needed for the correct functioning of all
economic relations in the international system. A trade regime is also
a public good, while a custom union is more similar to a club good as
it contemplates the possibility of exclusion (Kindleberger [26]). What-
ever the case, rules must, and have been, set up to enforce interna-
tional trade regimes (Lipson [35], Keohane [24]). We may also speak
of an international macroeconomic regime as the way in which
international effective demand is generated and to what extent (7).
Two kinds of international regimes may be considered for our
purposes, hegemonic regimes and multipolar (or oligopolistic)
regimes (Krasner [29], Keohana [23], Oye [39]).
In an hegemonic system, such as the one prevailing in the «long

decade» after World War II, the necessary and sufficient condition for
the provision of public goods is the existence of an hegemon, i.e. a
country whose economic and political power is large enough as to
allow the unilateral production of public goods in spite of free riding
policies pursued by other countries (8). The hegemon will act as the
“residual country” whose expansion ultimately allows the expansion
of the system as a whole by easing the international constraints to
growth (9). ‘
In a situation of multilateralism the conditions for the production
of international public goods are more complex — they will be
mentioned later — and require an increase in international cooper-
ation i.e. an agreement among the larger countries in the system (10).
An hegemonic system will resist as long as the hegemon will possess
enough economic power to exert international leadership. The defini-
tion of economic and financial power rises a complex and debated
issue and we will not consider it here at any depth (11). For our
purposes it is sufficient to establish some links among the international
financial position of a country and its ability to generate international
effective demand and to provide “ultimate liquidity”. The provision of
ultimate liquidity requires a series of conditions such as the esistence
of an international banking system supported by efficient lender-of-
last-resort facilities and international creditworthiness for the cur-
rency which denominates debt. A reserve currency country is interna-
tionally creditworthy (Minsky [38]) as long as it generates profits in
the international economy, that is its trade balance is in surplus. This
will assure international creditors that debt servicing will be guaran-
teed. If a country is creditworthy it is in a position to pursue
expansionary policies financed by its own currency. In the Bretton
Woods hegemonic system the US was in the position to act as
international source of effective demand, to issue the world’s cur-

rency, and to act as the base of the international financial system
succesfully as long as the US trade balance was in surplus (and as it
held a creditor position vis-a-vis the rest of the world). No wonder that
when the system was ufficially buried, in 1971, the trade balance had
turned into deficit for the first time after decades. The hegemonic
system, in addition, witnessed the expansion of a largely US based
international private banking system. In such a system the production
of the public good of financial stability was the main responsbility of
the US monetary authorities.
3. - From Declining Hegemony to Multilateralism
The Latin American debt crisis has developed in a period of
rapidly declining US hegemony. The foreign debt of Latin American
countries, as well as of many other Southern economies, has
developed in an international environment which favoured a process
of debt accumulation along the lines sketched in the previous Section.
Particularly easy monetary conditions prevailed in international
financial markets, reflecting easy monetary policy in the .centre
economy. Banks were eager to push loans onto what seemed an
extremely favourable business, lending to rapidly growing developing
countries.
More critical, however, were the conditions in which interna-
tional effective demand was generated. The breakdown of the Bretton
Woods system had shown that the US was no longer in the position to
provide unilaterally the public good of growth to the international
system for reasonably long periods of time. In the absence of close
coordination among the major industrialized countries US expan-
sionary policies would lead to a rapid deterioration of both her trade
balance and of the international position of the dollar. These two
facts, in turn, weakened the position of the US based international
banking system. The generation of a stable and sustained rate of
growth of demand required a new macroeconomic regime based on
multilateralism.
At the end of the seventies, at the Bonn summit, the declining
hegemon and the emerging powers, Germany and Japan, seemed to

North-North and North-South Debt etc. 155
have reached an agreement in the management of the world economy
(Putnam and Bayne [43]). This illusion soon broke down leading to
the drastic change in US policies both in the monetary stance (1979
Volcker shock) and in the fiscal stance (Reaganomics).
The consequences of this drastic change for the indebted coun-
tries were dramatic to say the least, (Sachs [46]). The international
environment become increasingly restrictive. Interest rates soared to
historic levels in real terms. Also as a consequence of the second oil
shock the world economy plunged into recession. The public good of
effective demand was no longer there to sustain a process of indebted
growth. The rise in interest rates had turned even the most conserva-
tive financial positions into prebankruptcy finances.
The provision of the public good of effective demand was made
more difficult also because the hegemonic regime had collapsed into a
multilateral system which did not meet the conditions for cooperation
without hegemony (Dye [39]). In this respect the debt crisis which
exploded in 1982 was the combination of international financial
instability mechanisms and an international regime not strong enough
to sustain them.
The declining hegemon, however, has produced a final effort to
provide the public goods necessary for the functioning of a financially
complex system. After the breakout of the crisis US monetary
authorities heavily intervened to avoid financial collapse by sustaining
the US banking system in heavy trouble due to exposure vis-a-vis the
Latin American countries. The recovery of the US economy, sustained
by an expansionary fiscal policy, later provided some relief to the
indebted countries. The global collapse which the world had feared
for so many months had been avoided (12).
Of course the management of the debt crisis was, and is much
more complex than what has been so rapidly suggested. It must be
recalled, among other things, the role provided by official institutions
such as the IMF in organizing the management of the crisis and
intermediating between indebted countries and the creditors (Padoan
[40]).
(12) An analysis of the management of the Latin American Debt crisis can be found
in PADOAN [40], [42].

The  “solution”  to the  debt  crisis  marked  once  again  the  impor-
tance  of leadership  in the  production  of international  public  goods.
The  new  event  which  has  come  to  general  attention  only  very
recently,  is that  the  new  act  of hegemony  represented  by the  US
unilateral  expansion  in  the  mid  80’s  has  further  deteriorated  US
financial  power  up to a point which  some  consider  of no  return  (13).
The  expansionary  policies  pursued  by the  US  administration  have
generated  a trade  deficit,  enhanced  by the massive  dollar  revaluation
of  1983-85,  which  have  produced  an  unprecedented  debt  accumul-
ation  (Gomel  [15]). The peculiarity  of this event  does not lie so much
in the total amount  of debt (or in the debt to income  ratio) but in the
fact  that  the  world’s  former  hegemon  has  turned  into  the  world’s
largest  debtor  and  that,  at  the  present  stage,  it is not  at  all  clear
whether  and  for how  long this  position  will  be sustainable,  to put it
differently  the  “management”  of  the  North-South  debt  crisis  has
produced a new North-North  debt crisis which is now closely linked to
the  former.
The position of the US as a debtor  reflects,  almost  symmetrically,
Japan’s  position  as  a world  debtor.  To stretch  things a little,  but not
much,  it is convenient  to say that Japan’s credit is US’s debt (14).  Let

nations, US and Japan (Bergsten and Cline [7]) (14). From the point
of view of the production of public goods the situation is now more
complex. After the transition to multilateralism the generation of
ultimate demand and of ultimate liquidity do not lie with the same
actor any more. While the United States still represents the most
important source of effective demand for the world market it is not in
the position to supply the public good of ultimate liquidity. This role is
rapidly being taken up by Japan. ‘
Such a statement would need a thorough documentation which is
beyond the scope and possibilities of this essay. So, only a few
arguments can be advanced. A support to the first point is implicit in
the facts which have been recalled above. A temporary relief to the
1982 debt crisis has come from the expansion of the US domestic
market. A similar relief could have not come from the Japanese
economy for both policy and structural reasons. Untill very recently
Japan’s economic policy stance has followed what might be termed a
form of “neomercantilism” by sustaining external competitiveness
and restraining the expansion of the domestic market. This has been
achieved both by tight fiscal policies and by a wide array of non tariff
protection measures, in the presence of a relatively high propensity to
save (15). Partly as a consequence of external pressures, arising
mostly from he US, this policy stance is being changed. Fiscal policy
has become more expansionary and promises have been made to
lower the explicit and less explicit barriers to domestic market
penetration. For the purpose of this paper, however, what matters is
that the capacity of Japan to act as a market for exports of indebted
countries may, until now at least, be defined as irrelevant.
The second element is more complex. As we have seen above the
supply of ultimate liquidity requires a number of conditions; the
existence of a widespread financial system supported by lender-of-last-
resort facilities, international creditworthiness of the currency, itself
based on a sound balance of payments position, as well as a sound
asset position. The financial system involved in Latin American debt is
still largely US based and lender-of-last-resort responsibilitis still lie

with US monetary authorities. The Japanese banking system, how-
ever, has been expanding internationally quite rapidly in the recent
past (Iwami [22]) while the Japanese financial system is undergoing
an extremely fast expansion and opening process (16). The Japanese
banking system, on the other hand, is only partially involved in direct
debt financing and, what is more important, the dollar, and not the
yen, is by far he leading international currency, denominating Latin
American debt as well as other international transactions.
However the dollar is issued by a country whese international
creditworthiness is greatly undermined both in flow terms (trade
deficit) and in stock terms. In other words, what is in question is the
long run sustainability of the US external debt (Gomel [15], Krugman
[33]).
As long as the international financial system is dollar based — and
we may assume that this state of affairs will prevail for several years to
come — ultimate liquidity must be provided in dollars. However the
soundness of this system itself depends on the willingness of other
countries, and of Japan in the first place, to provide credit to the US
(17).
The management of international debt today must, therefore,
face a double problem. Latin American countries are tied as debtors to
the US, while the latter is itself tied as a debtor to other countries, and
to Japan in the first place.
4. - Overlapping and Simultaneous Games
in the International System
Game theory has become extremely fashionable among econo-
mists. Its usefulness lies in the fact that is clarifies the interconnections
between the actors involved in complex interdependencies as is the
case of the problem under discussion. In what follows we will not try
(16) On the expansion of the Japanese financial system see e.g. SAKAKIBARA - NAGAO
[47], Iwai [22].
(17) US creditors face a currency risk rather than a country (or default) risk, see
GomEL [15].

North-North and North-South Debt etc. 159
to formalize it, rather we will use some concepts derived from game
theory to try to clarify the issues.
Several authors have addressed the debt problem in game
theoretic terms (18). In its simplest forms a game is set up between
the borrower and the lender. Players have the possibilities to defect or
to cooperate. For our purposes we may assume that lender here
means the country which provides both markets to debtors’ exports
and ultimate liquidity. For the borrower defection means debt repudi-
ation and cooperation means adjustment in the attempt to meet debt
service commitments. For the lender defection means refusal to
provide further liquidity and/or expansionary policies, and hence
imports and lower interest rates, while cooperation means the oppo-
site.
The financial picture presented in the previous paragraph may be
described in terms of overlapping games. Overlapping games arise (Alt
and Eichengree [2]) when the same game is played simultaneously by
one player vis-a-vis two different other players on the same issue. In
our case the US are simultaneously involved in a debt game with the
Latin American countries and with Japan. These two games, in
addition, are linked in the sense that the solution to one influences the
solution to the other.
Let us consider the US-Latin American debt game. If both
countries defect by, respectively, defaulting and not providing
additional liquidity, lower interest rates and larger markets the situ-
ation collapses into a debt crisis. If both cooperate the debt game can
continue and the conditions for the sound performance of a financial
system recalled in Section 2 are met. In a «sound» hegemonic regime
the system will function even in the absence of explicit cooperation on
the part of the debtor as both effective demand and ultimate liquidity
will be provided unilaterally by the lender-hegemon, while the debtor
may, and probably will, act as a free rider by meeting less than fully its
financial commitments, unless an efficient system of punishment can
be set up (Cohen [9]). This solution, as we have seen, is partially
possible in a situation of declining hegemony. In such a case, how-
ever, the exercise of hegemony will ultimately destroy the bases upon
(18) See e.g. KRUGMAN [31], COHEN [9], BuLOw - RoGorF [8].

160 Pier Carlo Padoan
which the system rests by further deteriorating the internationl
creditworthiness of the hegemon.
This brings in the game etween US and Japan. Here the issue at
stake is the maintenance of a dollar based financial system as a way to
provide ultimate liquidity, i.e. the sustainability of US debt in the long
run. The borrower (the US) may chose to defect by not adjusting her
economy, in particular not adjusting her trade deficit, or it may
cooperate by trying to turn her external deficit into a surplus in order
to meet her prospective debt service commitments and/or maintain a
level of the interest rate high enough to assure sustainability of debt
(Krugman [33]). The lender, in turn may choose to defect by stopping
to finance the US debt or to cooperate by continuing to do so. Note
that “adjustment” by the US here cannot mean an adjustment of the
trade deficit mostly or only through a substantive dollar depreciation
in the absence of the appropriate interest differential, as this will
endanger and ultimately destroy the value of the assets in the hands of
the lender and, probably, obtain a result that is opposite to the one
required, that is, the defence of a dollar based financial system. As we
mentioned above this implies that the creditors of the US face a
«currency» risk, i.e. the risk associated with a dollar denominated
debt (19). Adjustment by the US, then, requires — for a given level of
protection generation of trade surpluses by means of restrictive
policies in conjunction with an interest rate policy that is consistent
with the rate of dollar depreciation needed to support the effect of
demand cut on the trade balance. If both players cooperate the dollar
based system will survive, otherwise it will collapse. Note also that
cooperation is needed since we are not (yet?) in a situation of
Japanese hegemony, which would allow for the possibility of un-
ilateral provision of the public good of financial stability. In such a
case the Japanese economy would be ready to absorb US net exports
in an amount large enough to allow for a trade surplus to appear in
US trade balance.
It is easy to see that the solutions to the two games interfere with
(19) The amount of how much dollar devalutions needed to adjust the US trade
deficit remains an open question which is made more problematic if one takes into
account “hysteresis” effects, see BALDWIN and KRUGMAN [4], KRUGMAN [33].

North-North and North-South Debt etc. 161
each other. Cooperation in the second game requires a restrictive
policy in the US, to sustain the dollar denominated debt, which means
defection in the first game. If the US wishes to require creditworth-
iness vis-a-vis her major creditor she must pursue adjustment policies
which will mean restriction of her domestic market for Latin
American exports, as well as higher interest rates and heavier debt
service requirements for the South. This will be perceived by the
indebted countries as defection in their game to which they will
retaliate by repudiating their debt. In such a case the international
financial position of the US will deteriorate forther, as the value of her
international assets will shrink even further (20), thus making the
solution in the second game even more difficult to achieve.
On the other hand suppose that the US decides to cooperate in
the first game by keeping an expansionary course and low interest
rates. This will avoid defection by Latin American countries but it will
trigger retaliation by Japan as this will mean larger US indebtedness
and higher currency risk.
What are the solutions to this situation? Two general ways out
may be envisaged. One is overall cooperation and the other is the
introduction of simultaneous games in the picture.
Overall cooperation must be understood in different terms than
the ones sketched here. In the very simple terms of our example
cooperation in one game triggers defection in the other. This derives
from the fact that we are assuming implicitly one period static game
situations. Players have but one choice to make.
A different perspective arises if one considers the suggestions
artsing from the theory of cooperation “under anarchy” i.e. cooper-
ation without hegemony (Oye [39]; Axelrod and Keohane [3]). These
conditions, which may also be expressed in game theoretic terms, are
the following: a) players must take a “long shadow of the future”, i.e.
they must be involved in repeated games as this will minimize the
advantages from defection; b) players must be prepared to alter the
structure of their preferences which implies a change of the pay-off
matrices and hence the possibility of defining superior cooperative
(20) The dramatic fall of the value of Latin American debt on secondary markets is
a clear sign of such a possibility.

162 Pier Carlo Padoan
solutions); c) the number of players must be minimized so as to avoid
free-riding effects. In addition the role of institutions, as providers of
informations, must be enhanced (Runge [45], Langlois [34]).
If these conditions prevail a cooperative solution can be found in
the two debt games through a substantial change in the game
structure. If actors recognize the simultaneous nature of the games
they are involved in (Alt and Eichengree [2]), i.e. if they take a global
and long term perspective, they will not try to defect. However, this
will not be enough if the terms of the games described above remain
the same. In particular, adjustment must not be understood in simple
macroeconomic terms, either to expand or to deflate, to lend or not to
lend, but in much deeper structural terms. It is not possible to give a
full account of the structural trasformations required. A few obvious
hints may be advanced, (Sachs [46]). Latin American countries must
adjust their economies so as to decrease their dependence on external
finance. The US must increase her structural competitiveness to
improve her trade performance without resorting to massive devalu-
ation. Japan must gradually but rapidly open her markets to foreign
goods. If these conditions are met then a cooperative solution may
gradually emerge without the risk of triggering a worldwide recession
and financial crisis. At the same time it would be possible to design
and develop a financial system in which the role of the dollar is
gradually diminished without producing destabilizing shocks. This
solution is probably the most desirable one, but it is also the most
difficult to implement and surely the one that requires a very long
time horizon (Cohen [9]).
Let us now turn to the other possible solution related to the
inroduction of simultaneous games. Simultaneous games are played
by the same two players over two (or more) different areas at the
same time. The problem here is to discuss whether the existence of
simultaneity increases the prospects for cooperation. It is commonly
held that simultaneity increases the chances of cooperation, however,
as Alt and Eichengreen [2] warn, this is not necessarily so. Players
engaged in simultaneous games may have incentives to defect on both
games rather than only on one, knowing that defection on only one
game will trigger retaliation by the other player on all games they are
involved in. However if they recognize the existence of linkages

cooperative solution in the simultaneous games played by US and
Japan allows for the production of the public goods of ultimate
liquidity and of ultimate demand to the world system. Albeit partially,
the hegemonic role played by te US alone in the seventies and early

bilateral monopoly will have taken the place of hegemony.
5 - Cooperation in Trade
Let us now discuss the characteristics of a trade game between
Japan and the US. The international trade regime is of course
organized around GATT (Lipson [35]). However, notwithstanding the
global nature of international trade agreements, which are based on
the clause of the most favoured nation, over the past decade the two
major trading economies. US and Japan, have often been involved in
what may be defined as a creeping bilateral trade conflict (Bergsten
and Cline [7]). The increasingly unfavourable trade position has led
the US administration to use in different occasions the threat to the
recourse of overt protectionistic practices to face what are being
considered “unfair trade practices” on the part of the Asian industrial
power. The recently approved trade bill, indeed, offers to the
American administration a powerful weapon. This state of affairs is
also the result of declining US hegemony which, although it has not
destroyed the public good of free trade, it has made also cooperation
in trade more difficult, (Lipson [35]; Keohane [23], [24]).
Two things should be made clear about this new situation. First,
protectionist policies are invoked as a reaction to turbulence and
imbalances arising from the macroeconomic sphere, in terms of
persistent payments disequilibria and prolonged exchange rate mis-
alignements. Secondly trade policy should be analyzed taking into
account the new (oligopolistic) forms of industrial organization and
non-price competition. Economists have long since recognized the
fact that protectionist pressures may arise from macroeconomic
disequilibria (Robinson [44], Balogh [5], Corden [11]) especially
when poor macroeconomic results (trade deficits, high unemploy-
ment) are perceived to be determined by “aggressive” policies pur-

The initial equilibrium is at point A. Protectionist policies imple-

North-North and North-South Debt etc. 167
Suppose that point A represents the situation in which the US
trade balance is in deficit and Japan’s balance is in surplus as a
consequence of US expansionary policies described above. From a
financial point of view this is the situation in which the US is
cooperating in the North-South debt game and defecting in the
North-North debt game described above. At this stage Japan might be
tempted to defect by stopping to finance US’ debt. If the financial
game were played in isolation this would trigger further defection by
the US which would let the dollar devalue both heavily and per-
manently to make this a credible threat (27).
At this point a trade game can be played. In such a game coopera-
tive behaviour in the US can be represented as the refusal to adopt pro-
tectionist measures. Defection, on the contrary, would lead to the situ-
ation described by point B. Cooperative behaviour in Japan could take
the form e.g. of Voluntary Export Restraints (VER) but, more impor-
tantly, the adoption of import increasing measures at home. Defection
(or retaliation) by Japan could take the form of “unfair” (dumping)
practices in the US market — or even in third markets— which would
decrease the US’ share leading to a situation such as the one in point B,
as well as the refusal to open up her markets. However, given the par-
amount importance the US market represents for Japanese exports it is
doubtful whether Japanese retaliatory moves could fully and even more
than offset protectionist polices in the US. This is what makes the pro-
tectionist threat by the US a credible one.
6 - Interactions Between Financial
and Trade Cooperation
To recapitulate our arguments let us now reconsider the different
games which have been mentioned above and see how their intercon-
nections may or may not lead to cooperation in finance and trade.
Let us suppose that there are two games going on in the financial
area: a North-South debt game (NSDG ) played between the US and
the Latin American debtors and a North-North debt game (NNDG )
(27) This is necessary to offset “hysteresis” effects.

168 Pier Carlo Padoan
between the US and Japan. If the two games were not interconnected
one could envisage a situation in which a cooperative strategy (c)
would be the dominant one with respect to a non-cooperative one (nc)
in both games. This is represented in Table 1 in the games | and 2
where the total pay-off for the US, which is engaged in both games, is
14.
However, as we have argued at length, this is not the case in the
present international financial scene. The two financial games overlap
with each other, hence cooperative strategies cannot be pursued
simultaneously and the pay-off structures must then be modified. Two
different cases may be considered accordingly to whether the US
choses to cooperate in one game or in the other. Games 3 and 4 are
set up assuming that the US decides to cooperate (c) in the debt game
(Game n. 3) with the Latin American countries (possibly in the
attempt to sustain her own banking system) and hence defect (nc) in
the game (Game n. 4) with Japan. In such a case the total payoff for
the US is lower than the one obtainable in the case in which the two
debt games are separated. The opposite situation where the US
cooperate in the NNDG and default in the NSDG is represented,
symmetrically, in Games 5 and 6.
Let us now introduce a trade game (7G) between US and Japan.
In this new situation the US is playing overlapping games (with Latin
America and Japan) in the financial sphere and simultaneous games
(in finance and trade) with Japan. The introduction of simultaneous
games, as it has been argued above, alters the perception by the
players of costs and benefits of each strategy. If US and Japan agree to
cooperate on both games they will accept lower payoffs for the
cooperative solution to each game provided that they are played
simultaneously. In economic terms this means that, e.g. in the trade
game, cooperation will mean no strategy trade policy on the part of
the US and the opening up of the domestic market in Japan. The
maintenance if the status quo in trade relations will allow, at the same
time, cooperation in the financial sphere. Japan will continue to
finance the US trade deficit while allowing a more gradual financial
macroeconomic adjustment in the US which implies a sustainable
long run debt position. At the same time a gradual adjustment in the
US will allow a gradual adjustment in the North-South debt game

has been  accompanied  a North-North  debt  crisis,  i.e.  the transform-

170 Pier Carlo Padoan
ation of the former hegemon into the world’s largest debtor. The
solution to the North-South debt crisis is now closley tied up with the
solution of this new debt crisis. While some argue that the next
century (if not the next decade) will witness Japanese hegemony in
the world system, the present crisis requires some form of cooper-
ation between the two leading economies in order to provide support
for the dollar denominated debt mechanism. Such a cooperation may
be facilitated if one considers that relations between the two econ-
omies involve more than one field. In addition to finance, US and
Japan must cooperate in other critical fields such as trade and
security.
As new contributions in trade theory have shown, strategic trade
policies pursued by one country may enhance her overall competi-
tiveness at the expense of other countries and provide new justifi-
cations for protectionistic policies. Cooperation in trade therefore
must be sought for itself as well. In this paper we have offered an
example of how cooperation in trade may increase cooperation in the
financial sphere and how important benefits may derive for the whole
international system.

| 1.  -  Summary  |     | of Issues       |        |                      |               |            |        |     |     |
This  paper  extends  the  boundaries  of interdependence  analysis
beyond  the basic  North-South  or  North-North  foci  to  a more  global
South-North-North  perspective.  In particular,  it focuses  on  the impli-
cations  of the Latin American  debt crisis for the US economy  and US
|           |            |     |      |      | in     | turn  | affect  | US  affairs  | with  |

| economic  | policies,  |     | and  | how  | these  |       |         |              |       |
as well as its other OECD  partners.  Despite the limited  direct
Europe
economic  interaction  between  Latin  America  and  Europe,  for  ex-
ample,  it will be shown  that events  and policies in Latin America  can

| have  significant  |     | impacts  |     | on  | Europe  | through  | linkages  |       |          |
economy.
Increasingly  interdependence  in the  world  economy  is reflected
not  only in increased  flows  of capital  and  goods  and services  among
the developed  countries  of the Northern  Hemisphere  but in increased

LDCs  throughout  the  world.  In  some  cases,  policies  taken  in  the
industrial  countries  of the  North  can  have  effects  on  the developing
world  that in turn  rebound  to have  unforeseen  effects  on  those  same
| industrialized  | countries.  |     |     |     |     |
| --------------- | ----------- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
The  most  salient  example  of  a  phenomenon  exhibiting  this
interdependence  through multiple channels  is the debt crisis  affecting
Latin  America  and other  developing  countries.  Arguably  the  product
of US monetary  policy and the negative  real interest  rates  of the late
1970s,  as well as shortcomings in borrowing country policies,  the debt
has  created  a threat  to world  financial  markets  and  US  politico-dip-
lomatic interests.  This threat has added to the constraints  faced by the
Federal  Reserve  Board  in  its  formulation  of  US  monetary  policy
throughout the  1980s.  This constraint  has added to pressure  for lower
interest  rates  in the US, which  in turn  has implications  for exchange
| rates  and  | international  | capital  | flows.  |     |     |
| ----------- | -------------- | -------- | ------- | --- | --- |
But  this monetary  policy  feedback  is only one  of many  channels
through  which  the  Latin  American  debt  crisis  affects  the economies
and  economic  policies  of the  industrial  North.  The  initial  creditor
reaction  to  the  crisis  in  1982-1984  was  that  it  was  a  temporary
phenomenon  which needed to be financed  only on a transitional  basis
until  commodity  prices  recovered  as  part  of the  normal  trade  cycle
associated  with  economic  expansion  following  the  1981-1982  recess-
ion.  Unfortunately,  however,  the  terms  of  trade  did  not  recover.
Earlier  views  neglected  the  feedback  effect  from  increased  debt
service  requirements.  These  requirements  forced  the debtor  countries
to expand their output of primary products and dissipate their natural

2.1 Estimating Latin American Resource Rents
and Their Impact on International Capital Flows (1)
The following are some broad estimates of gross rent generation
from major primary product exports of selected Latin American
economies over the past two decades. Table 1 provides export values
(gross value of exports including manufactures) by country and major
commodity export values for selected years to show how the pattern
trade has changed between the 1970s and 1980s. It can be seen that
the trend in total exports (including manufactures) was sharply
upward through 1980 but subsequently remained at approximately
the same level in current dollars through 1988. But in the 1980s
(except for Chile) traditional commodity export values fell, to be offset
by non-traditional exports including manufactures and new raw
materials and primary products.
The estimates of resources rents in Table 2 indicate a highly
positive trend in the 1970s, not only for oil but for agriculture and
mineral exports. Non-oil export rents rise from $2.2 billion current
dollars in 1970 to $4.0 billion in 1975 and $10.9 billion in 1980. This
reflects the broad upswing in terms of trade for raw materials and
primary products over the course of the seventies, a rise which carried
the region forward and permitted Latin American economic growth to
outstrip most of the rest of the world during those years.

2.3 The Debt Crisis:
Reverse Transfer Problem of the 1980s
Almost overnight the dramatic expansion of resource rents was
reversed, beginning in 1981. While Table 2 shows benchmark data for
1985 and 1988, the collapse in terms of trade was very sudden. US
tightening of monetary policy, begun by the Fed in 1979, was imposed
for essentially domestic stabilization purposes, given the fiscal recalci-
trance of both Democtratic and Republican administrations. Dollar
interest rates rose from negative to strongly positive in real terms (see
Table 3) between 1980 and 1981. The global spread of interest rate
increases and related recession marked the second major indication,
after the 1970s oil shocks, that the international economy had reached
new levels of interdependence. For Latin America, much of whose
debt was indexed to LIBOR, there was a double squeeze, depressing
the commodity terms of trade and increasing debt service.
The drastic decline not only in the price of oil but for most raw
materials and primary products which depended on the advanced
industrial countries for their major markets had important feedback
effects. It is the degree of repercussion from South to North which
differentiates the earlier pattern of dependence from the new, albeit
asymmetrical, North-South interdependence. The impact on Latin
American countries of the simultaneous decline in terms of trade and
rise in real interest rates led to a sharp cut-back in imports from the

Latin American Debt etc. 187
equal or greater amount of GDP out of their societies in order to pay
back former loans at much higher real rates of interest. Those who
continued to receive the dwindling rents engaged in capital flight.
The rising value of the dollar increased the pressure for real
reverse transfer. The result was that Latin America’s raw materials
and primary products, facing relatively inelastic world demand, were
subject to virtual forced sale at falling prices even as the cost of
imports was rising. Underemployed labor and capital were shifted into
the production of tradeables for export at wages and prices that had to
compete with Asian suppliers. What had appeared to be a relatively
favorable transfer of resources into the region during the 1970s
became in a matter of months the basis for an historically un-
precedented net transfer out of Latin America to the advanced
industrial countries.
Partly because of the price declines associated with the need to
expand exports even as the world market weakened, non-oil resource
rents in Table 2 fell by more than forty percent, from $ 10.9 billion in
1980 to $6.4 billion in 1985. Circumstances still remain bleak at the
end of the decade. Resource rent estimates for 1988 show a slight
improvement for minerals, due to increased copper prices, offset by a
decline for agriculture, so that the total remains at $6.4 billion.
However oil prices have recovered somewhat from their eighties lows,
and there is some reason to believe that the downswing of terms of
trade in the eighties may lead to a modest reversal in the nineties,
though not before placing major burden on the economies and
societies of the region. (The rents earned from the export of drugs
which are returned to countries of the region such as Colombia,
Mexico, Peri, and Bolilvia have attendent social and economic
destabilization effects and to some extent are symptomatic of the lack
of opportunities for legitimate employment of labor, land, and capital
in the region. They represent a pathological form of interdependence).
The reverse transfer problem of the region could also be
measured in terms of drastic declines in real wages and living levels
for the majority of Latin America’s population. The feedback on
countries such as the US is only beginning to be felt, by migration
(especially from the nearer neighbors in Mexico, Central America, and
the Caribbean), social unrest, political instability, and increasingly

188 Clark W. Reynolds
hostile sentiments toward the creditor countries. As countries
attempted to adjust through measures that were intended to increase
exports and reduce imports, real exchange rates rose (currencies were
devalued in real terms) causing the price of exported labor services to
fall to one-half their 1981 dollar values in countries such as Mexico
and Brazil. Labor throughout the region is being embodied in exports
at wages below those of the Asian NICs. The impact is being felt as
much or more by skilled, professional, and white collar workers,
whose return on human capital has fallen by even more than half,
even as the real prices of public services rise (owing to fiscal adjust-
ment imposed by debt-induced austerity.) As election results and
popular demonstrations indicate, the degree of popular dissatisfaction
from all classes is growing. Those in a position to do so are increas-
ingly tempted to place their assets abroad owing to uncertainty about
economic recovery and political stability, even as domestic real
interest rates soar to more than two digits per month as governments
struggle to cover both internal and external deficits.
3. - Impact of the Latin American
Debt Crisis on the US
The United States remains Latin America’s largest trading part-
ner, with its exports to the Western Hemisphere (IMF: International
Trade Statistics) reaching 17% of total exports in 1980-1982 and
falling back to 14% in 1986-1987. This compares with an EC share of
around 2% of exports to the region in 1986-1987 (half of its 4% share
in 1968-1970.) Japan’s share has fallen even more dramatically,
reaching 3.7% of exports to the region from a high of 7.6% in
1974-1976 and 5.5% in 1968-1970. On the import side the trends have
been similar, with the Western Hemisphere share of total US imports
falling from 15% in 1980-1982 to 11.5% in 1986-1987. The region’s
share of EC imports fell from 4.4% in 1968-1970 to 2.6% in
1986-1987, while its share of Japanese imports aeclined from almost
7% in 1968-1970 to 4.4% in 1986-1987.
Hence as Latin America has struggled to reverse its trade balance
and become a net exporter, it has lost relative trade shares to the rest

190 Clark W. Reynolds
The US has been able to absorb imports from Latin America
without a signifiant increase in exports due to a combination of debt
service payments and depression in prices of the region’s exports This
is one of the more pathological examples of international market
comditions permitting some countries to run unwise domestic fiscal
policies without paying the cost, by taking advantage of what Marris
has called the “overfinance” of deficit by surplus countries. While it
may be true that savings in Europe and Japan reflect voluntary
decisions of its society to anticipate future consumption needs, unfor-
tunately a portion of Latin American savings have been squeezed from
those least able to tighten their belts (the wage share of the functional
distribution of a stagnating GDP has fallen by several percentage
points). To make things worse, some of the capital outflow represents
decisions of the more affluent to bet on the US or other industrial
regions in a possibly self-fulfilling prophecy of domestic doom. Such
outflows permit the US to sustain its fiscal and current account
deficits which rose dramatically in the 1980s and have only fallen back
slightly as a 1988 (see Table 5). The consumption share of GDP has
risen for the US from 1980 to 1988, while it has fallen for Japan and
Brazil. In the case of Mexico consumption in 1988 was several points
of GDP below its mid-1970s levels and over 9 percentage points below
the US rate (Table 6).
Meanwhile Latin America’s trade languishes, with exports forced
up in quantity and down in price, while imports have been drastically
cut back along with less domestic investment and social infras-
tructure. Even though birth rates have fallen sharply, along with rates
of urbanization, the legacy of a past “false boom” is reflected in
societies that are increasingly pressuring their governments to do the
impossible. It is more evident than ever that adjustment, recovery,
and restructuring will be impossible without major debt relief plus
substantial new increases in commercial credit and investment lend-
ing. Even the countries that have been most responsible in terms of
domestic adjustment and external debt service, such as Mexico, are
mired in a condition in which domestic capital markets are crowded
out by government borrowing. Real interest rates in such countries
are now at double digit monthly levels.
One of the consequences of the North-South linkages through the
