192 Clark W. Reynolds
rather than to long-term recovery and growth. Those countries most
capable of receiving concessional credit in the 1980s have been those
with the poorest growth performance, precisely because they have
complied with the conditionality of debt service and domestic adjust-
ment. This is not to criticize such conditions, but rather to point out
that when an entire region is suffering from the effects of a major
transfer problem, and all countries are attempting to cut imports and
raise exports in mercantilistic fashion, the consequences tend to
distort credit markets and to lead to capital flows in directions which
work against the long term “golden rule” of global growth and
distribution. The resources seem to be flowing from North to North,
and within the North from those countries most capable of saving to
those least willing to cut conspicuous consumption and investment in
research, development, economic capacity, and infrastructure. If this
distorted process is permitted to continue, then the “muddling
through” in the short run will lead to major global problems in the
medium and long run. It may be incumbent upon those countries and
regions most able to bring about their own internal adjusment,
integration, and restructuring, such as the EC and Japan, to take the
initiative in bringing about the recovery of a more balanced pattern of
trade, investment, and social development in the Americas-even though
the Western Hemisphere may not appear to be in their “backyard”, just
as in the immediate post-World War II period the US (almost unilateral-
ly, but with important allied suport) made decisions about Europe and
Asia. Latin American adjustment will require an approach that fully
considers its place in an increasingly interdependent global system.

and Brazil.  There  the propensity  to invest  suffered  a sharp downturn

been  to  the  detriment  of the  competitiveness  of the  local  manufac-

In spite of its semplicity, the example useful has two aspects: it
highlights the damage caused by the external debt and it offers
arguments in favour of the controversial thesis that the existing debt
should be sustained by means of international loans (Cooper and
Sachs [13]).
In any case, the fact that the payment of the external debt is
giving rise to serious difficulties can also be deduced from the figures
in the last column of Table 2. This column shows the price at which
the debts of the countries under consideration can be bought in the
international secondary market. The mean discount is of the order of
70%, the peak being represented by Argentina with 84%.
Nor is it really surprising that the market should prove so
cautious. Apart from the inflation data, it is also worth recalling the
data relating to the investment propensity in the present decade,
comparing them with corresponding figures for the seventies, and the
data illustrating the growth of per capita GDP during the same period.
This is done in Table 3 below.

The Unified European Market etc. 201
As can readily be seen, the backward slide recorded by Latin
America during the present decade is very significant, especially when
it is compared with the progress achieved in Asia. In fact, Latin
America has passed from a high GDP growth rate in the Seventies to a
negative rate in the Eighties, i.e. from a positive 3.1% in the Seventies
to — 0.8% in the latter decade. Moreover, the investment propensity
has fallen by almost five percentage points and is now at about 19%.
The comparison of the evolution of two countries representative of the
two continents, i.e. Korea and Brazil, only helps to confirm the
general trend.
One can only add that the Eighties have seen Asia overtake Latin
America even in the sense that its growth perspectives in the immedi-
ate future have become far better: in Asia, in fact, the investment
propensity has increased from 22% in the Seventies to a current 27%,
i.e. by as much as five percentage points, whereas in the Seventies
Asia still lagged behind Latin America as far as this indicator is
concerned (Sachs [30]).
In the light of these data, therefore, it is not by any means
surprising that there should be such widespread pessimism about the
future of the Latin American economy. Nor is it surprising that this,
almost as a natural consequence, should give rise to an equally
justified pessimism about trade relation between the EEC and LA.
This situation becomes even further enhanced when one considers the
differences between the respective growth and inflation rates briefly
referred to at the beginning.

EEC imports. Graph 3 provides a similar illustration of exports from
the EEC to these four Latin American countries.

is not  by chance  that  both  Brazil  and  Venezuela  saw  a reduction  in

As Sachs  [30] has noted,  a strategy of this “export-led”  type, even
though  it is not  by any  means  an  “easy job”,  is more  likely to prove
successful  than the strategy  that preceded it, especially if it were  to be
based  on  a system  of incentivating  exports.  Apart  from  the  general
monetary  and fiscal framework  that we  have already discussed,  there
still remain  two other conditions  that will have to be satisfied.  One of
| these  conditions  | is external,  | the other  | internal.  |     |     |
| ------------------ | ------------- | ---------- | ---------- | --- | --- |
The  first  is  related  to  the  reduction  of  the  neo-protectionist
measures  that  have  been  recently  adopted  by the  United  States  and
the  EEC.  The  second  concerns  the  national  policies  to  stimulate
| investments  | in the  export-oriented  | sectors.  |     |     |     |
| ------------ | ------------------------ | --------- | --- | --- | --- |
We  are  here  concerned  with  two  conditions  that  are  not  easy  to
implement,  especially the first one  (Grilli  [21], Onida  [27]). There can
be no  doubt  that  for the four countries  here  considered,  but also for
Latin  America  in  general,  a  return  to  export-stimulating  policies
would  be  meaningful  not  only  from  the  viewpoint  of  short-term
currency  benefits,  but  also  from  the  viewpoint  of investments  and
employment.  The  reason  why the  data  illustrating  the  negative  cur-

2.1  -  According  to  traditional  theory,  economic  integration  be-
tween two or more  countries will generally make possible —  assuming
competition  is  allowed  to  operate  —  a  more  rational  use  of  the
available  resources.  In  fact,  when  the  production  factors,  especially
capital  and  labour,  experience  perfect  mobility  from  one  country  to
another,  they  can  be  more  readily  utilized  in  the  most  profitable
activities.  It helps all the activities  that may contribute  in seeking this
| purpose,  | including  | investments.  |     |     |     |     |
| --------- | ---------- | ------------- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
The  European  Community  estimates  that  such  a  result  will  be
reached  through the introduction  of a single European  market  (Com-
mission  of the European  Communities  [10]), even  though the relevant
patterns  of coordination  of the national  economic  policies have yet to
be  defined.  The  manner  in which  these  policies  can  be  coordinated
will  therefore  affect  the  outcome  of  the  interdependence  of  the
various  economies  and,  consequently,  also the stability  of the under-
lying relationships.

2.3  -  These  brief remarks  about  coordination  of monetary,  fiscal
and  industrial  policies  within  the  Community  are  intended  to  stress
the complexity  of the  manoeuvre  that  has to be put into  practice  in
order to create  the single market.  They are  also intended  to highlight
the  various  phases  of this  manoeuvre:  growth  and  strengthening  of
the area  in the medium  and long term,  adjustment  in the short term.
As  of this  moment,  of course,  it is not  possible  to  foresee  the
precise  time  scale  of these  two  phases.  What  is certain,  however,  is
that  the  adjustment  phase  has  already  begun  for both  the  industrial
sector  and the financial  sector.  Firms,  banks  and other credit  institu-
tions  have  already  realized  or  are  currently  engaged  in processes  of
bringing  their  size  and  their  organizational  structure  in line  with  the

These figures are based on the estimated effects of the dis-
appearance of customs barriers and controls within the Community,
the liberalization of public tenders and purchasing and the liberaliz-
ation of the financial services and the capital markets, allowing also
for the associated supply effects (Commission of the European
Communities, [10]). The liberalization of the financial and banking
sector is expected to reduce the intermediation margins by 1%.
2.5 - On the whole, therefore, the single market implies a more
efficient organization of the financial sector and a lower cost of
money, a more efficient organization of the productive sectors,
especially industry, with a growing GDP and a reduction of prices,
features that should make possible more substantial savings and
greater funds available for investments at home and abroad.
The Report does not contain simulation exercises of the effects
that could derive from this general situation as regards trade with
areas outside the Community. Nor are there any other studies dealing
with this matter.
In general terms, however, one can say that, given the present
tariff system, the greater Community GDP implies an increase in
imports from the developing countries and therefore also from Latin
America. Furthermore, bearing in mind the greater competitiveness
of EEC products deriving from the generalized price reduction, there
will also be an increase in EEC exports to these areas. Latin America
will thus benefit by being able to count on less costly imports from the
EEC. Since capital goods account for a very substantial percentage of
these imports (see Tables 4.4 and 5.A in the Appendix), this will go to
the benefit of Latin American investments and the competitiveness of
the goods produced by these investments in both the domestic and the
overseas markets.
2.6 - This outlook can be approximatly quantified by using the
coefficients of elasticity. Estimating the elasticity with respect to GDP
of EEC imports from LA on the basis OECD data covering the period
from 1971 to 1987, i.e. 17 observations (Table 11), one obtains-a
coefficient of 1.7.

Lastly, one should also bear in mind that these estimates are
based on constant prices and no chages in legislation. In other words,
no account has been taken of the possible competitive effects deriving
from the expected downturn in EEC prices, and the estimates also
ignore the possible expansive effects on trade that would derive from
a lesser degree of protectionism within the EEC market.
2.7 - What we have just done is therefore a first assessment of the
“1992 effect”. It provides a first indication, a positive one, though
strictly speaking it relates only to the foreseeable development of
exports.
But there is yet another aspect that is connected with the better
organization of the financial services and the readier availability of
loans at an expense that is likely to be below the present level. This
aspect could well enhance the forecast we have just made, because it
could improve the relations between the two areas both in terms of

The Unified European Market etc. 247
awareness of opportunities and in terms of capacity for exploiting
such opportunities.
The first part of this paper has shown us just how heavy a burden
the precarious financial condition is for the present phase of the
economy of the most representative countries of the Latin American
continent. A larger, better equipped and more efficient financial
market, like the one that is now being visualized for the EEC, cannot
but represent a benefit for developing industrial countries like Brazil,
Venezuela and Argentina, who have always been anxious to
collaborate with the EEC (Sylos Labini [32]).
Furthermore, since their requirements in this sector go, above all,
in the direction of importing technology, it seems obvious that the
more the unified European financial system will be able to offer its
support in the form of “financial packages” in keeping with the
development rhythm of the necessary technology, the more will these
countries find it possible to satisfy these needs. This would be a further
stimulus for productive collaboration between the EEC and Latin
American firms, a collaboration that in recent years has already been
tending to gain ground. In this connection it has often been held that
joint ventures of this type were greatly facilitated by the fact that raw
materials, sare in Europe, are plentifully available in Latin America.
What has been achieved in practice, however, is only a tiny part of
what could effectively be done in this field, and one of the reasons for
this sluggish progress is undoubtedly the relative weakness that, by and
large, still remains a characteristic of the European financial system.
Divisions and structural weaknesses, system differences and often only
a very limited capacity for overseas initiatives have made the European
system, taken as a whole, far less efficient that its North American
counterpart, which has always covered a dominant position in LA.
Liberalization, together with the rationalization, will undoubtedly
stimulate also the financial sector, it will work in the direction of a
larger average size among European banks and, above all, will induce
them to acquire a more international vocation. This will go to the
benefit of firms and enterprises who propose to enter joint ventures
abroad, not least those who wish to collaborate with Latin American
firms, who will henceforth feel themselves to be more closely sup-
ported with finance and services (Secchi [31]).

In short,  not only will trade in goods and services  be advantaged
by the  new  situation  in  Europe,  but  productive  and  technological
cooperation  between  the two  areas  will also be greatly facilitated  and
will  henceforth  be  able  to  develop  along  lines  and  models  that  will
undoubtedly be able to capitalize all the experience  that the members
of the European Community have gained in recent years in the field of
technological  development  and  industrial  restructuring  (CEPAL-
ICEPS  [9]).

The Unified European Market etc. 219
Of course, a greater opening of the future European market, with
appropriate antiprotectionist revisions of the present regulations de-
signed to limit the import of Latin American products, could not but
further enhance these effects. On the other hand a hypothetical loss of
competitiveness of the Latin American products currently being
imported into Europe (especially if it occurred in the adjustment
phase of the single European market, i.e. before the unification
process could produce its beneficial effects) would tend to reduce the
impact of the measures mentioned above. Whereas the second
hypothesis assumes a further worsening of the debt crisis of the Latin
American countries, which the United States — above all — seem
anxious to avoid (so much so that the Brady Plan sees them lined up
in the front rank of those trying to find a way out), the first hypothesis
requires a deliberate trade policy decision on the part of the Com-
munity.
Paragraph 36 of the Delors Report reminds us that the Treaty of
Rome assigns foreign trade policy to the Community. The Delors
Report also sustains that the growth potential in international trade
that the single market is likely to bring about can be fully exploited
only if foreign supply will hold free access to the Community market,
just as exporters from the Community area have free access to
third-country markets.
In general principle, therefore, seeing that the export develop-
ment policies adopted by the principal Latin American countries
(through the liberalization of their own markets) make it possible for
the “free-access-for-EEC-exporters condition” to become a reality, it is
now up to the Community authorities to ensure full reciprocity.
2.10 - As far as the Community trade policies are concerned,
there is yet another aspect that has to be analyzed: the cooperation
policies adopted by the various member countries.
Liberalization will have repercussions also as far as these policies
are concerned. At present, all the economically stronger EEC coun-
tries have cooperation systems for promoting growth in the
developing countries (ICEPS [23]) and use them to finance invest-
ments and services of particular social utility for the beneficiary
countries. As a general rule, these operations assume the form of

| 220  |     |     |     | Michele Bagella  |     |     |     |
| ---- | --- | --- | --- | ---------------- | --- | --- | --- |
assistance  credits  and  donations,  which  are  very  often  accompanied
by export  credits  plans.  Many  countries  have  also  signed  bilateral
agreements  specifically  designed  to  facilitate  even  closer  forms  of
economic  cooperation  with  the  receiving  countries  (Italy,  for  ex-
ample,  has  such  agreements  with  Brazil  and  Argentina).
Hitherto  these  initiatives  have  been  promoted  on  the  basis  of a
rigid division of the EEC countries,  this in the sense  that each country
has  used  its financial  resources  not  only  in support  of an  economic
policy  designed  to  strengthen  its own  presence  in particular  geogra-
phic areas,  but also with a view to providing working opportunities for
national  enterprises  and  thus  facilitating  their  degree  of penetration
| into  these  | areas.  |     |     |     |     |     |     |
| ------------ | ------- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
This condition  of exclusivity  in favour of national  enterprises,  this
barrier preventing the enterprises of other Community countries  from
competing  in tenders  for some  major projects  promoted  in this way,
has  already  been  formally  removed  as  a  result  of the  liberalization
process.  Nevertheless,  they have  not  yet completely  disappeared  and
there  still  remain  difficulties,  especially  those  connected  to  informa-
| tion  and  | effective  | transparency.  |     |     |     |     |     |
| ---------- | ---------- | -------------- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

ly expect  that  even  the  goals  hitherto  pursued  by means  of cooper-
ation policies will disappear.  It will no longer be possible to use  major
projects and the public tenders

|             |              |          | national      | businesses  |       | by  this  means  | and  thus  |
| distorting  | the rules    | of free  | competition.  |             | When  |                  |            |
|             |              |          |               |             |       | this happens,    | many  of   |

The Unified European Market etc. 22)
the existing agreements with Latin American countries will have to be
revised. It will not be sufficient to extend the existing incentives to the
other EEC countries, but action will have to be taken to ensure that all
‘interested parties from within the Community will have equal oppor-
tunity of access to these bilateral cooperation programmes, including
those involving industrial and technological cooperation, no matter
which country actually provides the funds.
Yet another novelty that the single market will usher in is the
complete overhaul of the Community’s existing cooperation system,
which will have to be rethought from scratch, taking account of the
new goals and the new rules implied by the unified market. So here
we have a fourth indication that has to be borne in mind on account
of the not by any means secondary repercussions that it could have in
the Latin American area.
Indeed, this overhaul and redefinition of the cooperation policies
could be highly innovative if it were to take the form of a “strong”
choice and lead to the decision to set up a European Fund for
Cooperation with Latin America. Such a proposal could be studied
with a view to eventually channelling into this Fund all the national
funds provided on the basis of the existing bilateral or general
agreements of the European countries; growth mechanisms could
also be devised to ensure that the Fund will automatically grow as the
GDP of the Community goes up.
However, no matter what specific operating mechanism might be
chosen in this connection, the setting up of such an organism would of
itself open a new phase in EEC-LA relations, which would largely
benefit. Apart from representing a new source for financing and
coordinating initiatives, such a fund would be particularly suitable for
incentivating all operations of collaboration among firms, especially
those that use debt capitalization (“equity swaps”) financing.
Indeed, the political and economic importance of such a fund is
too obvious to require further words to stress the benefits it would
provide.
2.11 - At the beginning of these reflections we said that one of the
fears aroused by the present difficult situation of the Latin American
economies is that their relations with the European Community and

| 222  |     |     | Michele Bagella  |     |     |     |
| ---- | --- | --- | ---------------- | --- | --- | --- |
—  more  generally  —  with  all the  more  advanced  economies  might
| decline  gradually  | further.  |     |     |     |     |     |
| ------------------- | --------- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
The considerations made above tend to stress that the setting up of
the single market  will*have  a positive  impact  on  the evolution  of the
relations.  All the same,  one  has to  add  that  this  does  not  mean  any
significant  change in the present  trends  of the trade between  the two
areas.  Indeed,  a quality  “jump”  in this trend  would  call for a modifi-
cation  of the  exogenous  conditions:  the external  tariff regime  of the
EEC  (which  will  have  to  be  decisively  orientated  towards  liberaliz-
ation);  revision  of the trade policies that the individual  member  states
have hitherto pursued vis-a-vis  the Latin American countries, with the
perspective  of the creation  of  a European  Fund for Cooperation  with
Latin America,  which will bring under the same  roof all the financial
resources  hitherto  made  available  by individual  European  countries
and channel  them towards  productive initiatives  capable of increasing
income  and  employment  and,  above  all,  creating  new  credibility  as
regards the capacity of the most representative countries in this region
to adjust their balance of payments.  As Reynolds  [29] has pointed out,
the  strengthening  of the  collaboration  between  the  EEC  and  Latin
America could trigger a rebalancing of the overall interdependence  of
the North-South  system,  and therefore  also of the US-LA relationship,
and it is only such  a rebalancing  that could lead to a gradual  attenu-
ation
of the “perverse”  effects  that the policies  pursued by the indus-
| trialized  countries  |     | have  | unleashed  |                 |           |          |
| --------------------- | --- | ----- | ---------- | --------------- | --------- | -------- |
|                       |     |       |            | in  the  Latin  | American  | economy  |
during the last decade.  Indeed, interdependence  is the dominant char-
acteristic of the present phase of the world economy.  It is therefore up
to  the  will  and  the  capacity  of the  United  States  and  the  European
| Community  | to  avoid  |      |           |        |              |                  |
| ---------- | ---------- | ---- | --------- | ------ | ------------ | ---------------- |
|            |            | the  | measures  | taken  | to  control  | their  national  |
economies having negative “effects” outside the areas of their immedi-
ate competence,  effects that invariable end up by producing further —
and not  always desirable  —  distributive  and reallocative  feedbacks  in
the countries
|                         | that  | originally         | gave  | rise  to them    | (Cooper  | [13]).     |
| ----------------------- | ----- | ------------------ | ----- | ---------------- | -------- | ---------- |
| The  creation           | of a  | European           |       | Fund  for Latin  |          |            |
|                         |       |                    |       |                  | America  | would  be  |
| entirely  in line with  |       | this perspective.  |       |                  |          |            |
And  with  this  last  indication,  our  analysis  of the  relations  be-
tween the EEC and Latin America,  rather than coming to an end, has
| really  reached  | a new  | starting  | point.  |     |     |     |

Exchange-Rate Regimes
and the Desirability
of International Cooperation (“)
Carlo Carraro - Francesco Giavazzi
Universita di Venezia Universita di Bologna
and CEPR CEPR and NBER
1. - Introduction
Applications of game theory to closed and open economy macro-
economics have proceeded along two parallel directions. In the
analysis of closed economies the attention has focused on the interac-
tion between policy-makers and wage-setters (Barro and Gordon [4])
and among different policy-making institutions within the same
country (Tabellini [34]; Carraro [11]). Open economy models have
studied the interaction among policy-makers in different countries,
assuming that there is only one policy-making institution in each
country, and that prices and wages are set according to simple rules
(Hamada [23]; Sachs [33]; Canzoneri and Gray [9]). Open economy
models have also mostly considered static games, while an important
area of research in the closed economy literature is the analysis of
repeated games.
Attempts to extend the analysis of international policy interac-
tions to allow for a domestic as well as an international game, or for
the evolution of the game over time, have found an obstacle in the
difficulty of computing analytical solutions. There are two reasons
(*) Some of the considerations which are developed here may be found in CARRARO
and Giavazzi [14].

236 Carlo Carraro - Francesco Giavazzt
why the study of international games becomes very soon very
complicated. One reason is the different channels through which
policy actions in one country are transmitted to another: income
effects, relative price effects, and interest rate effects through financial
markets. This is in contrast to a typical closed economy model where
the interaction between wage-setters and the policy-maker usually
occurs through one channel only-the price level. Another reason is
that in a two-country model the number of players increases very fast.
Consider for example a model in which output in each country is
produced using two factors, domestic labor and the output of the
partner country. In each country labor demand will depend on
domestic monetary policy-to the extent that it can affect the real
wage-and on the real exchange rate that determines the relative price
of the imported input. The wage-setting process in each country is
therefore a game in which the two unions-one in each country-and the
two policy-makers play simultaneously. A branch of the literature has
therefore taken the direction of investigating the properties of more
complete open economy models by means of numerical simulations
(Levine and Currie [28]). Others (Canzoneri and Henderson [10])
have instead chosen to study more simple open economy models,
ruling out, for example, the international linkages that occur through
financial markets.
Although limited either by the assumptions made to keep the
models analytically tractable, or by the impossibility to go beyond
numerical simulations, the analysis of open economy models has
raised a number of issues that are less obvious in a closed economy.
By increasing the number of players, open economy models have
raised the question of the desirability of cooperative behaviour when
cooperation cannot be extended to all players in the game. Rogoff
[31] was the first to point out that international policy cooperation
may not be desirable in the absence of “domestic” cooperation
between wage-setters and the domestic monetary authority. Another
issue that emerges naturally in open economy models is the optimal
choice of a policy instrument. The reason is that the choice of the
exchange-rate regime, a crucial element in the decision process of
monetary authorities, is really a choice over the optimal policy
instrument. In a two-country world, for example, under flexible rates

both central banks use  the money  supply as their instrument  and the
exchange rate is endogenous.  In a regime of managed exchange rates,
in contrast,  countries  choose  different  instruments:  one  country  sets
the  money  supply,  the other  sets  the bilateral  exchange  rate  (1).
This paper  addresses  both the issue  of the desirability  of interna-
tional  cooperation,  and  the  issue  of the  optimal  choice  of a  policy
instrument.  The  purpose  of this  paper  is to introduce  the two  prob-

and that are not known at the time wages are set. We show that
allowing for the international regime to be part of the outcome of the
game modifies in an important way the comparison of alternative
regimes. We claim that the solution we propose is the only rational-ex-
pectation-subgame-perfect solution of the international game.
The remaining sections of this paper are organized as follows. In
Section 2 we present the model. Section 3 discusses alternative
international regimes assuming, as commonly done in the literature,
that the regime that will prevail in period one is known at the time
wages are set. Section 4 assumes that the international regime is
endogenously determined as part of the outcome of the game. In
Section 5 we briefly discuss the case of “domestic” cooperation, when
wages in period zero, and monetary policy in period one, are the
resulto f a bargain between the union and the domestic central bank.
Finally, Section 6 discusses possible extensions.
2. - The Choice of Instruments
in a Simple Two-Country Model
In this section we describe, by means of a simple example, the
problem of the optimal choice of a policy instrument, and the
incentives to form a coalition in an international game. The basic
structure of our example is a simple two-country model with six
decision makers: a representative firm, a union, and a central banker
in each of the two countries. Such a model has been analyzed by
Canzoneri and Henderson [10] and, in a different framework, by
Giavazzi and Giovannini [22].
First of all, we provide an explicit game-theoretic derivation of
the model, in order to emphasize several implicit assumptions, that
play an important role in computing the equilibrium of the game. The
normal form of the constituent game is determined by the number of
players K (K =), their strategic space and payoff function. The basic
equations of this game are laid out in Table 1. Lower case letters
indicate variables expressed in logs and in deviations from equilib-
rium. Upper case letters indicate the level of the same variables. The

Domestic and foreign money are the only assets, and they are

Equations (5), and (5’), (6), and (6’), (7), and (7’) describe the
objectives of the players in each country. The representative firm in
each country maximizes one period profits, and the union aims at

banks have two objectives: they minimize the fluctuations of the

ive to affect real variables in the economy. The power to affect real
variables is given to them by the assumption that wages are preset.
The strategic variables in the game are the following: n and n* for
the representative firms, w and w* for the unions. The central bank
can choose either the money stock or the exchange rate as a strategic
variable. Each strategic variable belongs to a finite interval So =
[— S’, S’], where S’ is a positive number. The strategy space of the
constituent game is therefore S = S6.
The “rules of the game” are as follows: (i) The game is sequential.
In period 0 unions set nominal wages; then, in period 1, firms decide
employment and, consequently, the level of output, and central
bankers set the policy instruments. The realization of the productivity
shock is known to firms and central banks before they take their
decisions, but is unknown to unions: the expectation of x when unions
set wages is equal to 0. Hence, unions maximize the expected value of
eqs. (6) and (6’). This implies that wages are set based on the
expectation of the price level that will prevail after wages are set, i.e.
w = p* and w* = p**. Because expectations are rational, unions
anticipate that equilibrium prices will be the outcome of the game
involving domestic and foreign firms, and the domestic and the
foreign central bank. We shall restrict ourselves to subgame perfect

(iii) each central banker sets his policy instrument given the domestic
nominal wage and the reaction function of domestic firms, and given
the other central banker’s policy decision. Central bankers observe the
productivity shock before taking their decisions. Two different
regimes may arise as a consequence of the possible combinations of
policy instruments: either both central banks set their money stock
(flexible exchange rate), or one sets the money stock and the other
one sets the exchange rate (managed exchange rates).
The above “rules of the game” simplify the structure of the
constituent game by defining only two strategic interactions among
the players in the game: one between the union and the central bank
in each country, and one between the two monetary authorities. If we
allowed for all possible interactions, it would be impossible to
compute the equilibrium analytically. Notice, for example, that
foreign output does not enter in the domestic production function
(and viceversa): this implies that, given wages, employment only
depends on the domestic price level, so that unions do not have to
take into account what happens in the other country (4).
(3) Notice that these assumptions imply that all outcomes of the game must belong
to the firms’ reaction functions.
(4) If foreign output entered the domestic production function, a real appreciation
would improve the output-inflation tradeoff by lowering the relative price of imported
intermediate goods. Here, instead, the tradeoff is improved because a real appreciation
lowers the domestic CPI. The two assumptions capture quite different channels for the
transmission of exchange-rate changes: their implications for the effects of international
strategic interactions are however qualitatively similar and have been used alternatively
in the literature. The choice is here determined by analytical tractability.

The above assumptions and “rules of the game” define the

the ‘payoff vector. Its normal form, however, can be completely
defined only after having specified the policymakers’ decision vari-

domestic game between unions and central bankers is non coopera-

(flexible or managed exchange rates) and derive the normal form of
the sequentia] game. Then we compute the subgame perfect equilibria
of each game both in the case of non cooperation and of international
cooperation.
3. - Precommitment to a Policy Regime
In this section we assume that central banks announce in period
0, when wages are set, the policy regime that will prevail in period 1,
‘and that such an announcement is binding. There are in principle four
possible regimes: cooperation and non cooperation, under flexible and
managed rates. The relevant regimes, however, are only three be-
cause the exchange-rate regime is irrelevant when central banks
cooperate. The reason is that the cooperative solution is computed
maximizing a single objective function by choosing two out of three
possible instruments (e, m, m*), which are linearly dependent.
3.1 No Cooperation
In this case, each central bank sets its policy instrument taking
the partner’s instrument as given. Under flexible exchange rates they
both use the same instrument—the domestic money stock. Under
managed rates one country sets the money stock, the other’ sets the
bilateral exchange rate. In the flexible exchange rate regime each
central bank takes the other partner’s money supply as given: there-
fore it believes that a change in its own money stock can affect the
exchange rate. Because the exchange rate feeds back into domestic
prices, the central bank believes that monetary-policy can improve the
output-price level tradeoff. In a regime of managed exchange rates, in

economy’s  tradeoff  between  output  and  the  price  level.  The  other
country,  on the contrary,  believes —  as in the case  of flexible rates —
that it can affect the price level with a smaller output loss by changing
the  exchange  rate.  No  coalition  is formed  within  each  country:  the
subgame  perfectness  of the  equilibrium  thus  implies  that,  in equili-
brium,  the incentive to achieve  n  =  k, n*  =  k by fooling the union is

As remarked by Rogoff [31], the presence  of an externality  at the
international  level  affects  the  outcome  of the  game  that  takes  place
between  the union  and the central  bank within  each  country.  This is
clearly  seen  by noticing  that  in  a  closed  economy  the  equilibrium

Exchange-Rate Regimes etc. 247
The Nash interaction under managed exchange rates gives rise to
two interesting properties. The first is pointed out by Canzoneri and
Henderson [10]. Consider eqs. (21) and (21’). In the country that con-
trols the money supply (the starred country), the inflationary bias
associated with the central bank’s incentive to raise output (the first
term of eq. (2/’)) is larger than in the country that controls the ex-
change rate, and is larger than in the flexible exchange rate regime. This
is because the starred country’s asymmetric position prevents it from
attempting to affect the real exchange rate in order to improve its
tradeoff between output and prices. As we have seen above, the public’s
recognition of such an incentive is precisely what keeps price expecta-
tions lower under flexible exchange rates, relative to the fixed exchange
rate case. On the other hand, the incentive to affect the exchange rate is
still there in the country that controls the exchange rate — and this still
helps to keep price expectations down. In the non-stochastic case, this
country is indifferent between flexible and managed rates. As pointed
out by Canzoneri and Henderson [10], the above remarks suggest that
managed exchange rates are an inferior regime if the problem is the
correction of the “domestic” inflationary bias. When no productivity
shock occurs, a country that joins a stable monetary area, but main-
tains the ability to affect the exchange rate, does not improve upon the
flexible rate outcome. In the country that controls the money stock, on
the contrary, price expectations are higher than under flexible rates
because the public recognizes that the central bank has lost the ability
— and thus the incentive — to affect the real exchange rate.
These conclusions are modified by the introduction of a produc-
tivity shock. Suppose x > 0. The country that controls the exchange
rate now achieves a lower CPI than in the flexible exchange rate
regime, as can be seen comparing eqs. (/8)-(21); its value is also lower
than in the country that controls the money stock. Therefore, it is no
longer true that managed exchange rates are an inferior regime if the
main target is the domestic CPI. Furthermore, as far as employment is
concerned, both countries achieve higher employment under man-
aged than under flexible exchange rates. Comparing eqs. (/9) and
(22), we can conclude that the country that controls the exchange rate
is better off under managed exchange rates, whereas the other
country prefers flexible rates.

4. - Endogenous Policy Regimes
The assumption that the policy regime that will prevail in period 1
is known with certainty in period 0, when unions set wages, contrad-
dicts the result, shown above, that the optimal regime may depend on
the realization of the productivity disturbance. The comparison be-
tween cooperative and non cooperative equilibria discussed in the
previous section, and usually computed in the literature (8), is thus
incorrect. In computing the non cooperative equilibrium, for ex-
ample, we have assumed that central banks announce at the begin-
ning of the game that they will not cooperate, and that unions set
wages in the expectation that the two policymakers will indeed not
cooperate. When the realization of the exogenous shock occurs,
however, it may turn out to be in the banks’ interest to cooperate, for
example if the shock happens to be very large. Their announcement
not to cooperate is thus not credible. The best unions can do at the
time when they set wages is to rationally anticipate the decision

This result rules out the possibility that cooperation may be
counterproductive. The superiority of a non cooperative equilibrium
can be obtained comparing non cooperation given wages set in the
expectation that central banks would not cooperate, with cooperation
given wages set in the expectation that central banks would coop-
erate. We have shown however that the first cannot be a subgame
perfect equilibrium of the game: indeed it has not been constructed by
backward induction. Such a comparison is thus inappropriate. Real-
izing that unions must set wages before knowing the policy regime
that central banks will choose next period modifies the way in which
the equilibrium is computed. For any given wage and productivity
shock, in period | central banks are always better off if they form a
coalition. By anticipating this, in period 0 unions set x = 1 and thus
w = ok/a. Then, in period 1, the cooperative outcome defined by
eqs. (34) and (35) is actually achieved. Having used backward induc-
tion, this equilibrium is subgame perfect (Carraro-Giavazzi [15]).
There are two remarks to be made.
The first is that we have excluded managed exchange rates from
the set of possible policy regimes: the reason is that managed ex-
change rates have been shown to be unstable (10). The second remark

that the policy regime was known with certainty in period 0, when wages are set. It is

managed exchange rate regime.

with respect to w and w* respectively, where V; (m (w, x), w, x) and
Vp (m (w, x), m* (w*, x), w, x) are the union’s and central bank’s
payoff at the begining of the game, when wages are not yet set, and V;,
(ok/(a + ©)) and Vg(ok/(a + ©) ) are the payoffs in the absence of
cooperation between union and central bank. The solution of this
sequential bargaining is not easy to compute (12). We cannot thus
provide an explicit comparison between the players’ payoffs in the
presence of domestic cooperation. However, it is easy to see that in
the presence of domestic cooperation, the equilibrium in period one is
the same under cooperation or non cooperation. The reason is that
domestic cooperation removes both the inflationary bias, and the
incentive to run “beggar-thy-neighbor” policies. Hence, domestic
cooperation, by ruling out the need for international cooperation,
yields the Pareto optimal outcome.
6. - Remarks and Extensions
The results obtained in the three previous sections support the
following two conclusions. The first concerns the optimal choice of
instruments; the second concerns the desirability of international
policy coordination.
a) In the absence of exogenous supply shocks managed exchange
rates are always dominated by flexible exchange rates. This is because
no matter what coalitions prevail in the game, neither country is
worse off, and some may be better off under flexible exchange rates
than under managed rates. However, in the presence of supply
shocks, the country that controls the exchange rate is better off under
managed exchanged rates, whereas the other country prefers flexible
rates. Furthermore, under managed exchange rates, the country that
controls the exchange rate achieves a larger payoff. Managed ex-
change rates are thus an unstable regime because each country would
like to be the one who sets the exchange rate.
(12) See MANNING [29] for a different application of the sequential bargaining
equilibrium concept.

The important  assumption  we  made when  we  defined  the “rules
of the game” is that firms are  atomistic  and competitive,  so that they
can  neither  form  coalitions  nor  be threatened  by the other players of
the game.  If we  assume,  in contrast,  that the market  structure  is not
competitive,  firms  become  active  players  of the  game;  its  outcome
must therefore account  for the strategic interactions among all players
in a more  complicated  way.  In particular, coalitions  between, firms
and the union or between  firms and the central bank can be formed in
This is likely to change our results on the profitability of

subset  of  the  players  cooperate,  cooperation  is  generally
counterproductive.  As  shown  in  Section  4, this  is not  true  in  our
model  and suggests  that a more  precise evaluation  of the profitability
of international  cooperation  must  rely either  on  a general theoretical
model  where  firms  are  allowed  to form  coalitions.  Empirical  analysis

258 Carlo Carraro - Francesco Giavazzi
based on a general econometric model can provide preliminary
evidence on this matter (this is done, for example, in Levine [27]).
Another crucial element of the particular “rules of the game” we
have assumed is the hierarchical position of the six players. We have
assumed that unions and central banks have the same strategic
power, that is, both can raise threats in order to achieve the desired
cooperative outcome. The introduction of asymmetric strategic power
(for example, only central banks can raise threats) affects the possible
outcomes of the games, giving central banks the possibility to achieve
their most desired outcomes (Carraro [12], Cahuc [8]) (15). In this
case, international cooperation is certainly productive, because the
coalition among the central banks improves their strategic power with
respect to the unions.
6.3. Model Specification
The results of the previous sections may also depend on the
structure of the model we used. Even if our game captures the main
features of most international policy games, it would be interesting to
see how our results depend on the simplifying assumptions we made,
and, in particular, on the assumption of no financial linkages between
the two countries.
A partial answer to this problem is contained in Laskar [25]
and in Hughes Hallett [24]. The first paper studies the optimal
choice of instruments; the second paper the profitability of interna-
tional cooperation. Laskar’s |25] modifies the central banks’ tar-
gets, by substituting the domestic CPI with the level of international
reserves. Furthermore, unions are excluded form the game. In this
setting he analyses the problem of the optimal choice of a policy
instrument.
Hughes-Hallett [24], in contrast, provides an empirical assess-
ment of the profitability of cooperation in the presence of uncertainty
about the true structure of the model. In particular, it investigates
how robust are the estimates of the gains from cooperation to
variations in the model and in the objective functions used.

| 6.4  Incomplete  | and Asymmetric  |          | Information  |     |
The last issue we want to deal with concerns  the introduction into
the game of the hypothesis of incomplete and/or asymmetric informa-
tion.  Incomplete  information  was  already introduced  to sustain  coop-
erative  outcomes  in finitely repeated  games  (Backus  and  Driffill  [3]).
Another  important  implication  of this  hypothesis  is that  it gives  the
policymaker an incentive to masquerade his own prefences in order to
achieve  a larger payoff. This problem was first studied by Vickers  [36]
for a closed  economy  model.  Levine  [27]  and  Blackburn  [7] extend
the analysis to an  open  economy  model with policy interdependence.
Both  papers  show  that central  banks  have  an  incentive  to conceal  or
misrepresent private information  in order to disguise their intention to
export  inflation.  In particular  Blackburn  [7] by using  the  signalling
equilibrium  concept,  is able to identify separating and pooling equilib-
ria  which  explicate  conditions  under  which  private  information  is
revealed.  In  this  setting  he  also  explores  the  implications  for  the
profitability  of international  cooperation.  This  is an  issue  that  will
deserve  further  attention  in the future both in the game-theoretic  and
| international  | economics  | literature.  |     |     |

1.  -  Introduction
Among  industrial  countries,  the  joint  dynamic  properties  of
exchange  rates  and price  levels  are  remarkably  similar.  The  purpose
of this  paper  is to  illustrate  what  appear  to  be  the  most  important
statistical  facts  about  the joint behavior  of aggregate  price levels  and
nominal  exchange rates,  both in the short run  and in the long run  (1),
and  to discuss  alternative  theoretical  models  that  might  explains  the
facts.  Rather than coming to a conclusion on «which  family of models
best  explains  the evidence»,  I intend  to highlight  the questions  raised
by the  current  theories,  and  take  stock  of the  available  empirical
results.
This paper  offers  a status  report  on  the research  first outlined  by
Flood  [4],  who  attempted  to  verify  to  what  extent  mainstream
open-economy  models  can  explain  some  of the empirical  regularities
on  the behavior of exchange rates  and prices.  In addition  to the issues
discussed  by Flood,  I concentrate  on  the  covariance  of prices  and
exchange rates over  time,  as well as on their behavior  across  different
| nominal  exchange  | rate  regimes.  |     |

Equation (4) is the goods markets equilibrium condition, with
output supply y exogenously given, and w representing an aggregate
demand disturbance. The real exchange rate r is defined in equation
(7) (foreign prices are assumed constant and equal to 0 for simplicity).
Equation (5) is the equilibrium condition in the domestic money
market. m is the consumer price index, defined in (8). Money demand
is a function of the nominal interest rate, real income, i.e. the value of
real output in terms of domestic residents’ consumption basket, and a
velocity disturbance, v, Equation (6) is the usual interest parity
condition. While this equation clearly does not hold exactly in the
data, empirical researchers have so far failed to relate deviations from
interest rate parity to economic models of the risk premium (11).
In order to simplify the algebra of the reduced form equations, I
assume that all forcing variables, including the two stochastic disturb-
ances, follow univariate random walk processes. As I argued above,
this assumption does not appear to be an unreasonable approximation
of the actual data. More complicated processes for the forcing
variables would only make their coefficients in the reduced form
equations more complex algebraically, but would not affect the basic
results. The reduced-form equations for the real exchange rate, the
nominal exchange rate and the price level are:

and  (//) show that shocks  in the money  market  are  reflected  equally
in the  exchange  rate  and  the  price  level.  On  the  other  hand,  goods
markets  shocks  affect the nominal  exchange rate more  than the price
level.  Indeed,  if goods markets  were  dominant  i.e.  if the variance  of
the three terms in square brackets were much larger than the variance
of the  last  three  terms  on  the  right hand  side  of equations  (10) and
(11), the variance of the nominal exchange rate would be greater than
the  variance  of  the  price  level,  and  the  correlation  between  the
nominal  and  the  real  exchange  rate  would  approximate  1.  This
happens  because  changes  in the  real  exchange  rate  unambiguously
generate  an  excess  demand  for  money,  and  produce,  other  things
equal,  nominal  exchange  rate  appreciations:  this  property  has  been
| noted  by Flood  | [4] and  | Obstfeld  | and  | Skockman  | [12].  |     |

First,  the  conditions  that  shocks  in  the  goods  markets  have  to

| exchange          | rate  is determined   |                |              |                    |          |                  |

Prices and Exchange Rates etc. 271
determination of the real exchange rate. Specifically, equation (9)
implies that the flexible-price model can explain the behavior of real
exchange rates depicted in Graphs 1-3 only under the condition that
the variance of goods markets shocks during the flexible exchange
rates period increased approximately tenfold relative to the Bretton
Woods years. Stockman [15] has tested precisely this proposition, by
estimating a cross-section time series model of real exchange. rates
across a number of countries. For each country-year pair, the real
exchange rate is explained by a variable representing the year
(common across countries) and a variable representing the exchange
rate regime. This method controls for country-specific real shocks, as
well as worldwide real shocks. Stockman is able to reject the null
hypothesis, that the nominal exchange rate regime does not affect
the behavior of the real exchange rate, after controlling for worlwide
real shocks and country-specific shocks, at very high confidence
levels. Indeed, he finds that, other things equal, a typical country
experiences a 40% increase in the variance of the real exchange rate
in correspondence of the adoption of a flexible exchange rates
regime.
Thus reconciling flexible-price models with the empirical regu-
larities presented in Section 1 requires to identify nonneutralities
associated with nominal exchange rate regime that can have very
large effects on relative prices. One attempt in this direction has
recently been made by Stockman [16]. Relying on the empirical
observation that countries tend to impose controls on international
transactions more frequently under pegged exchange-rates than
under flexible rates, he shows that the effect of real shocks on real
exchange rates is mitigated in the fixed-rate regime. This happens
because large shocks increase the probability of exchange controls
(13), and therefore bias the expectation of the future real exchange
rate, since exchange controls improve the equilibrium real exchange
rate. Through intertemporal substitution, the antcipation of better
future terms of trade mitigates the negative effect of adverse real
shocks on current terms of trade.
(13) Controls are imposed when central-bank reserves are significantly depleted.

| 3.2  The  | Sticky-Prices  | Model               |     |     |     |
Models  with  sticky  nominal  prices  can  clearly  account  for  the
asymmetric  behavior  of real exchange  rates  across  nominal  exchange
rates  regimes presented  in Graphs  1 to 3. However,  the pure  natural
rate  models,  with  fixed  long  run  output  (or  fixed  long-run  output
growth)  and  purely  nominal  disturbances  are  clearly  at  odds  with
| Graphs  4 to  | 15.  |     |     |     |     |
| ------------- | ---- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
Rather  than  working  out  the solution  of a sticky  price  model,  I
use  equations  (/0) and  (/1) to infer the long run  variance-covariance
matrix  of p and e in a sticky  price  model.  If nominal  rigidities  are
absent in the long run,  output is fixed, and the sources  of disturbances
are purely monetary,  equations  (/0) and (11) predict that the long run
variance  of the price level and the exchange rate should be equal even
in the  presence  of short-run  nominal  rigidities.  Thus  the  correlation
between  the nominal  and the real exchange rate should decrease  with
the  forcast  horizon.  This  prediction  is clearly  in  contrast  with  the
evidence  of Graphs  4 to  6:  the  Graphs  show  that  the  correlation

decrease  slightly  in the long run,  but converges  to steady-state
values
that  are  above  0.9.  The  long-run  variance  of the  nominal  price  level
remains  a fraction  of the long-run  variance  of the nominal  exchange

hypothesis  within  a more  general  model  that  allows  the presence  of

|             |              |          |          |               |         | definitely  | establish  |       |

| confidence  | levels.      | These    | papers,  | however,      | cannot  |             |            |       |

Centro Studi Confindustria
Between  the two  wars,  consultation  among  developed  countries
on  issues  such  as  international  trade  and  taxation  was  frequent
although it did not always lead to effective  cooperation.  On the other
hand,  fixed  exchange  rates  implied  automatic  constraints  on  mon-
etary policies,  although they were  not always accepted.  Since the post
World  War  II  period,  industrialized  countries  have  experienced
policy  coordination.
| several     | kinds  of explicit  | economic  |     |
| ----------- | ------------------- | --------- | --- |
| 1.  -  The  | Bretton  Woods      | System    |     |
The  Bretton  Woods  regime  was  the  first  and  perhaps  the  last
example of a global restructuring  of international  monetary  relations.
As such  it can  be considered  an  example  of global cooperation.  As a
matter of fact, it fixed general rules for the exchange rates and for the
payments  system.  National  monetary  policies  became  largely  depen-
| dent  upon  | this  set  of rules  | as  well.  |     |
| ----------- | -------------------- | ---------- | --- |
The  Bretton  Woods  period  can  be  divided  in two  parts.  From
1945  to  1958  the  international  monetary  regime  was  dominated  by
accounts  prevailed
| exchange  | and  capital  | controls,  while  | bilateral  |
| --------- | ------------- | ----------------- | ---------- |
under the payments system.  During that period the United States had
a hegemonic position,  given the leadership of the US economy  and the
role of the dollar as reserve  currency.  The US dollar also had to carry

| 284  |     | Antonio  |     | Colombo  |     |     |     |     |
| ---- | --- | -------- | --- | -------- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
the  burden  of convertibility  into  gold on  demand.  The  international
payments  mechanism  was  dependent  upon  the  quantity  of dollars
supplied  by  the  US  economy,  hence  there  was  a  problem  of  the
adeguacy  of  the  quantity  of  international  liquidity  created  by  the
United  States.
During  the  second  part  of the  Bretton  Woods  period,  between
1969  and  1973,  several changes  were  introduced.  The  system  of
multilateral  payments  was  extended.  Exchange  rates  were  allowed  to
fluctuate,  according  to an  adjustable  peg regime,  1% from the parity.
Larger  capital  flows  and  increasing  international  banking  activities
reduced  the effectiveness  of controls.  The  leading  role  of the  United
States  and  its ability  to provide  the world  economy  with  the  appro-
priate  amount  of international  liquidity,  in  a  more  inflationary  en-
| vironment,  | became  more  | and  | more  | questionable.  |     |     |     |     |
| ----------- | ------------- | ---- | ----- | -------------- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
The  Bretton  Woods  system  was  a scheme  in which  international
coordination  was  confined  to preserving  fixed exchange  rates,  hence,
| national  | economic  policies  |     |       |           |         |           |           |     |
| --------- | ------------------- | --- | ----- | --------- | ------- | --------- | --------- | --- |
|           |                     |     | were  | affected  | by the  | external  | balances  | of  |
the economies  and by their impact on official reserves.  Changes in the
parities were  allowed only if the external balance was in “fundamental
disequilibrium”.  The system  also included  the possibility  of borrowing
| from  the IMF  | in order  | to finance  |     |             |     |                   |     |           |
| -------------- | --------- | ----------- | --- | ----------- | --- | ----------------- | --- | --------- |
|                |           |             |     | short-term  |     | current  account  |     | deficits  |
and  to  counteract  speculative  attacks  against  individual
currencies,
provided  that  the economic  policies  were  appropriate.  The  financing
could  not  cover  capital  outflows  which  were  to be prevented  using
| controls.  | After  1962,  | another credit facility,  |        |             |                        |             |      |         |
| ---------- | ------------- | ------------------------- | ------ | ----------- | ---------------------- | ----------- | ---- | ------- |
|            |               |                           |        |             | the General Agreement  |             |      | to      |
| Borrow,    | was  set  up  | for  the                  | major  | industrial  |                        |             |      |         |
|            |               |                           |        |             |                        | countries.  | The  | credit  |
facilities  were  usable  under  a system  of mutual  surveillance,  within
| the  Group  | of Ten.      |         |                |     |          |             |              |     |
| ----------- | ------------ | ------- | -------------- | --- | -------- | ----------- | ------------ | --- |
| Since       | the          |         |                |     |          |             |              |     |
|             | Bretton      | Woods   | system         |     | implied  | an  almost  | automatic    |     |
| mechanism   | of economic  | policy  | coordination,  |     |          |             |              |     |
|             |              |         |                |     |          | mostly      | constrained  | by  |
changes  in the  external  balances  and  in the  official  reserves,
in the
60s,  most  of the  efforts  for  cooperation  were  concentrated  on  the
problem
of the  adequacy  of international  liquidity.  While  in the  50s
| the problem  | was  “dollar      | shortages”,  |            |              |       |                   |     |         |
| ------------ | ----------------- | ------------ | ---------- | ------------ | ----- | ----------------- | --- | ------- |
|              |                   |              |            | in the late  |       | 60s  the concern  |     | was     |
| that world   | trade  financing  | was          | dependent  |              | upon  | an                |     |         |
|              |                   |              |            |              |       | increasing        |     | supply  |
of dollars,  deriving from persistent US payments deficits which threat-
ened confidence  in the US currency.  The debate,  then, concerned  the

|              | International Economic  |          |         | Coordination  | etc.     |               | 285  |
| ------------ | ----------------------- | -------- | ------- | ------------- | -------- | ------------- | ---- |
|              |                         |          |         | based  on     | a  more  | controllable  |      |
| achievement  | of  a                   | payment  | system  |               |          |               |      |
source  of world liquidity.  In 1967, at the general assembly of the IMF
in Rio de Janeiro,  an agreement was reached for the creation of a new
reserve  asset,  the  SDR,  not  directly  dependent  upon  the balance  of
The creation
| payments      | and the monetary  |     | policy of the United  |           | States.   |         |      |
| ------------- | ----------------- | --- | --------------------- | --------- | --------- | ------- | ---- |
|               |                   |     | it required           | the  85%  | majority  | in the  | IMF  |
| of SDRs  was  | discretionary;    |     |                       |           |           |         |      |
Board.  This was the last example of an agreement on general rules for
a global payments  system  reached within  an institutional  framework.
The position of the United States within the described  set of rules
has often been considered a privileged one,  given the role of the dollar
|     | currency  |     | and  as  | an  internationally  | accepted  | means  | of  |
| --- | --------- | --- | -------- | -------------------- | --------- | ------ | --- |
as  the reserve
payments.  It has often been argued that, because of this privilege,  and
its virtually unlimited  ability to finance  its imbalances with the supply
|                |           |     |            |              | States  | could  | put  off  |
| -------------- | --------- | --- | ---------- | ------------ | ------- | ------ | --------- |
| of  a  highly  | demanded  |     | currency,  | the  United  |         |        |           |
its balance  of payments  adjustment  and  could  avoid  any
indefinitely
constraints  on its domestic  policy.  In fact because  of the commitment
to convertibility the United States position was a very difficult one.  Its
adequate
| monetary  | policy was  | caught between  |     | the need to supply an  |     |     |     |
| --------- | ----------- | --------------- | --- | ---------------------- | --- | --- | --- |
amount  of liquidity,  proportionate  to  the  volume  of trade,  and  the
necessity to keep this supply in check, so to avoid inflation and doubts
about  its ability  to fulfill  the  convertibility  requirement.
As  a  matter  of  fact,  persistent  balance  of  payments  deficits,
starting in the 60s, led to several crises of confidence  in the dollar and
to speculative  surges  in the demand  for gold.  The very  fact  that  the
system  was  dependent  upon  the US dollar  supply,  and hence  on  the
US monetary  policy,  was  the reason  for its instability.  The  US policy
|                     |     |           |                     | stability,  |     | and  an  | orderly  |
| ------------------- | --- | --------- | ------------------- | ----------- | --- | -------- | -------- |
| had  to  reconcile  |     | internal  | and  international  |             |     |          |          |
and  international  economic  expansion.  The  end  of dollar
domestic
convertibility  in  1971,  and of fixed  exchange  rates  in  1973,  were  the
inevitable  results  of the unstable  equilibrium  the  system  was  relying
upon.
| 2 -  The  | First  Oil  | Shock  | and  the 70s  |     |     |     |     |
| --------- | ----------- | ------ | ------------- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
The collapse  of the fixed  exchange  rates  system  and the first  oil
in 1973-1974,  marked  the beginning  of a period characterized
shock

| 286  |     |     | Antonio Colombo  |     |     |     |     |     |
| ---- | --- | --- | ---------------- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
by high volatility of exchange rates,  together with high and diversified
inflation  rates.  In the  second  half of the 70s,  discretionary  forms  of
economic  cooperation were  developed,  the annual economic  summits
replaced  the routine  consultations  within  the  Bretton  Woods  institu-
tional  framework.
The oil shock,  which  affected mostly the supply conditions  of the
developed  economies,  found the authorities unprepared.  Inflation was
first  fought  with  monetary  restrictions.  This  strategy  proved  insuf-
ficient.  In  1975  it was  clear  that  it had  aggravated  the  recession
resulting from the sudden change in the terms  of trade.  Furthermore,
the flexible exchange rates immediately  showed their inability to cope
with  the  large  current  account  imbalances.  Ad  hoc  agreements  for
stabilizing  inflation  and  growth  rates  and  for enhancing  the external
adjustment  process  appeared  necessary  in order  to face  the difficult
| situation.  | The idea of ad hoc coordination  |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |
| ----------- | -------------------------------- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
was replacing the necessary
| interdependence  |     | of  | economic  | policies  |     | implied  | by  fixed  |     |
| ---------------- | --- | --- | --------- | --------- | --- | -------- | ---------- | --- |
exchange
rates.  From  that  period  on,  cooperation  was  meant  as  a process  by
which agreed-upon policies were  adopted in order to overcome  global
| problems,  | impossible     |     |              |                  |        |             |            |     |
| ---------- | -------------- | --- | ------------ | ---------------- | ------ | ----------- | ---------- | --- |
|            |                |     | to be dealt  | with             | using  | individual  | measures.  |     |
| In         | that  period,  |     | given        | the  inadeguacy  |        | of          |            |     |
|            |                |     |              |                  |        | monetary    | policies   | in  |
dealing with the mixture of inflation  and recession  caused by a supply
shock,  the  coordination  efforts  mostly  involved  policies  of the  Ke-
ynesian type.
|            |           | To a large extent  |     | the debate  |            | concerned  | the roles of low      |     |
| ---------- | --------- | ------------------ | --- | ----------- | ---------- | ---------- | --------------------- | --- |
| inflation  | (surplus  | countries),        |     |             |            |            |                       |     |
|            |           |                    |     | and  high   | inflation  |            | (deficit  countries)  | in  |
demand  management  policies.  When  the  first  summit  took
place  in
Rambouillet  (November,  1975),  many  countries  had  already  reacted
to the shock with tax cuts.
Expansionary policies to maintain the level
| of demand  | were  | highly  | diversified  |     |                     |     |           |        |
| ---------- | ----- | ------- | ------------ | --- | ------------------- | --- | --------- | ------ |
|            |       |         |              |     | and  insufficient,  |     | however.  | More-  |
over,  the productive systems showed different attitudes to adjusting to
the  new  terms  of trade  and  to  the  new  patterns  of world  trade.
Current  account  imbalances  reached  unprecedented  levels and unem-
| ployment        | rose  | generally.  |              |           |               |           |                   |      |
| --------------- | ----- | ----------- | ------------ | --------- | ------------- | --------- | ----------------- | ---- |
|                 |       |             | The summit   |           | concentrated  |           | on  the exchange  |      |
| rates,  ruling  | out   | the         | possibility  | of going  |               |           |                   |      |
|                 |       |             |              |           |               | back  to  | fixed  parities   | and  |
emphasizing  the  need  for  stabilization  measures  and  for  orderly
market  conditions.
In  July
|     | 1975,  | OECD  |     | stressed  | the  | need  to  | fight  the  current  |     |
| --- | ------ | ----- | --- | --------- | ---- | --------- | -------------------- | --- |
recession,  the deepest one of the post war period, with much stronger

International Economic Coordination etc. 287
expansionary measures which, if coordinated, could have a cumula-
tive impact. The recovery of 1975-76 was weaker than expected and
inflation rates remained highly diversified. In the years 1976 and 1977
economic policy reactions became more differentiated: low inflation
countries adopted moderately expansionary fiscal policies and neutral
monetary policies; both fiscal and monetary policies were restrictive
in the high inflation countries. Although appropriate in the direction
they took, but not in their magnitude, in 1976-1977 those policies
were, to a large extent, still the result of independent national choices.
High inflation rates differentials and differences in external imbal-
ances led to the idea that the low inflation countries had to assume a
leading role in sustaining the global economic growth according to
what was soon called the “locomotive approach”. At the summit held
in London in May 1977, the United States maintained that their
economy could not take the burden of leading the world economy
growth, due to the already record level of their current deficit and to
pressures on the dollar. As a matter of fact, the growth path of the
United States started to be seen as too fast, keeping the US current
deficit too high, while the demand for oil in the United States was too
strong and contributed to sustaining its price. Pressure was put on
Germany to undertake expansionary policies but the Germans resisted
the pressure for specific policy measures claiming that expansionary
policies would bring about higher inflation rates. Japan agreed to seek
an annual growth of 7% and introduced an expansionary budget.
During the July 1978 Bonn summit an agreement was reached
including anti-inflationary measures in the United States and expan-
sionary policies both in Germany and in Japan. Germany in particular
agreed to an increase in government spending of 1% of GNP; Japan
accepted to keep the export growth equal to zero; the United States
accepted to liberalize its energy prices so that they would reach the
world level. The consequent reduction of energy demand in the US
was expected to lower oil prices. The United States also agreed to
reduce the planned tax cut for 1979.
While conclusions of the London summit had been general, the
Bonn Agreement was more specific, except for the Japan growth
target, for which again there was no commitment to policy impli-
cations. Its results were more readily verifiable. As a matter of fact,

| 288  |     |     | Antonio Colombo  |     |     |     |     |
| ---- | --- | --- | ---------------- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
the  expansionary  package  was  approved  in  Germany  within  one
month;  the United States moved more  slowly in their commitment  on
energy  prices,  but  the  administration  proved  later  to  be  convinced
that  it was  necessary,  Japanese  exports  increased  only slowly  in the
following  year.  The  Agreement  led  to  more  optimistic  economic
| forecasts,  for instance,  |     | the one  | by the  | OECD.  |     |     |     |
| -------------------------- | --- | -------- | ------- | ------ | --- | --- | --- |
A rather  pessimistic  interpretation  of the Bonn  summit,  the first
example  of  specifically  coordinated  policy  measures,  is  that  the
agreement made possible decisions which faced quite strong domestic
opposition.  As a matter  of fact both the energy  prices liberalization  in
the US, and the fiscal expansion in Germany,  were  not at all generally
| accepted  in the  | two  | countries.  |     |     |     |     |     |
| ----------------- | ---- | ----------- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
Although  in  the  right  direction  and  quite  specific,  the  agreed-
upon  decisions  were  still  insufficient.  Fiscal  expansion  in  Germany
and  Japan  was  quite  limited.  No  decision  was  made  on  monetary
policies,  so that the fiscal measures  in Germany were  largely offset by
monetary  restrictions.  The second oil shock which followed  made the
effects  of  the  agreed-upon  measures  on  inflation  and  on  current
| accounts  impossible  |      | to evaluate.  |               |     |     |     |     |
| --------------------- | ---- | ------------- | ------------- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3 -  The  Second      | Oil  | Shock         | and  the 80s  |     |     |     |     |
The  second  oil shock,  in the  first  half of 1979,  with  the  conse-
quent surge of inflation,  slower  growth and exchange rates  instability
gave  origin to the new  scenario  in which,  in the first half of the 80s,
| economic  policy  | coordination  |     | took  | place.  |     |     |     |
| ----------------- | ------------- | --- | ----- | ------- | --- | --- | --- |
The continuous  exchange rate fluctuations helped to enhance the
|
creation  of an  area  of monetary  stability  in Europe.  This project  had
been  previously  attempted  with  the  “snake”,  in  1974.  In  1978  the
| creation  of a European  |          |           |     |              |          |             |           |

| implementation           | started  | in March  |     | 1979.  The   |          |             |           |
