restricted  fluctuation  of  the  European  currencies  within  a  band
around the central parity. The Italian lira was granted the exception of
a larger fluctuation
|                  |         | band,  in consideration  |           | of the higher inflation  |             |      | rate        |
| ---------------- | ------- | ------------------------ | --------- | ------------------------ | ----------- | ---- | ----------- |
| of  Italy.  The  | System  |                          |           |                          |             |      |             |
|                  |         | also                     | included  | credit                   | facilities  | for  | structural  |

International Economic Coordination etc. 289
adjustments of the economies and the embrio of a common currency
unit, the ECU.
The agreement on the exchange rates mechanism was considered
as the first step towards further strengthening of the process of
monetary unification, which in future steps would have included also
institutional changes. The process was supposed to be accompanied
by the gradual lifting of the controls on capital movements. The deal
had direct implications in terms of monetary policies independence:
fixed or stabilized exchange rates, together with free trade and capital
movements necessarily implied that monetary policies of the member
countries would be interdependent. In particular, given the unques-
tionable leading role of Germany, the System implied that France and
Italy would accept the leadership of Germany in monetary policy,
accepting much more severe conditions than their autonomous
policies would have created. By restoring, at least at a regional level, a
system of fixed exchange rates, the EMS can be considered as an
agreement on authomatic policy coordination by the member coun-
tries.
At a global level, in absence of clear macroeconomic deals to be
reached, the Tokyo and Venice summits in 1979 and 1980 concent-
rated mostly on energy and on the principle that inflation had to be
controlled. As a matter of fact, in those years, there was a consider-
able agreement on the priority to be given to the fight against
inflation, with a lower emphasis on the consequences on unemploy-
ment; some economists and government officials even believed that
anti-inflationary policies would have no lasting effects on employ-
ment.
In 1979, in the presence of rising inflation rates and of a declining
dollar, after having tried to convince the Bundesbank to intervene in
support of the dollar, the Federal Reserve inaugurated the era of a
strictly anti-inflationary monetary policy, quickly imitated by the
majority of the other industrialized countries. This led to a general
increase in interest rates. The subsequent recession was stronger than
expected. In the US the economic slow-down accelerated the decision
of a large tax cut. Thus the severe monetary restriction was combined
with a mythologized fiscal expansion, strongly advocated by the
supporters of “supply side economics”. Tax cut plans were soon

299 Antonio Colombo
followed by public expenditure increases, especially in armaments.
While keeping monetary conditions tight, starting in 1981, Germany
and Japan followed restrictive fiscal policies in order to reduce budget
deficits and to stabilize public debt.
The subsequent developments were dramatic and became shortly
unsustainable. The US fiscal and current account deficits began to rise
continuously. The interest rate differential and the good growth
prospects for the US economy led to large capital inflows in the US
which caused the beginning of a continous dollar appreciation. The
US currency continued to climb, due also to a speculative bubble,
even when, in 1984, the interest differential vis-a-vis the other cur-
rencies decreased. The continuous appreciation of the dollar made the
adjustment of the current deficit of the US impossible. It reached the
unprecedented level of 140 billion dollars in 1986, while in the same
year the surpluses of Germany and Japan reached 80 billion dollars
respectively.
Large disequilibria in the major economies and high interest rate
differentials were leading to a pattern of exchange rates conflicting
with the need for international adjustment. In the US high interest
rates were necessary in order to attract capitals and to finance the
fiscal and current account deficits. The dollar appreciation was a
result of the conbination of persistent imbalances and of the restrictive
monetary policy. The final solution of this contradictory and un-
sustainable situation could only be achieved with the adjustment of
the federal deficit. Its consequences in terms of exchange rate distor-
tion could only be controlled with more coordinated foreign exchange
interventions and economic policies.
Having reached the record level in February 1985, the dollar
started to depreciate due to coordinated interventions of the major
central banks. The beginning of the dollar depreciation had no effect
on the US current account deficit. De facto coordinated interventions
to push the dollar down were formalized in September of the same
year, when, during the Plaza summit the five major industrialized
countries stated that the level of the dollar exchange rate had reached
its record high. The announcement of the agreement itself helped the
decline of the US currency.
In the following months interest rates started to decrease, parti-

International Economic Coordination etc. 291
cularly in the US. The pattern of the fiscal imbalances remained
unchanged. Germany and Japan refused fiscal expansion, needed to
help increase demand for US exports. Most of the burden was put on
the need for fiscal adjustment and for slower growth in the US;
pressure was put on the American authority so that fiscal policy would
become restrictive and monetary policy would be eased, so as to let
the dollar decline. In those months the debate about policy coordi-
nation sounded like those in 1976-1978, although in the presence of
much lower inflation rates than in the 70s: surplus countries were
asked to follow fiscal expansion and deficit countries, namely the US,
were urged to adjust their budgets.
In May 1986, during the Tokyo summit, there was an awareness
of the difficulties due to the slow coordination process. Decision was
made that the finance ministers of the G-7 would meet at least once
every year in order to review economic policy performances.
Strengthening of the cooperation with the IMF for multilateral surveil-
lance was also decided, and the use of a set of economic indicators in
order to monitor the individual economies was approved. These
decisions led to some relevant results: in October of the same year
Japan agreed to reduce its discount rate, the US accepted to resist
protectionist pressures while the yen — dollar exchange rate was
considered to be consistent with the existing fundamental conditions
of the two economies. Meanwhile Japan had started to implement
expansionary measures.
The continuous depreciation of the dollar, though, started to
cause deep concern among the other countries, because, while not
followed by any relevant adjustment of the US current account, it
started to deteriorate the other economies’ exports. In February 1987,
during the G-7 meeting in Paris, it was stated that the current pattern
of exchange rates was appropriate, implying that the monetary
authorities were committed to sustain the dollar. Coordinated actions
to correct differences in demand growth were decided, including
fiscal policy measures, besides monetary instruments. In the following
months it became clear that the market was not convinced of any
effective change in the relative impact of the fiscal policies, while a
further monetary restriction by the Fed and expectations for a
worsening of the US current account created distrust in the markets

| 292  |     |     | Antonio Colombo  |     |     |     |     |     |
| ---- | --- | --- | ---------------- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
and fear of a recession.  Doubts  about  the willingness  of the German
monetary  authority  to  sustain  the  dollar  and  increases  in  the  US
interest rates led to large sales of bonds and to the consequent collapse
of their prices in the New York  stock  market  on  October  19th which
spread to the other major markets.  As a consequence,  the Fed stopped
sustaining  the dollar,  and  financial  market  stability  became  its main
objective.  The dollar started  to depreciate  again vis-a-vis  all the major
currencies.

International Economic Coordination etc. 293
Council of Hannover, in June 1988, it was decided to study ways,
procedures and timing of the steps in order to achieve monetary union
in Europe, evaluating the necessary link with the harmonization of the
real economies. A committee was created, chaired by Mr. Delors, and
its report was scheduled to be discussed during the following
European Council of Madrid, in June 1989.
The Report of the Delors Committee envisages a process divided
in three stages, starting with the completion of the current exchange
rates agreement, with the participation of all the currencies in the
System and the equalization of the fluctuation band for all the
member currencies. The process would continue with further institu-
tional steps, including the creation of a federation of the central
banks, up to the point where the exchange rates would be definitively
fixed and the federation of the central banks would be given the
necessary power to exercise full functions as the European monetary
authority. Precise steps are planned for enhancing, in a parallel way,
further policy coordination and real economic harmonization.
The Delors Report can be seen as the first comprehensive plan for
economic unification in Europe. It very efficiently compromises be-
tween economic and monetary union, establishing parallelism be-
tween the two procedures. Most importantly, it is a clear statement of
how it is technically possible to achieve the ambitious result, if the
political will is strong enough.
The Madrid European summit substantially approved the Report,
or at least it fixed a schedule for the beginning of its implementation.
As a matter of fact most of the discussion was on the calendar rather
than on the subject matter. The summit confirmed its willingness to
pursue the objective and agreed to adopt the Delors Report as a
guideline. It was also decided that the first stage of the procedure
would start on July 1 1990, while preparatory works for an inter-
governmental conference were announced. The conference, to be
held in order to discuss the full implementation of the procedure, was
not precisely scheduled, but there was a commitment to start it as
soon as the preparatory work would have been completed.
The prospect for the completion of the process depends crucially
on the way the intergovernmental conference will agree on the
objective of a parallel and complete monetary and economic union

| 294  | Antonio  | Colombo  |     |     |
| ---- | -------- | -------- | --- | --- |
and on how strongly it will pursue  it. It would be naive to say that the
process  is now  irreversible.  However,  from  a technical  point of view,
it is out  of question  that  Europe  is well  ahead  in going  beyond  the
simple coordination  of economic  policies and in trying to establish  an
order for sistematic  and fully accepted integration.  The success  of this
effort  relies on  the achievement  of a higher degree of convergence  of
| the economic         | performances.   |     |     |     |

The current  economic  scenario,  although  affected  by many  inter-
dependent  problems,  is free  from  dramatic  emergencies  and  strong
fluctuations  of the  growth  rates.  However,  domestic  problems,  like
the persistence  of a large fiscal  deficit  in the  US and  in other  major
economies,  together with large current  account  imbalances,  although
| changing  in    | their  allocation,  |                |         |                   |

|                 |                     | need  actions  | to  be  | pursued  in  the  |
| common,  other  | than  national,     | interest.      |         |                   |

nation is still not long enough.  A few considerations can be made.  The

policy
measures  are  easier to be agreed-upon  in emergency  situations,  it still
has to be proved that the willingness to cooperate  is strong enough in

much  more

International Economic
Interdependence
and World Income Distribution
Giovanni Palmerio
Libera Univ. Int. degli Studi Sociali
One of the basic characteristics the present-day international
economic situation is the interdependence of the various countries, a
feature that has become more and more pronounced ever since the
end of the Second World War.
Individual countries (like the United States) or groups of coun-
tries (the oil producers, for example) are in a position to transmit
pulses to other economic areas and to exert an influence both on the
state of the world economy and on the structure of the various
markets and economies. Such first pulses, of course, will generate
consequences and these, in their turn, will generate others and may
also give rise to feedback effects affecting the centre of original
propagation. The transmission channels may be both of the real type
(for example, increases or decreases in the prices of raw materials or
manufactured products) or of the financial type (effects of rates of
interest and exchange rates on capital movements).
The first point to be taken into consideration is the influence that
the state of the American economy exerts on the evolution of the
world economy. Experience, especially in recent years shows that the
world economy begins to boom whenever the United States pursues a
policy of global demand expansion: such a policy tends to drive up
raw material prices and thus promotes the growth of the developing
countries. If not carefully governed, however, this expansion leads to

302 Giovanni Palmerio
inflation and therefore induces the United States authorities to adopt a
restrictive economic policy. This, in turn, triggers a world recession
and exerts negative effects on production and employmant in the
other countries.
In recent years expansions of the American economy have un-
doubtedly brought about an increase in raw material demand and
therefore an upturn in prices, but have done so less markedly than in
similar growth phases in the more distant past. This phenomenon has
been attributed to the increasing degree to which synthetic materials
are taking the place of raw materials, a process that is being pushed
unremittingly shead by scientific and technological research in the
industrialized countries and, above all, in the United States
Analyses of this theme normally remain within the limits of a
logic of the Keynesian type, which concentrates its attention exclu-
sively on the effects that American economic policy has on income
and employment in the rest of the world. In actual fact however,
United States policy in this way exerts an effect on the inflation rate in
the world and on the terms of trade between manufactured goods and
raw materials, and thus ultimately also on the way income is distri-
buted among the various countries in the world.
This conclusion is further enhanced when one extends the exam-
ination to the part that is played by the monetary policy of the United
States. Since this policy regulates the dollar supply, it will influence —
not least via the effects it exerts on interest and exchange rates — both
the level of economic activity in the world and the distribution of the
resulting income between the various international areas.
The basic elements that sustain these conclusions regarding the
effects of American economic policy on the rest of the world are
constituted by the size of the United States economy (and its conse-
quent weight in the general framework of the interdependence of the
great world areas) and the part that the dollar plays in the interna-
tional financial markets.
Events of the eighties have made it quite clear that the United .
States, relying solely on financial manoeuvres, is in a position to bring
about a considerable appreciation of the dollar, that is to say, an
increase in its purchasing power with respect to goods and services
originating outside the country; and very recent experience has also

The  structural  deficit  of the  United  States  vis-a-vis  Japan,  Ger-
many  and  the  newly  industrialized  countries  in  the  Pacific  area  is
aggravated  by the fact that these  countries  enjoy comparative  advan-
tages,  because  they import  raw  materials  at a low cost,  add value  to
them and then re-export them as manufactured products, whereas the
United  States  are  net exporters  of raw  materials  and net importers  of
manufactured  goods.  The  terms  of trade  tend  to  deteriorate  in the
course  of time  to the disadvantage  of raw  materials,  and  the  United
| States  therefore  |     | tends  | to chalk  | up deficits.  |     |     |     |

ratio continue-dt o rise to the peak of 3.4% in 1987 and then slightly

Second: on macro economic performance. The annual growth
rate of Japan’s real GNP slowed down to 2.5% in 1986 and then
accelerated to 5.7% in 1988, in sharp contrast to a great concern
about a depression which might have been caused by the rapid yen
appreciation. Prices remained very stable, and private consumption
deflator rose at annual rate of less than 1%.
The growth rate of US GNP accelerated to 3.9% in 1988 from
2.9% in 1986 in the due course of the dollar depreciation. Prices were
relatively stable in the face of the substantial dollar depreciation, and
consumption deflator rose by 4.1% in 1988. Short-term interest rate
declined from 7.5% in 1985 to 5.8% in 1987, then increased to 6.5% in
1988. Long term interest rate declined from 11.4% to 9.0% in 1986,
and then increased to 9.9% in 1988.
The above observations lead us to the following issues. First,
external imbalances of both Japan and the US in nominal dollar terms
increased in 1986 and 1987, and then declined in 1988. Where did this
initially reversed and thereafter only small adjustment of the nomninal
current account imbalancers come from? This issue is important not
necessarity to economists but to politicians and others who pay
attention rather exclusively to the absolute nominal amount of imbal-
ances.
Second, adjustments of the real net exports/real GNP ratio in
both Japan and the US were much greater than those of the nominal
current account imbalance/GNP ratio. Why did they differ so much?
This question is important because it is net exports in real terms that
actually affect domestic production and employment, and because
much larger real adjustments are required for a given decline of the
nominal external imbalances.
Third, the rapid and unprecedentedly large changes in exchange
rates caused great concerns on a serious recession in Japan and an
acceleration of inflation in the US. But neither of the problems
became serious. What factors lessened the problems?

The last treatment raises an important question as to the validity
of simulation results. Are changes in the exchange rate totally in-
dependent of those in the exogenous variables? Oil price decline will
cause yen appreciation and probably dollar depreciation. It can not be
justified to assume that fiscal and monetary policies in Japan and the
US do not affect exchange rates. However, in view of the fact that the
exchange rate changes after 1985 were much more pronounced than
those usually projected from model simulations for oil price changes
and alterations in fiscal and monetary policies, we have treated
exchange rates exogenously for the simulations presented in this
paper.
Simulation results are reported in Tables 3-6 and they are all
expressed in terms of differences of each case from the preceding
case. In case 1 deviations from the standard case simply represents
actual values of economic variables which are influenced by actual oil
price declines, actual exchange rate changes and actual macro
economic policy changes in 1985-88.
Some details of the assumptions made for each simulation case
will be given at the outset of the following sections which describe

3. - Effects of the Oil Price Decline:
Case «i» Simulation Results
In general, three mechanisms are at work through which oil price
decline affects current account imbalances:
1) through directly reducing the value of imports due simply to
the import price decline; .
2) through inducing higher volume of imports due to import
demand response to import price decline (price elasticity effect) and;
3) through inducing larger volume of imports due to higher real
income caused by the improved terms of trade (income effect).
Table 3 indicates the simulation results for all of the combined
effects of these three.

4.1 Main Features and Problems
Table 4 indicates that the yen appreciation alone would have
caused Japan’s current account surplus in dollar terms initially, to
increase till 1986, and then to decline in 1987 and 1988. The current
account surplus/nominal GNP ratio, after having increased by 0.1%
point in 1985, would have declined by 2.7% points in 1988 as
compared with the case in which the yen had not appreciated. By
contrast, adjustment of the current account in real terms would have
advanced rather swiftly: real net exports/GNP ratio would have
decreased by as much as 6.5% points in 1988 under the yen appreci-
ation.
These simulation results demonstrate that the exchange rate
changes (the yen appreciation) contributed to reducing the current
account surplus/GNP ratio both in nominal and real terms. As
compared with this Japanese case, the effect of the exchange rate
changes (the dollar depreciation) on the US current account was
found very weak, according to the simulation results. It is, however,
important to note that changes in the real net export/GNP ratio were
found much less for the US than for Japan.
An important issue involved here is why the nominal external
adjustment is very slow compared with the relatively rapid real
adjustment under exchange rates changes. In the following, this issue
will be discussed systematically by examining pass-through ratios, the
Marshall-Lerner condition, endogenized changes in incomes and pri-
ces under the exchange rate change, and their influence on the
effectiveness of the exchange rate.
4.2 Pass-Through Ratio
It is sometimes claimed that the adjustment of the volume of
Japan’s exports has been slow due to low pass-through ratio under the
yen appreciation and that the adjustment of the volume of US imports
was also slow due to small rises in US import prices under the dollar
depreciation. Let us examine how the EPA model shed light on this
issue.
First: Japan’s export prices. Yen actually appreciated by 99.5%
from 255.5 yen/$ in January-March 1985 to 128.1 yen/$ (annual

Evaluation of Actual Mechanisms etc. 315
average) in 1988. Japan’s export price in dollars, however, cumula-
tively increased only by 49.6% in 1988 over January-March 1985.
Pass-through ratio, defined as export price increase/currency appreci-
ation ratio, is only 49.7% (=49.5/99.5). An issue is whether this
actual pass-through ratio is abnormally low.
Japan’s export price (in yen) function is specified and estimated
as follows in the EPA model, all the variables are expressed in the rate
of changes:
export price (in yen) = 0.42 exchange rate (yen/$)
.+ 0.33 private inventory deflator
+ 0.36 export price of foreign countries (in
dollars)
From the yen appreciation of 99.5% by 1988, export price in
dollars can be expected to rise by about 58% from the first term in this
export price function, with other variables remaining unchanged.
However, private inventory deflator (the second term) declines due to
import yen price fall of materials and to a deflationary impact on
aggregate demand are both attributed to the yen appreciation. Jud-
ging from the third term in the export price function, some increases
in export prices of foreign countries under the dollar depreciation will
offset at least part of the dampening effect on export prices of the
lower private inventory deflator.
The simulation results for exchange rate changes (case ii) show
that export price would have increased by 60.4% in dollars in 1988
under the yen appreciation (Table 4), resulting in the pass-through
ratio of 60.7% (= 60.4/99.5) in the year. This simulated pass-through
ratio is about 11% points higher than the above mentioned actual one.
But, if we take into account the impact of oil price declines on unit
prices of Japan’s exports which was a 3.5% decline according to our
simulations (Table 3), the discrepancy between the actual, pass-througt
and the simulated one narrows down to 7-8% points. Though this
disrepancy is still subject to further examination, the actually obser-
ved low pass-through ratio is largely a result of historically observed
“normal” pricing behavior of Japanese exports. US import price
increases which have been much lower than generally expected in the

exporter’s  pricing  behaviour  in general,  unless  they have  adopted  a
grossly  differentiated  pricing  strategy  by export  destination.
| 4.3  The  Marshall-Lerner  | Condition  |     |     |     |
| -------------------------- | ---------- | --- | --- | --- |
The  Marshall-Lerner  condition  is generally  satisfied  for both  the
US and Japan,  since the sum  of the long-run elasticity  of exports  and
imports  exceeds  unity  for  the  US  (0.62  for  exports  and  0.95  for
imports)  and Japan (1.40  and 0.52,  respectively  (2), according  to the
estimations  in the EPA model.  However,  two  modifications  are  to be
noted for a better assessment  of the effect of the exchange rate on the
nominal  value  of the trade  account.  One is the existence  of the large
initial Gap between exports and imports which has made it difficult to
satisfy the Marshall-Lerner  condition,  given the price elasticities.  The
other  was  a  series  of  J curve  effects  due  to  the  continuation  of
exchange  rate  changes  throughout  almost  all the simulation  period.
J curve  effects  are  referred  to  as  reversed  adjustments  of the
nominal  imbalances  in  the  short  run  and  hence  slow  adjustment
tempo  of the  nominal  imbalances  for the  initial  first  few  years.  But
such  effects  do  not  necessarily  explain  all  about  smaller  nominal
adjustments  than  real  adjustments  in the  long-run,  i.e.  long  after  J
curve  effects  have completely  worked  out.  To examine  the issue why
nominal  adjustments  are  very  small compared  with real adjustments,
it is useful  to  clearly  distinguish  not  only between  nominal  and  real
but also between  the “partial”  equilibrium  effect of the exchange  rate
on  the  external  imbalances  and  its  “full  and  general”  equilibrium
| effect,  as  explained  | in the  following.  |              |     |     |

short)  is defined  as  the  trade  volume  effect  exerted  by changes  of

Evaluation of Actual Mechanisms etc. 317
export and import prices alone which are directly caused by exchange
rate changes. In this case, incomes and prices other than those of
exports and imports are assumed to reimain unchanged. By contrast,
the full equilibrium — trade value effect (“full-value” effect in short) is
defined as the full effect on the nominal value of the trade or current
account balance when all the incomes and prices are influenced
endogenously by exchange rate changes. In between these two- ex-
tremes, there are two intermediate cases: one is the trade value effect
in partial equilibrium solutions. This effect is associated with the
assessment of the efficacy of the exchange rate in terms of meeting
the Marshall-Lerner condition or not. The other intermediate case is
the trade volume effect in general equilibrium solutions. These four
effects are summarized in Table 7.
The table shows that, in the case of Japan, the effect of a
sustained 10% yen appreciation on real trade balance in partial
equilibrium solution (i. e., the case in which only export and import
prices move to the extent of the exchange rate change, and other
prices and incomes are assumed to remain constant) amounts to
1.53% of GNP. Since the effect on nominal trade balance in the same
partial equilibrium solutions amounts to 0.7% of nominal GNP, it is
clear that the Marshall-Lerner condition is indeed satisfied. However,
the effect of the yen appreciation on the trade account is already
different between real and nominal terms: the effect on the nominal
trade balance is only half the effect on the real trade balance.
Furthermore, the effect of exchange rate changes in full general
equilibrium solutions (i.e. the case where all the prices and incomes
endogenously move by exchange rate changes) on the nominal trade
balance gets increasing smaller by another half, hence amounting to
only 0.36% of GNP.
The differences between these effects in the case of the US are
even more pronunced. In the partial equilibrium solutions, the trade
value effect is much smaller than the trade volume effect. The
difference between the two effects is more pronounced than the case
of Japan. This difference between the US and Japan may be explained
by the difference of the sum of long-run export and import price
elasticities between the two economies (1.57 for the US and 1.92 for
Japan) estimated in export and import functions in the EPA model.

As shown in Table 4a, the dollar depreciation of 1985-1988 would

| volume  | of US  | exports  | decline  | despite  | the dollar  | fall.  |

It is indeed true that the dollar depreciation would have raised US
export  price  since  the  US  private  inventory  deflator  increased  by
11.5%  in  1988  due to the dollar  depreciation.  But international  price
competitiveness  of US  exports  is strengthened,  due  to  the  relative
decline  of  US  export  prices  by  20.3%  compared  with  its  trading
partner  countries.  Judging  only from  the price elasticity  (0.62)  of US
exports,  the volume  of US exports  ought to increase  by as  much  as
12.6% (= 20.3 x 0.62).  Yet, the reason  foy the export volume  decrea-
ses  in the simulation  results  is that  the world-wide  deflation  effect  of
| the dollar  | depreciation  |     | adversely  | affects  | US exports.  |     |

The simulation  results indicate  that the dollar depreciation would

Evaluation of Actual Mechanisms etc. 319
have caused US import price to rise by 29.2% in 1988 and its import
volume to decline by 17.9%. Judging only from the price elasticity
(0.95) of US imports, the import volume should decrease by 27.7% (=
29.x 02.95 ), which is therefore much more pronounced than the
above full simulations result. This US import decline is caused by
weaker US domestic demand which is, in turn, caused at least
partially by the dampening effect of the dollar depreciation on world
trade and hence on US income. The simulated rate of rise in US
import price is much larger than its actual rate of increase (only 5.1%
in 1988 over 1985). In fact, the volume of US imports actually
incresed by 26.4% in 1988 over 1985, as against the simulation result
of its large decline. A reason why the actual import price did not rise
much is the oil price decline which lessened the US import price by
10.9%, according to the simulation results (Table 3a). However the oil
price decline alone is not sufficient enough to explain a relatively small
rise in the US import price, which remains a puzzle.
Turning to the effects of exchange rate changes on incomes in
Japan, it is useful to distinguish between the effect on GNP through
changes in the volume of exports and imports and that on domestic
demand through the terms of trade changes. According to the simula-
tion results, Japan’s GNP would have decreased by 10.2% in 1988 due
to the yen appreciation, while her domestic demand would have
decreased only by 3.8%.
Our simulation results concerning the effects of exchange rate
changed indicate that the yen appreciation should absolutely reduce
the volume of Japan’s exports due to higher export prices in dollars
and that the dollar depreciation should absolutely reduce the volume
of US imports due to higher US import prices. However, what
actually happened is almost the complete reverse of the simulation
results (Tables 1, 1a). Namely, in actuality, while the volume of
Japan’s exports remained virtually flat from 1985 to 1988, the volume
of its imports surged. In contrast to this Japanese case, the volume of
US exports expanded substantially, whereas the volume of its
imports grew moderately. These contradictions between the simul-
ation results and what actually happened may probably be attributed
to the over-estimated deflationary impact of the dollar fall, but this
issue is subject to further examination.

320 Masaru Yoshitomi
5. - Counter-Factual Simulation Results
for Macro-Economic Policies
One of the policy implications of the large discrepancies between
the «partial equilibrium - trade volume effects” and the “full equili-
brium - trade value effects” is that domestic demand management
policies should be complementary to exchange rate changes, if exter-
nal imbalances are to be reduced effectively. Let us now turn to
counter-factual simulation results concerning fiscal and monetary
policies.
It is difficult to properly assume hypothetical cases of macro-eco-
nomic policies which would have been adopted if the exchange rate
and the oil price had not changed. In our simulations we simply
assume that difference between the macro-economic policies actually
undertaken in 1985-1988 on the one hand and those unchanged from
1985 is the discretionary «changes» in the macro-economic policy
under exchange rate changes. The assumed policy changes are shown
in Table 2. Fiscal policy is represented only by government expendi-
ture, and monetary policy only by official discount rate and monetary
aggregates, due to the limited availability of policy variables in the
EPA model.
5.1 Effects of Japan’s Fiscal and Monetary Policies:
Case «tit» Simulation Results
The above assumptions imply that, in the case of Japan, public
fixed investment (nominal) increased by 6.3% in 1987 and by 8.6% in

together with a 1%-2% point increase in the annual rate of increase in -
monetary aggregates (M2+CD), from 1987 to 1988. The combined
effects of these fiscal and monetary policy changes are shown in Table
5:
The expansionary policies in Japan contributed to reducing the
current account surplus by 9.2 billion dollars in 1988. The policies
reduced the current account surplus/nominal GNP ratio by 0.8%
point in 1988. Since the terms of trade remain practically unchanged
under the macro policy alterations, the effect on real net exports is

Evaluation of Actual Mechanisms etc. 321
similar to that or on the nominal balance, namely, the real net
export/real GNP ratio declines by 0.9% point in 1988.
The effect of Japan’s expansionary policy on the US trade balance
is limited. As shown in Table 5a the US trade account deficit declines
by 2.1 billion dollars in 1988 due to the expansionary policies of
Japan. The current account deficit/GNP ratio shrinks by 0.06% in
nominal terms and by 0.09% in real terms in 1988.
The simulation results show that Japan’s real domestic decid
would have increased by 4.3% in 1988 by the macro-economic
policies. This effect together with the positive effect of the oil price
decline on real domestic demand (0.9%) exceeds the 3.8 deflationary
effect of the yen appreciation, but cannot offset the deflationary effect
of the yen appreciation on Japan’s real GNP of 10.2%.
Japan’s budget deficit (general government) would have increa-
sed by 5 trillion yen, or 1.4% of GNP in 1988 under expansionary
macroeconomic policies. The private consumption deflator would
have risen by 1.5% in 1988. Of course, this price increase is far more
than offset by the simulated declines of the consumption deflator of
9.7% caused by the yen appreciation (Table 4) and on additional 2.1%
decline due to the oil price fall (Table 3).

of increase in monetary aggregates (M2) at 9.1% from 1985 to 1988,

The US current account deficit would have decreased by 14.3

point in 1988, compared with a 0.4% improvement of the real net
exports/real GNP ratio.
The assumed non-expansionary macro-economic policy changes
induced US real domestic demand to decrease by 2.5% in 1988 and
the private consumption deflator to decline by 1.7%. This price decline
together with a 2.6% decline due to the oil price fall offset about three
quarters of a 5.8% inflation effect of the dollar depreciation, which
may account for relatively stable actual inflation rates in the US in

The US general government deficit decreases by 32.4 billion
dollars or 0.7% of GNP in 1988 under the assumed macro-economic

6. - Overall Assessment
The main features of the simulation results for Japan are summa-
rized in comparison with actual changes in the relevant economic
variables in Table 8.
First, the actual current account/nominal GNP ratio rose from
3.6% in 1985 to the peak of 4.3% in 1986 in the face of the rapid
appreciation of the yen. According to the simulation results, large
J-curve effects are observed only in dollar terms (Table 4) in 1985 and
1986. The yen appreciation worked for decreasing the GNP ratio of
the nominal surplus by 0.7% point already in 1986. What actually
reversed Japan’s external adjustment in the nominal ratio in 1986 was
the oil price decline, not J-curve effects. The simulation results suggest
that the actual decline in the nominal ratio to 2.7% in 1988 from the
peak of 4.4% in 1986 can be accounted for by the yen appreciation
(reducing the ratio by 2.7% points) and by the expansionary macro-
economic policies (reducing the ratio by 0.8% point).
Second, the actual real net exports/real GNP ratio steadily
decreased by 3.9% points from 1985 to 1988. This actual decline in the
real net exports/real GNP ratio can be explained mainly by the yen
appreciation, which would have reduced the ratio by 6.6% points by
1988 according to the simulation results. The effect of Japan’s
expansionary macro-policies and the oil price fall contributed to the

Evaluation of Actual Mechanisms etc. 323
actual decline in the real surplus ratio to GNP, but much less than the
effect of the yen appreciation.
Third, the actual growth rate of real GNP slowed down from
4.8% in 1985 to 2.5% in 1986, and then recovered to 4.2% in 1987 and
accelerated to 5.7% in 1988. The simulation results show that Japan’s
real GNP would have cumulatively decreased by 10.2% by 1988 under
the yen appreciation, which can be only partially offset by the
expansionary policy (3.3%) and the oil price decline (0.3%). It is
possible that the deflationary effect of the yen appreciation is over-esti-
mated by the EPA model simulation. However, it is suggested by the
same simulations that the dampening effect of the yen appreciation on
Japan’s domestic demand was offset by the favorable impact of the oil
price decline and the expansionary macro-economic policies.
Finally, the actual fact that the real balance/GNP ratio declined
much more greatly than the nominal balance/GNP ratio can be traced
to the similation results concerning the oil price decline (the real and
nominal ratio moved in opposite directions and the yen appreciation
(the decline of the real ratio was more than twice as large as that of
the nominal ratio), both of which altered the terms of trade in favor of
Japan.
For the US, its main features are summarized in Table 8a. First,
the actual current account deficit/GNP ratio expanded from 2.9% in
1985 until 1987 and decrease to 2.8% in 1988. The simulation results
indicate that the dollar fall indeed aggravated the nominal deficit/GNP
ratio until 1987. However, the EPA model may have underestimated
the effect of the dollar fall on US’s own exports due to the over-esti-
mation of the deflationary impact of the dollar fall on world trade and
therefore.
Second, the actual, real net exports/real GNP ratio shrunk by
0.5% point in 1988 over 1985 after having expanded in 1986. The
simulation results show that the oil price decline has exerted the affect
of reducing the net export ratio to GNP through 1986 to 1987 due to
domestic demand expansion, but that the dollar decline and the
non-expansionary policy of the US contributed to improving the real
net export ratio by 2.3% and 0.4% point respectively, offsetting more
than the deterioration of the ratio (— 1.1% in 1988) caused by the oil
price fall.

| 7.  -  Some      | Policy  Implications  |                   |     |     |
| ---------------- | --------------------- | ----------------- | --- | --- |
| 7.1  Sources     | of Frustrations       | with  Inefficacy  |     |     |
| of the Exchange  | Rate                  | Change            |     |     |
Recently,  frustrations  appears  to have arisen  from the disappoin-
tingly  small  external  adjustment  after  1985.  It is felt  that  exchange
rates  and  macroeconomic  policies  have  not  worked  either.  Is this
feeling  correct?
It is an iron law of economics  that at full employment,  exchange
rate  changes  can  not  are  substitute  for domestic  absorption  policies
but complementary  to each other (Krugman  1987).  That is, deprecia-
tions  of the  dollar  (i.e.  switching  policy)  can  only  be  effective  in

Evaluation of Actual Mechanisms etc. S25
reducing the external deficit of the US if restrictive fiscal policies
simultaneously reduce domestic expenditure (i.e. absorption policy)
to release part of otherwise fully absorbed domestic resources for
greater net exports. The US economy has been at full employment
and full capacity in 1988 and early 1989 when the effects of exchange
rate changes have been potentially still at full work.
Unfortunately, a large reduction of the fiscal deficit in 1987 ($70
billion or so) was totally offset by an increase in the propensity to
consume. In 1988 and early 1989, the fiscal deficit did not decline.
More seriously, improvement of the US trade deficit has stalled
regrowith over the recent half year or so in the face of a world trade
boom. In 1988 world trade expanded by 9% and is expected to
increase by near 8%. However, this extremely favorable world trade
environments has not well been exploited by the US economy,
probably because it has been at the edge of overheating as indicated
by tight monetary policy adopted by the Fed. This phenomenon
suggests that domestic demand has been too strong for the US
productive capacity to export more by exploiting the world trade
expansion. Hence recent stalling of the US trade deficit can be a result
of its own supply constraints.
Therefore, it is wrong to claim that drastic exchange rate changes
have not worked to reduce imbalances. This is wrong, because
exchange rate changes have not been simultaneously supplemented
by required domestic absorption reduction policies, particularly at the
time of full employment and full capacity in the US. Frustrations with
ineffectiveness of exchange rate changes can not be justified, since the
exchange rate alone can not work effectively. In other words, since
the Plaza Agreement, three basic policies have been advocated for
reducing current account imbalances: 1) promoting a drop in the
dollar; 2) expanding domestic demand in surplus economies; 3)
reducing the US federal deficit and improving domestic savings —
investment imbalances. However, the last policy has not well been
implemented, which has reduced the efficacy of exchange rate
changes.
The inaction on the US fiscal front has caused monetary policy to
be tightening since early 1988 in order to prevent a possible accelera-
tion of inflation rates. While such monetary policy has been successful

| 7.3  The  Issue  | of “Sustainability”  |     |     |     |
External  imbalances  in the  1980s  are  often  discussed  in terms  of
their  sustainability.  This  issue  is  composed  of  two  elements:  1)
associated  with  trade  deficits;  2)  “financiability”  of
protectionism
imbalances.
It is commonly thought that trade deficits adversely affect domes-
tic  production  and  employment,  hence  inducing  protectionist  trade
measures.  Domestic  production  and employment  can  be impaired by
the  penetration  of imports  and  stagnation  of exports,  i.e.,  by  net
import  expansion  in  real  or  volume  terms.  It was  exactly  this  net
import  expansion  that contributed  to strengthening  protectionist  sen-
|                                  |     |               | for various  attempts  | to  |
| -------------------------------- | --- | ------------- | ---------------------- | --- |
| timents  in the US and provided  |     | a background  |                        |     |
legislate  protectionist  trade  bills.  From  1982  to  1985,  the  volume  of
US exports  were  totally stagnant  and that of US imports increased by
60%.  As  net  exports  declined  in  volume,  the  nominal  value  of the
| external  balance  | worsened.  |     |     |     |
| ------------------ | ---------- | --- | --- | --- |
Since  1985,  however,  this parallel movement  between  net exports
in volume  and  the trade  account  in value  has  not  been  the  case  any
more  in the US. The distinctive  feature  after  1985 is that net exports in
volume  has  been  improving,  whereas  trade  deficits  in  value  remain

328 Masaru Yoshitomi
large. The volume of US exports of goods expanded by 40.2% in two
years from 1986 to 1988, and the market share of US exports of
manufactured goods in the world economy is expected to reach by
1990 the peak registered in the mid-1960s (OECD 1988). The volume of
US imports of goods increased by 13.8%, i.e., much less than that of
exports during the same period. The slow improvement of the US trade
deficit in value despite the rapid expansin of net exports in volume is
simply due to the terms of trade deterioration under the dollar,
depreciation and the large initial Gap in value between imports and
exports.
The net export expansion has benefited industrial production and
employment since 1986, hence quickly undercutting the base of
protectionist sentiments. Therefore, the large trade deficits in value
per se do not have any meaningful relationship with domestic produc-
tion and employment and hence protectionism.
The other element of the sustainability issue, i.e., the financibility
of imbalances can be judged not in terms of the absolute value but in
terms of GNP ratios of external imbalances. This applies to domestic
fiscal imbalances as well. This is simply because any fixed nominal im-
balance in value, however large it is, will get smaller in relation to in-
comes and savings as an economy grows. Therefore, the financibility of
the fixed nominal imbalance can be increasingly enhanced. Of course,
the sustainability can not simply be determined by imbalances relative
to GNP or savings, but what is important here is to recognize that the
absolute number will get increasingly meaningless as economies grow
over time. What does matter more importantly is the stock of net exter-
nal liabilities relative to GNP. However, even this stock ratio will de-
cline so long as the imbalance/GNP ratio steadily falls over time.
7.4 The Stalling of External Adjustment,
Even in Real Terms-Since Mid-1988
The reduction of trade imbalances in real terms has stalled since
mid-1988, in both the US and Japan. For the US, the supply constrain-
ts in the full employment economy have been a predominant reason:
the tempo of increases in the volume of exports has decelerated
(halved) and that of imports accelerated (nearly doubled).

Evaluation of Actual Mechanisms etc. 329
For Japan, the volume of exports and imports have grown more
or less parallel with each other. Exports have picked up due to
stronger world demand on Japan’s capital goods and components,
reflecting business investment based world trade boom. The volume
of imports has decelerated as the Japanese economy enters a steady
growth path at full employment after a sharp expansion at the
recovery phase. However, the volume of imports of manufactured
goods have still increased about 20% per year, as mentioned earlier.
The stalling of US net exports expansion due to its own supply
constraints should have nothing to do with a source of renewed
protectionist sentiment, simply because the problem is its own supply
shortage. A stronger yen is required for Japan to maintain both
domestic equilibrium (non-inflationary growth at full employment)
and net import expansion in real terms. However, without altering the
inappropriate macroeconomic policy mix, the US’s, desirable exchan-
ge rate relationship would not easily be brought about by Japan’s
single action on the monetary front, nor would the US external deficit
be reduced.

| Cooperation               | in Managing       |                             |          | .   |
| ------------------------- | ----------------- | --------------------------- | -------- | --- |
| the  Dollar (1985-1987):  |                   | Interventions               |          |     |
| in Foreign                | Exchange          | Markets                     |          |     |
| and                       | Interest          | Rates                       |          |     |
| Eugenio  Gaiotti          | -  Paola  Giucca  | -  Stefano                  | Micossi  |     |
| Banca d'Italia            |                   | Centro Studi Confindustria  |          |     |
| 1.  -  Introduction  (1)  |                   |                             |          |     |
In this paper we study the experience of cooperation between the
United  States,  Japan  and  Germany  in  managing  the  dollar  in
1985-1987.  The basic  facts,  with  emphasis  on  the  role  played  by the
different  policy  tools  (interventions  in  foreign  exchange  markets,
monetary  and  fiscal  policies)  are  reviewed  in Section  2.  In Section  3
we  discuss  the  channels  of monetary-financial  interaction  between
countries  participating  in  a managed  exchange  rate  system,  based on
the  model  presented  in  the  Appendix.  In  particular,  we  show  that
interest  rate  differentials  (short  and: long-term)  across  countries  and
their  maturity  structure  within  countries  may  depend  (together  with
many  other  factors)  on  intervention  policies  in  foreign  exchange
markets (that is, on the degree to which market trends are  “resisted”);
and  the  degree  of sterilization  of interventions.  This  result  could  be
relevant  for establishing  a connection between exchange rate manage-
ment  under the Louvre  accord and the steep rise in long-term  interest
rates  in  the  US  that  “detonated”  the  October  1987  stock-market
crash.  We  then  present  empirical  evidence  on  intervention  policies
(Section  4),  monetary  policies  and  sterilization  (Section  5),  interest
rates  (Section  6) in the period  under  review;  the critical  relationships
(1) The  authors  are  grateful  to Alessandro  Giustiniani  for help in developing  the
model  in  the  Appendix,  and  to  William  Branson  for  useful  comments.  The  usual
disclaimers apply.
Advise: the numbers in square brackets refer to the Bibliography in the appendix.

348 Eugenio Gaiotti - Paola Giucca - Stefano Micossi
identified by the model are examined in some detail, with various
quantitative techniques, to see whether actual developments lend any
support to the propositions derived from the model. Our conclusions
are summarized in Section 7.
2. - Return to Cooperation
period 1985-1987 marked the return to cooperation by the
United States and the other major industrial countries in exchange
rate management (Graph 1), in the (narrow) sense that: (7) on various
occasions these countries took, and announced publicly, a common
“view” on the desirable range or direction or pace of change of the
key exchange rates (dollar-DM and dollar-yen); (ii) they intervened
increasingly actively in foreign exchange markets, in a number of
cases jointly, to achieve these goals; (iii) they recognized increasingly
the resulting constraints for their domestic policies and to an extent
changed these policies accordingly.
It is useful, to start with, to stress what this return to cooperation
was not. The US policy of neglect of the dollar exchange rate was
abandoned because of the protectionist pressures generated by the
high dollar. Meanwhile, a consensus had emerged that exchange rate
“misalignment” was due principally to the divergent mixes of mon-
etary and fiscal policies followed in the US, Germany and Japan
during the phase of disinflation (2). Accordingly, much emphasis was
placed, in the recipes for adjustment, on the need for fiscal policy
changes (restraint in the US, stimulus in Japan and Germany).
Monetary policy was to remain geared to the objective of price
stability. Interventions in foreign exchange markets were assigned a
subsidiary role on grounds that they would be ineffective in
countering market trends if they were sterilized, and would otherwise
come soon to conflict with domestic monetary objectives (3).
At the official level the exchange rate regime was not in itself
called into question. International institutions and working groups
(2) A forceful presentation of this view is in MARRIS [23]; the analytics are more
fully discussed in BRANSON [7] and KRUGMAN [21]. This view found official sanction, as a
basis for restored cooperation in exchange rate management, in the June 1985 Report
on the Functioning of the International Monetary System of the Group of Ten
Deputies.
(3) See JURGENSEN P. [18].

(G-10, G-7, G-5) concentrated their efforts on setting up multilateral
surveillance procedures — based on joint monitoring of “objective”
indicators — to bring about greater “international consistency” of
national policies and policy-mixes (4). Altogether, the image of coop-
eration presented to the public was one of fully-fledged coordination
of domestic policy objectives (growth, inflation, external balance) and
instruments (monetary, fiscal and structural policies) (5). The ex-
change rate was apparently confined to backstage either because its
level would be determined by “fundamentals” or, more simply,
because it was not considered appropriate to let the public know the
precise content of agreements in this area.
The reality of cooperation was different. Three phases can be
identified in the period under review. During the first one, in 1985, the
authorities of the industrial countries aimed at bringing the dollar
down. Substantial interventions by the European central banks, with
some assistance from the Federal Reserve (Graph 2), took place in
February to accelerate a turnaround in market sentiment that ap-
peared under way. However, following action by the Federal Reserve
to halt the decline in short-term rates in the third quarter, in Septem-
ber the dollar started to rise again. This prompted the authorities of
the G-5 to sit together — at the Plaza Hotel, in New York — and agree
on a joint announcement to the effect that «... in view of the present
and prospective changes in fundamentals, some further orderly appre-
ciation of the main non-dollar currencies is desirable. They (i.e., the
Ministers and Governors) stand ready to cooperate more closely to
encourage this when to do so would be helpful» (G-5 Communiqué of
September 22, 1985, para. 18). While registering national policy
objectives and intentions, the Plaza communiqué did not involve
commitments to change current domestic policies, that were judged
already to «provide a sound basis for continued and more balanced
(4) A formal endorsement of the indicators approach came with the Tokyo
Economic Declaration of the Group of Seven (May 1986). The typical list of indicators
would include growth (GDP and domestic demand), inflation, external balance, fiscal
balance, monetary aggregates, interest rates and exchange rates.
(5) Coordination prevails when policy-makers in different countries agree on
common objectives and together take joint policy decisions that differ from those they
would have taken on their own. The game-theoretic approach to international policy
coordination, cherished by academic economists, entails policy plans and policy rules
that would apply far into the future and thus has contributed to a notion of coordination
as a commitment binding participants together for a protracted period. Cooperation is a
much looser concept that involves information exchanges, consultations, and possibly
common assessments of the international economic picture and the external reper-
cussions of national policies. See KENEN [19] and Dini [10].

Cooperation in Managing the Dollar etc. he |
expansion with low inflation [and] for redressing the external imbal-
ances that have developed».
Substantial interventions in foreign exchange markets were
carried out (jointly) only in late September and October (Graph 2); the
Bank of Japan pushed up, sharply but temporarily, short-term rates,
while little change in monetary conditions took place in either the US
or Germany until early 1986. As for fiscal policies, measures of
moderate restraint were already being enacted in the US (where in
1985 the federal government deficit reached 5.3% of GNP). Expan-
sionary measures were announced in Japan and were under discuss-
ion in Germany as part of the tax reform; the actual impact turned out
to be negligible, and fiscal balances actually improved in 1986 in both
countries. The depreciation of the dollar accelerated in early 1986
(Graph 3).
The second phase, lasting through 1986, saw a market-led de-
preciation of the dollar, with the Bank of Japan intervening to slow
the rise of the yen in the central part of the year, and the Bundesbank
and the Federal Reserve hardly intervening at all. Monetary policies
were progressively eased in the US and abroad after the first quarter,
and interest rate differentials moved against the dollar. The drop in
the oil price, in early 1986, and (outside the US) the depreciation of
the dollar had contributed to reducing fears of inflation and to tilting
priorities in favour of growth. Measures to increase public spending
and stimulate domestic demand were approved by the Japanese Diet
in November that, however, fell short of previous announcements by
the government; steps to reduce the federal deficit were adopted in
the US under the Balanced Budget (Gramm-Rudman-Hollings) Act;
the German authorities continued to stick to their public deficit
reduction objectives and to overly optimistic forecasts of domestic
demand growth. Meanwhile, trade imbalances between the three
major countries were growing larger in volume, and even more in
dollar terms, owing to the depreciation of the US currency.
In November the Ministers of the Treasury of the US and Japan
issued a joint statement that, after describing policies that were
already in place in their countries, «expressed their mutual under-
standing that .. . the exchange rate realignment achieved between the
yen and the dollar since the Plaza Agreement is now broadly consis-
tent with the present underlying fundamentals» and reaffirmed their
willingness to cooperate on exchange market issues. The changed
attitude on the dollar was signalled by half-a-point cut in Japan’s

discount rate. This statement marked the transition to the third phase,
that lasted through 1987 and was characterized by growing resistance
to dollar depreciation and, at the same time, by increasing conflict
between domestic and external objectives of monetary policies.
When the dollar fell sharply, in January 1987, the Bank of Japan
intervened heavily; the Bundesbank helped with some interventions
and joined in easing monetary conditions. With the Louvre Accord the
authorities of the Group of Six (6) agreed that “the substantial
exchange rate changes since the Plaza have now brought their
currencies within ranges broadly consistent with underlying economic
fundamentals and agreed to cooperate closely to foster stability of
exchange rates around current levels”. (Louvre Communiqué of
February 22, 1987, para. 10). The communiqué also contained, once
again, a detailed statement of policy actions already implemented
(para. 7), as well as fresh promises to strengthen mutual surveillance
over national economic policies (para. 9). In practice the Accord was a
“holding operation” to stabilize exchange rates based on the belief: (1)
that substantial improvement in real trade imbalances was already
implicit in exchange rate and policy adjustments since the Plaza that
required time to become visible; and (ii) that there was a risk of
exchange rate overshooting that could rekindle inflation in the US and
depress growth elsewhere.
Joint interventions in foreign exchange markets were substantial
in March and April but tapered off in May; short-term rates continued
to decline gently in Japan and Germany through the second quarter,
and short-term differentials widened in favour of the dollar. Long-
term rates, on the other hand, were coming down in the US and were
rising in Japan and Germany, increasingly so as the stabilization
operation gained credibility and the long-term capital flows towards
the US accelerated.
In May the Japanese government approved strong stimulative
fiscal measures; meanwhile the US federal deficit was improving more
rapidly than originally envisaged. Neither development, however, was
fully appreciated at that time, and there was growing disillusion with
fiscal policy commitments undertaken in international fora. Monetary
aggregates, on the other hand, were expanding rapidly, well beyond
(6) The Group of Seven minus Italy, whose delegation did not take part in the
meeting on grounds that all the relevant decisions had already been agreed upon by the
Group of Five (US, UK, Japan, Germany and France).

Cooperation in Managing the Dollar etc. 355
targeted growth rates, both in Germany and Japan, raising fears of
monetary tightening; monetary restraint was also expected or feared
in the US as a result of the need to support the dollar. And, indeed,
during the summer monetary policy turned restrictive (albeit gently)
in all the three countries; long-rates rose sharply, particularly in the
US, as the markets saw their fears coming true.
Meanwhile, pressure was building up in foreign exchange
markets, fueled by bad trade balance figures and by the perception
that interest rates were now less likely to respond to international
considerations. At the end of September a new G-7 Communiqué
failed to dispel mounting concern on the implementation of domestic
fiscal policy commitments.
On October 19, the US stock market fell by 23%, all the main
world stock markets followed suit in the ensuing days. Shortly
afterwards, the Louvre Accord was suspended, as interest rates were
pushed down aggressively by the Federal Reserve to circumscribe
damage to the financial system. During the last two months of the
year the dollar depreciated by some 10% despite substantial interven-
tions; it was eventually stabilized around the turn of the year, partly
thanks to joint interventions, partly because the descent of the dollar
had made the new exchange rates more credible.
On the whole, the process of international cooperation has been
much more in the nature of “regime preserving” (7) or crisis manage-
ment operations than of coordination of national policies; its burden
has fallen mostly on intervention and, increasingly, on monetary
policies; policy commitments in other areas have reflected more often
than not actions and intentions that had already been decided or
responded anyway to domestic requirements. Fiscal policies, in par-
ticular, did move in the right direction in the period under review, but
only in Japan in May 1987 visibly as a direct consequence of external
objectives bending national priorities. Over time, the credibility of
public announcements was damaged by failure to live up to the image
of fully-fledged coordination that had been created in the public
opinion. This has contributed to bringing about a less sanguine and
more realistic view of international cooperation, both in the official
and the academic world (8); that, however, is a development of 1988,
out of the range of observation of this paper.

3. - The Main Channels of Monetary Interaction
In this section the channels of monetary interaction between
countries participating in an exchange-rate arrangement are discussed
based on a simple two-country, portfolio model so as to place in
proper context the evidence presented in the ensuing sections.
The model (see the Appendix) describes the financial sectors of
two countries (“domestic” and “foreign”), made up in each case by
markets for three assets, monetary base (“money”, M ), bills (B ) and
long-term securities (S). The demands (by residents and non-
residents) for these assets are a function of wealth (domestic and
foreign), the vector of returns, the expected change in the exchange
rate and a vector of real exogenous variables. The assets are gross-
substitutes (own-yield coefficients are positive and substitute-asset
yield coefficients are negative, when non-zero); an expected appreci-
ation of one country,s currency increases the demand for assets
denominated in that currency (9).
The total supply of securities is exogenously fixed; the supply of
bills is also fixed but the central bank can alter the quantity in the
hands of the private sector with open market operations. Money
supply in each country is the sum of a foreign and a domestic
component of creation. The central banks of the two countries
intervene in the foreign exchange market to limit the divergence
between desired and current exchange rate level; the change in the
foreign component is determined by the total interventions of the two
central banks; by definition (the model is “closed”) an increase in one
country’s foreign component of money supply entails a corresponding
decrease in the second country. This is a first, direct source of
monetary interaction.
The monetary base effects of interventions can be “sterilized”, in
each country, with open-market operations in the bills market. Thus, ©
money creation through the domestic channel is described by central
banks reaction functions that include, among their arguments, dom-
estic policy objectives (growth, inflation) and the foreign component
of the base; these functions also determine the supply of bills (dom-
estic and foreign) to the public (residents and non-residents).
(9) A number of restrictions on the matrix of substitution coefficients are intro-
duced to make the model more manageable (without loss of generality); see the
Appendix.

What is happening here is that the “foreign” country is effectively
setting a floor not only to its own, but also to the world’s interest rate
structure: since the increase in the interest rate differential cannot
spread symmetrically in the two countries, a tightening of aggregate
monetary conditions (higher average interest rates) is brought about.
4. - Intervention Policies
Very seldom, since the transition to floating exchange rates, did
the leading countries’ central banks admit the existence of a target-
level for the exchange rates of their currency (bilateral or effective).
The stated purposes of intervention have included the maintenance of
orderly market conditions (“smoothing”) and, on occasion, the
“breaking” of destabilizing market behavior (13).
1985-1987 were no exception in this regard (14). In practice,
however, the Plaza Agreement involved a joint decision to encourage
depreciation of the dollar, and a joint decision that depreciation had
gone far enough was reached between November 1986 (US-Japan)
and February 1987 (G-6). The Louvre Accord entailed de facto
(although not formally annouced) limits on the permissible range of
(12) A particular case of this property is the “reserve currency” case as stated in
MarsTON [24], pp. 76-7.
(13) During the floating years the US Treasury was “interventionist” when the
dollar was weak, most active in 1977-1979; an explicit policy of non-intervention was
adhered to between 1981 and the beginning of 1985. With the exception of the Carter
years (1977-1979), the Federal Reserve’s operations aimed at “giving signals” in special
circumstances rather than offering continuous guidance to the market. The presence of
the Bank of Japan and the Bundesbank in the foreign exchange markets was more
continuous, on both sides of the market (Graph 4), leading in the end to much larger
numbers. On average intervention rates are much higher (more than double) for Japan ©
than Germany. The Bank of Japan appears to have been more active during dollar
depreciations and the Bundesbank during dollar appreciations. In the 1977-1979 period
(dollar depreciation), for instance, the former central bank intervened on average at a
monthly rate of about $1,075 million, as against 435 millions of interventions by the
latter; in 1981-1984 period (dollar appreciation) the Bundesbank intervened at a
monthly rate round 570 million dollars and the Bank of Japan at a 310 million rate.
(14) For a semi-official description of leading countries’ exchange rate policies see
SMITH - MADIGAN [31], DUDLER [11], MASUNAGA [27]. This last author carries the notion
of smoothing quite far, arguing that “when external surpluses are already very large ...
there will be a great deflationary effect if we try to bring exchange rates to levels that
could eliminate surpluses within a short period”, and therefore “... first of all the role of
intervention policy would be to allow market trends to take their own course ...
stemming at the same time any disruptive or too quick movements” (p. 134).

variation of the dollar vis-a-vis the two other key currencies. Against
the background of these broad objectives, interventions were typically
“leaning into the wind”, with the major exception of the post-Plaza
operations. In the presence of strong market pressures, in some
occasions a response of strong announcement-cum-joint-intervention
was adopted to “break” market trends (as in February 1987); in most
instances, however, rigid pegging of exchange rates was avoided (15).
Flexible intervention policies were increasingly accompanied by sup-
portive (sometimes joint) changes in money market conditions (see
following Section).
During the period not only Japan and Germany but also the US
intervened more frequently and for increasing amounts (notably in
1987): average monthly interventions in 1985-1987 were around 350
million dollars for the US and Germany, and 1,400 dollars millions for
Japan; they were respectively about 800, 400, and 2,900 million
dollars in 1987. The Bank of Japan was most active in resisting
depreciations and participated with enormous purchases of dollars in:
the joint operations. The Bundesbank’s pattern of intervention appear
more balanced, with the largest operations observed when the goal
was to push the dollar down (in 1985). As for the Federal Reserve
(that intervenes under the instructions of the Treasury), increasing
activism went along with a shifting focus from the DM to the yen as
“pivotal” rate; however, its relative role, in terms of shares of total
interventions, was bigger in the DM than in the yen market (Graph 2).
We have tried to ascertain whether the intervention policies of
1985-87 entailed a departure from past practices (16) by estimating
intervention reaction functions. The Fed does not publish the
(monthly) time series of interventions (and these cannot be mean-
ingfully approximated by published data on its foreign official posi-
tion); therefore, we restricted the exercise to Japan and Germany.
The model of central bank behaviour, following Artus [3] and —
Black [5], is as follows:
INT= ao(S — S*) + a, AMS + a2 TB + U Qo, a, a2, > 0 (4.1)
Su s00 TU Abas a!) bo, bi, a2, > O (4.2)
(15) Joint interventions were resorted to in four occasions (Graph 2), twice in 1985
(February and September-October) to consolidate the turnaround of the dollar, twice in
1987 (March-April, after the Louvre, and after the stock-market crash of October) to
break downward pressure on the dollar.
(16) Regardless of whether they were successful or not. An influential voice
arguing indeed they were not is FELDSTEIN [12].

Cooperation in Managing the Dollar etc. 361
Interventions (purchases of dollars) increase with positive
divergences of the exchange rate (dollars per foreign currency) from
the target (S*),the (percentage) rate of change of S (to measure the
resistance or “leaning against the wind” behaviour), the trade balance
(TB ); u is an error term (normally and independently distributed).
The 7B variable is included since in the short-term, with the central
bank managing both the exchange rate and the money market interest
rate, changes in the trade balance will in general be offset less-than-
fully by private capital flows, and will thus lead to interventions
without this necessarily implying a change in the target-exchange
rate. The target exchange rate S* moves around a constant (bo) with
relative (wholesale) price changes (foreign/US). The equation to be
estimated is obtained by sustituting (4.2) into (4./):
INT = —- Aobo Sie aoS = aAob, (BP Pu: i 1) F (4.3)
+ a, ANS + ag TB + u
Equation (4./ ) may involve problems of simultaneity, since — to
the extent that interventions are effective — one may also expect that:
A%S = % + a, INT + v, a, < 0 (4.4)
The negative correlation between A% S and INT through equa-
tion (4.4) may thus impart a downward bias to the estimated coef-
ficient a, obtained with OLS. Therefore, equation (4.3) was estimated
(in the specifications without dummy variables) both with OLS and
with instrumental variable methods to account for simultaneity on
A%S.
Estimation results are presented in Table 1 for the periods
1973-1987 and 1973-1984 (monthly data); the “leaning” coefficient
(a,;) has also been allowed to vary in periods of sustained appreciation
of the dollar (17); the “basic equations” have been estimated with OLS
and instrumental variables (IV) (18). Dummy variables have been
inserted for the three episodes of large concerted interventions in
November 1978 (Carter), September 1985 (Plaza) and February 1987
(Louvre). The equations’ fit is fairly good and the residuals show little
(17) The variable DUM takes value = 1 in the period 1980-3 to 1980-5.
(18) The following variables were used as instruments: the exogenous variables in
equation (4.3), and, in addition, two lagged values of A%S, and the contemporaneous
and lagged values of changes in interest rate differentials vis-a-vis the United States (see
also Artus [3]).

the contributions  to base growth in 1985-1987.  In 1985 both Germany
and Japan were  keeping monetary reins rather tight, while the US was

easing
(with interest  rate  differentials  moving  against the dollar-Graph  3). In
both years there was in fact no conflict between domestic  and external
objectives  of  monetary  policy;  interventions  either  contributed  to
monetary  base  creation  in  the  desired  direction  or  were  sterilized
without  much difficulty.  The story is different  in 1987: dollar interven-
tions,  very  substantial,  were  sterilized  by the  US  (where,  however,
bank  reserves  and  monetary  aggregates  were  slowing  down  growth),
but  were  increasingly  reflected  in base  and  money  supply  growth  in
Japan,  and,  to a lesser  extent,  also in Germany  (notably  in the fourth
quarter).

(23)  Both  Japan  and  Germany  raised  their  money  market  interest  rates  in the
weeks following the Plaza, and lowered then subsequently once the downward trend in
the dollar was established (Graph 7). In March  1986 interest rates were lowered jointly
by the US, Japan and Germany;  from this moment  onward  the US was  leading in a
general relaxation  of monetary  policy,  after the fall (in January)  in the oil prices had
dampened inflation fears. The October  1986 US-Japan accord to halt the decline of the
dollar  was  marked  by the  Bank  of Japan  lowering  interest  rates;  both  Japan  and
Germany  lowered  their  discount  rates  at  the  time  of the  Louvre  Accord  (February
1987).
(24) Our results for Germany are broadly in line with those obtained for the period
1979-1987  by MasTROPASQUA  -  Micossi -  RINALDI  [25], for 1973-1975  by Artus  [3], and
for 1960-1971  by HERRING - MarsTON  [15]. For Japan,  most estimates  indicate  steriliz-
ation coefficients greater than  1 during the 60s and 70s. See  LANEY e WILLET [22] for a
survey  of the  main  empirical  results  for  sterlization  coefficients  in  the  industrial
countries.
