to  (and  not  significantly  different  from)  the  one  for  Japan,  and
somewhat lower for Germany (significantly different from  1) (25). The
inflation  effect in  both  countries  confirms  the  role’ played  by  this
variable in the decision to relax monetary policy in 1986 (when INFLR
was  negative).
Stability  tests  were  performed  on  the monthly  data  equations  to
check  for  possible  structural  “breaks”  in  1985-1987  or,  within  this
period,  in  1986-1987.  The  results  do not  lend  support  to the hypoth-
esis  of structural  break,  particularly  in the  case  of Japan  (the Chow
test  for  Germany  is slightly  above  the  95%  confidence  interval  for
1986-1987).
Out  of sample  simulation  over  1985-1987  of the  equations  esti-
mated  over  1973-1984  shows  an  underprediction  of domestic  base
growth  (that  is,  reduced  sterilization)  for  both  countries  in  1986
(when  Germany  did  not  intervene  very  much)  and  for  Germany  in
1987,  and an overprediction  for Japan in this latter year (that is,  Japan
sterilized  more  than expected).  Some  short-run  oscillations  in steriliz-
ation  coefficients
|     |     | are  | confirmed  | by  | the  estimates  | from  | three-year  |
| --- | --- | ---- | ---------- | --- | --------------- | ----- | ----------- |
rolling  regressions  (Graph  8).  As  may  be  noted,  for  both  countries
sterilization  coefficients  are  below  sample  average  in  1985-1987,  but
close  to or above  average  in 1987.  Germany’s coefficient
shows wider
oscillations  (greater  short-term  flexibility),  with  a drop  in  1985-1986
| (external  | and      | domestic  | objectives  | coincided)  |      |              |          |
| ---------- | -------- | --------- | ----------- | ----------- | ---- | ------------ | -------- |
|            |          |           |             |             | and  | a  recovery  | at  the  |
| beginning  | of 1987  | (26).     |             |             |      |              |          |
All in all, our
|     |     | results  | confirm  | flexibility  | in sterilization  |     | behaviour  |
| --- | --- | -------- | -------- | ------------ | ----------------- | --- | ---------- |
in the short-run  and a tendency  to revert  to “normal”  behaviour  over
longer periods.  Once again,  however,  1987  stands  out as a case  when
increased  pressure  on money  supply from the foreign component
was
matched  by increased  resistance  to let domestic  money  market  inter-
| est  rates  | adjust downwards  |     | (in fact,  |                 |     |              |          |
| ----------- | ----------------- | --- | ---------- | --------------- | --- | ------------ | -------- |
|             |                   |     |            | after mid-year  |     | a rise took  | place).  |
(25)  As for the policy variables, in the German case only the residual component of
inflation  is significant,  with  the expected  negative  sign,  indicating  a monetary  policy
| mainly  aimed  | at  |     |     |     |     |     |     |

contrasting  inflation  accelerations.  For  Japan,  the  three  policy
| variables  | are  generally all significant.  |     | The signs seem  |     |              |                |         |
| ---------- | -------------------------------- | --- | --------------- | --- | ------------ | -------------- | ------- |
|            |                                  |     |                 |     | to indicate  | that monetary  | policy  |
accomodates  variations  in  output  and  in  the  trend  component  of
|     |     |     |     |     |     |     | inflation,  while  |

| 6.  -  Interest  | Rate Differentials  |               |                     |     |     |
and Maturity Structure
We  have  suggested,  with  the  help  of  the  model  sketched  in
Section  3, that changes  in exchange  rate  expectations  may  influence
differently  interest  rate differentials  across  countries,  and their matur-
ity  structure  within  countries,  depending,  among  other  things,  on
interventions  (degree  of resistance)  in foreign  exchange  markets  and
| the degree of sterilization  |     | of their monetary  | effects.  |     |     |
| ---------------------------- | --- | ------------------ | --------- | --- | --- |
Two  sets  of propositions  are  involved  here.  First,  interest  rate
parity is an equilibrium  condition;  as such it cannot  identify  causation
chains,  and  is  consistent  with  a  different  observed  dynamic  rela-
tionship  between  interest  rate  differentials  across  currencies  and
exchange  rate  changes.  Indeed  during  1985-1987  we  observe  interest
rate  differentials  (dollar  minus  foreign)  sometimes  shrinking  and
sometimes  widening  in  the  presence  of  dollar  depreciations.  The
former  case  implies  that  the  exchange  rate  is  moving  to  reduce
expected  depreciation  (27),  the  second  that  actual  changes  in  the
exchange  rate  are  lagging  behind  expected  depreciation  (we assume
that changes in any risk premium  or discount  on the three currencies
| played a minor role in observed  |     | changes in differentials).  |     |     |     |
| -------------------------------- | --- | --------------------------- | --- | --- | --- |
Second,  as  shown  in  our  model,  interventions  in  foreign  ex-
change  markets  shift  more  of  the  burden  of  adjustment  of  any
emerging  portfolio  disequilibrium  (due  to  a change  in exchange  rate
expectations)  onto interest  rate differentials,  increasingly with increas-
ing resistance  to exchange  market  trends;  sterilization,  in turn,  shifts
more  of  the  burden  of  adjustment  onto  the  long-term  end  of  the
| market;  | and,  finally,  | if the  country  |                  |               |     |
| -------- | --------------- | ---------------- | ---------------- | ------------- | --- |

Some elements  consistent  with these two sets of propositions  can
be  recognized  in  observed  developments  in  1985-1987.  First,
long-
term  differentials  were  higher  in  1985,  up  until  the  Plaza,  when  a
large depreciation was discounted by private agents but uncertainty as
to  the  actual  course  of  monetary  policy  in  the  US,  (would  it  ac-
| comodate  | the depreciation  |                            |       |               |     |
| --------- | ----------------- | -------------------------- | ----- | ------------- | --- |
|           |                   | or  not?) kept the dollar  | from  | falling more  |     |
than it did (Graph  3 and Table  5). They went  down consistently  from
(27)  A similar distinction  is that made  in MCKINNON  [26], if one
relates expected
depreciation to inflation expectations.

Cooperation in Managing the Dollar etc. ew
the last quarter of 1985 through most of 1986, when a market led
depreciation was restoring portfolio equilibrium; they went up again
in 1987, as confidence in the Louvre Accord was faltering.
The observed pattern of net capital flows (Table 5) could also be
related to changing expectations on the dollar (the alternative explan-
ation of a rising risk premium on this currency is also plausible, and
would not change the substance of the argument). The slowdown of
net inflows in the US from Japan corresponds to a “bump” along the
interest-differential declining trend in the fourth quarter of 1986, and
to a sharp widening of the differential in the third quarter of 1987. The
phenomenon is less clear vis-a-vis Germany, where aggregate flows
are the result of bilateral movements of opposite sign with other
European countries; however, rising outflows do coincide with de-
clining long-term differentials through 1986, and declining outflows
from Germany with rising differentials vis-a-vis the US in the first and
second quarter of 1987.
The behaviour of short-term interest differentials is somewhat
different (Graph 3), notably in the case of Japan in 1985-1986 (Japan
raised its money market rates in the first half of 1986, after lowering
them more pronouncedly in late 1985), and in the case of Germany in
1987 (when the Bundesbank moved its money market rates more
actively): these differences signal the attitude of monetary policies
relative to changing exchange rate expectations.
As it was mentioned, resistance to exchange rate depreciation
really starts at end 1986 - early 1987. In the first half of this year short-
(and long-) term interest rates moved consistently with the objective of
supporting the dollar (in line with the symmetric widening- or shrink-
ing-case of our model). In the summer and early autumn, however,
short-term interest rates were creeping up everywhere while ex-
change rate expectations were turning again against the dollar; the
two foreign countries were “setting a floor” to the world interest rate
structure, thus shifting more of the burden of monetary adjustment
into US markets. The steepening yield curve in the US seems to imply
— in terms of our model — that the Fed was moderating the rise in
short-term interest rates relative to what would have been required by
portfolio balance (28).
(28) According to the OECD, “over this period, given the efforts of the authorities
to stabilize exchange rates at the then-current level, practically all the financial
adjustment took place in terms of a change in long-term interest rates and differentials”
(OEcD [30], p. 76). On long-term interest rates as an emerging constraint to monetary
policy, see the considerations in Bis [4], ch. VI.

of the  above.  During  the  period  1985-1987,  the  correlation  between
long and short  term  rate  differentials  is lower  than  that observed  for
the  previous  floating-rate  period  1973-1984.  In  1985-1986,  a positive
correlation  was  observed  between  interest  rate  differentials  and  the
exchange  rate,  particularly  strong  for  long-term  rates  (0.95  for  Ger-
many,  0.96  for  Japan).  In  1987,  the  correlation  is  negative  (the
expected  depreciation  is  resisted,  not  necessarily  with  success);  in
absolute  terms  long-term  rates  are  more  strongly  correlated  with

382 Eugenio Gaiotti - Paola Giucca - Stefano Micossi
interest-rate differentials seem to contribute somewhat to the explan-
ation of the yen-dollar exchange rate (31).
With monthly data we were not able to analyse separately the
1985, 1986, and 1987 periods, as it would be required to find formal
evidence of our theses. We estimated separately the VAR model over
1985-1988; the results, however, are inconclusive due to the limited
number of degrees of freedom and hence low significance levels.
Further research using higher frequency data seems required. Keep-
ing this caveat in mind, the impulse-response functions derived from
the estimated VAR models over the two periods 1973-1984 and
1985-88 were calculated; some of their characteristics are shown in
Graph 9 (32). For both countries, a shock on the exchange rate has a
lower effect on short-term differentials in the more recent period,
while the effect on long-term differentials is somewhat stronger; this
result is at least consistent with our interpretation of the facts.
7. - Conclusions
The return to cooperation in managing the dollar between the
United States, Japan and Germany in 1985-1987 mainly involved joint
announcements, interventions in foreign exchange markets and, to an
extent, supporting changes in monetary policies. Fiscal policies did
play some role, but much less than is envisaged in official statements
and communiqués, with the exception of the expansionary package
adopted by Japan in May 1987. Furthermore, cooperation did not live
up to the image of fully-fledged coordination of macro-policies and
policy-mixes advocated, by international institutions and described by
academic economists in their models. Rather, what prevailed was
flexible “muddling through” with monetary instruments, and effective
crisis management operations concentrated in short-time spans.
Through most of 1985 and 1986 national policy objectives were
broadly consistent with the common goal of bringing about an orderly
depreciation of the dollar, so that pursuit of the latter did not imply an
(31) A significant role of the term structure of interest rates in predicting move-
ments in the (real) exchange rate is found by BOUGHTON [6]. Unlike our results his
estimates show a dependence of the exchange rate on long-term interest rates in
Germany but not in Japan. Boughton’s model assumes different processes of formation
for long and short-term exchange rate expectations.
(32) Data for 1988, otherwise not considered in this paper, had to be included to
gain degrees of freedom.

Cooperation in Managing the Dollar etc. 383
important constraint on national policies. The story was different in
1987, when the desire to halt depreciation of the dollar came to
conflict increasingly with domestic monetary policy objectives in
Japan and Germany. Large interventions, the resulting pressure on
monetary growth, actual and feared policy reactions to this pressure
and their impact on long-term interest rates, eventually took their toll,
possibly becoming an important factor in “detonating” the stock-mar-
ket crash.
The general lesson seems to be that there is considerable leeway
in the use of monetary instruments to accomodate diverging domestic
and external requirements, but that after a point the inconsistency
may show up (the inconsistency obviously arising from failure to act
on the fiscal policy front).
The traumatic suspension of cooperation in October 1987 also
seems to point to another conclusion. Non-intervention and pure
floating had been abandoned because of emerging imbalances in
international trade. A consensus then developed that exchange rates
cannot be left by themselves and need to be managed. After the return
to cooperation, however, there is ground to argue that central banks
may have overdone it, falling into the opposite sin of an excess of
intervention both in the foreign exchange and the domestic money
market, simply because it is very difficult to determine when precisely
to stop intervening under growing market pressures.
As long as there is an underlying “fundamental” disequilibrium
(in external balances or fiscal policies) the possibility of making similar
mistakes is a risk inherent in any cooperative arrangement to manage
exchange rates.

1.  -  During the ten years of its existence  the European  Monetary
System has survived  the ups and downs  of the business  cycle, which,
within the period, was also characterized by substantial changes in the
price  of oil and consistent  imbalances  in the  system  of international
| payments.  |     |     |     | ;   |
| ---------- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
As  far as  duration  is concerned,  in any  case,  the  EMS  may  be
considered  as  one  of  the  principal  results  of  the  commitment  to
European  unification.  The project for the further growth of European
integration  assigns to the EMS and the developments  that may spring
from  it the task  of constructing  the  starting  point  for the process  of
monetary  union.
But what have been the effects of the system on the economies  of
the countries  participating  in this exchange  rate  agreement?  In other
words,  it will be useful to ask ourselves  whether the system,  over  and
above  the  invariably  recalled  monetary  stability  and  the  consequent
disinflation  process  that  the  exchange  rate  mechanism  (ERM)  has:
induced  in the member  countries,  has  also  had  other  effects  on  the
(*) Though the present paper is the result of joint research,  Section  I was written
| by C. Imbriani  and Section  | B by R. de Luzenberger.  |     |     |     |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------ | --- | --- | --- |

| 394  | Raul de Luzenberger -  |     |     | Cesare Imbriani  |     |
| ---- | ---------------------- | --- | --- | ---------------- | --- |
economies  of the member  countries,  what  is the magnitude  of these
effects  and, more  particularly,  whether  these effects  have been distri-
| buted  in a symmetrical  |     | manner  | among  | the countries.  |     |
| ------------------------ | --- | ------- | ------ | --------------- | --- |
As regards  the  real  consequences  induced  by the  system,  it has
recently  been  observed  that  “between  1974  and  1985  the  growth  of
the  countries  participating  to  the  exchange  rate  mechanism  has
deteriorated  in the ERM period as compared with another group of 15
| countries  who  | are  not  | members  | of the  | ERM”  | (1).  |

This  has  been  happening  in  a  context  in which  a  continuous
increase  of the  German  advantage  in trading  exchanges  took  place.
For example,  an  indicator  like the one  given by the German  trading  ~
surplus  with  respect  to  the  other  EEC  countries  expressed  as  a
function  of the  total  German  trade  within  the  Common  Market  has
grown  steeply  during  the period  of the EMS.  Indeed,  it passed  from
values comprised between  3.5 and 4.0% in 1978-1979  to little short of
15% in 1988 (see Table  1); Italy, on the other hand, has seen this index
(1) See CockLe P. [4], p. 9; see also UNGERER et AL.  [23], ch. V, and GuITAN et AL.
[10].

EMS Membership Under etc. 395
deteriorate during the same period from more or less similar values in
1978-1979 to almost —7% in 1988.
This index provides a summary measure of the German trading
“success” in the EMS period. And all this has taken place within an
exchange rate regime in which some countries have experienced a.
continuous appreciation in real terms vis-a-vis the mark in recent
years. Therefore, it has been said that «Germany seems to benefit
from a competitive advantage constructed within the system that is
highlighted by the ever greater trade flows directed to the country».
Given this situation, it is probable that the tensions the system will.
have to face «will not be primarily the ones associated with the
recurring crises in current balances or with the lack of enthusiasm the
countries are showing in adjusting their interest rates, but rather
those deriving from the real implications for regional economies of
maintaining the exchange rates at levels that seem to be above their
equilibria» (2).
At the Community level it is generally said that it is up to the
countries in difficulty to fall into line with the optimal standard. But it
remains to be seen, especially within the ambit of the enlarged
Community, whether this is wholly realistic when one bears in mind
the imbalance regarding the trade flows within the Community and
also the rapidly emerging issue of catching up. The issue of the
regional differences in the Community or of rebalancing territorial
dualisms, the latter being of particular interest to Italy, will certainly
not be solved with policies that tend to impose demand control, even
though such policies are obviously important for short and medium-
term control. Therefore, rather than continuing at the Community
level with an approach of the good and bad boys type, the construc-
tion of the Community stands in need of a contribution that, as far as
possible, will internalize the existing differences.
If this is true, some comments are in order about the exchange
rate system and the effects it has produced within the member
countries. Although its mechanisms are well known, as also the
interrelations that the ERM has induced, it may be helpful to recall
them briefly.
(2) See COcKLE P., ibidem., p. 10.

396 Raul de Luzenberger - Cesare Imbriani
First of all, it is well known that the Bundesbank exerts a great
influence in this ambit, because it lays down monetary targets,
whereas the other countries, for the purpose of maintaining an
external balance and keeping inflation in check, limit themselves,
albeit with some autonomies, to an exchange rate control policy.
These different disciplines (i.e. monetary control and exchange
rate control) have hitherto implied that, face to face with the tendency
of the leader country to rely on restrictive policies that have induced a
generalized deflationist bias in the system, the cost of adjustments has
to be borne by the countries in structural deficit, since they are
committed to pursuing an adequate exchange rate discipline.
It is also true that a decisive part in this mechanism is being
played by the exchange rate relationships that recent years have seen
become established between the mark and the dollar. It has been
noted that when interest rates begin to rise in the USA, this represents
a new external constraint within the ambit of the countries of the
ERM. More specifically, «the European countries have succeeded in
producing a partial detachment of their interest rates from those
practiced in the United States, leaving the [...cost of the...] adjust-
ment to be borne, at least partially, by the appreciation of the dollar.
There has thus become configured a mechanism that is transmitted
from US economic policy to the local rate of interest, and thence to
either the German interest rate or the mark-dollar exchange rate - to
the extent to which the Bundesbank had succeeded in bringing about
a partial detachment of its interest rates - and therefore to the entire
exchange and interest rate structure within the EMS» (3).
This operating mode has highlighted an asymmetry, because —
depending on the particular state of the mark-dollar relationship —
there would occur changes in the position of the mark vis-a-vis the
other currencies of the system. More specifically, in periods of dollar
weakness «the mark becomes stronger vis-a-vis both the dollar and the
other currencies in the EMS, while a strong dollar leads to the mark
becoming weak vis-a-vis, once again, both the dollar and the other
EMS currencies» (4)

398 Raul de Luzenberger - Cesare Imbriani
In recent years, therefore, the real appreciation of the exchange
rate in countries with an income growth rate greater than the German
one has gone hand in hand with the coming to the fore of trading
imbalances within the Community. This forms part of a sequence of
events that has its exogenous starting point in the German growth
rate, which — given the careful policy of domestic demand manage-
ment — is sustained primarily by foreign demand (5). The manifest-
ation of imbalances in intracommunity trade, always in favour of
Germany and to the disadvantage of all the others, has found an
important panacea in the role that was performed by the US economy
until a few years ago and, more generally, is now being performed by
the rest of the world, which not only compensated the trading space
conquered by Germany within the Community, but also represented
an important outlet that enabled countries like Italy to achieve
particularly significant growth rates in recent years.
At the same time, however, — and here we come to the final
effect — Germany increased her surplus vis-a-vis all the other EMS
countries, and this not only by virtue of growth differentials, but
thanks also “to the real-term depreciation of the mark vis-a-vis all the
other currencies, which enabled the mark to compensate the effects
of its initial revaluation with respect to the dollar” (6).
3. - What will be the end of this story? As a general rule, people
today concern themselves with the operational aspects of the EMS, or
with new mechanisms that could be created on the basis of the
process of monetary union; but the problem of the trading imbalances
within the Community remains an open one.
Let us for the moment delve a little deeper into the analysis of the
evolution that the trading positions of the various EEC countries have |
undergone in recent years. Given the tendency of the ERM to be
transforme from an “adjustable peg” regime into a fixed exchange
rate system, a future situation of substantial stability of exchange rates

In short,  one  has to ask oneself whether  there  may be a possible
conflict  between  the exchange  rate  agreements,  which  may  induce  a
revaluation of the real exchange rate of the countries that tend to have

exchange  rate,  which  may  come  to the  fore  as  part  of development
acceleration  processes  in the  face  of trading  imbalances.
Leaving  aside  the  question  of  the  validity  of  the  model  that
Krugman  used  to  estimate  the  relationships  between  real exchange

This aspect can significantly condition the Italian trading position.
We have
already  seen  that  in the early eighties  a partial  solution  for
| the  problems  | of competitiveness  |              |             |                |

EMS Membership Under etc. 403
manufactured products was found by diverting the flow of Italian
exports from the EMS area to other areas, especially the United
States. However, the improvement in trade with the rest of the world
only masked a tendential worsening of the Italian trading imbalances
with the countries of the EMS area (10). This worsening was further
aggravated from 1987 onwards, when the nonpositive trend with the
countries that had signed the exchange rate agreements became
supplemented by a deterioration of Italy’s position vis-a-vis countries
outside the EMS area.
4. - Against this general background, concern has recently been
expressed regarding the part that participation in the exchange rate
mechanisms has played in promoting real convergence of the
economy of the member states. The growth rates experienced by the
various countries in the EMS period have been anything but uniform;
on the other hand, however, monetary convergence and stability have
been greatly facilitated by the non-repetition of the great shocks of the
seventies and the favourable trend of trade with the rest of the world.
Nevertheless, the rebalancing of the economies that in a certain sense
has been achieved is of a rather precarious nature: indeed, it is hardly
likely that productivity growth rate differentials will in future succeed
in compensating structural inflation differentials that are still very
appreciable without, at one and the same time, causing changes in
competitiveness in a situation in which economies have to face each
other in a fixed exchange rate regime.
If such a situation can persist, it is abundantly clear that the
inflation and competitiveness differentials of the industrial sectors will
continue to be decisive factors as far as trade is concerned. In the
short term, moreover, the present growth rate of our country, albeit
accompanied by a new upturn in the inflation rate, could promote a
deterioration in the trade balance; though we are at present compen-
sating this trend by attracting foreign capital, this inflow is implicitly
volatile and it is not easy to evaluate whether it represents a desirable
feature over the medium term. Therefore, we find ourselves in a
squeeze between our growth trends and our Community commit-
(10) See BINI, SMAGHI and Vona [12].

404 Raul de Luzenberger - Cesare Imbriani
ments with respect to the logic that the ERM has produced in
exchange rate matters.
5. - The analysis here performed is intended to stimulate further
consideration rather than to furnish cut and dried results. Neverthe-
less, bearing in mind the general trend to assess the ERM as an
element of order for a number of riotous countries and, consequently,
as an element of Community cohesion in the medium and long term,
it quite consciously adopts a different stance, wondering whether an
effective medium and long-term cohesion is possible when the mon-
etary mechanism can be a contributory cause of real imbalances that
are becoming ever more accentuated, especially as regards the trade
flows within the Community. A question of this kind, asked at a
moment when Europe seems to be on its way to monetary union, may
well prove to be far from trite.
On the other hand, the question of the compatibility of the trends
and divergences just described, given the passage to a system of
virtually fixed exchange rates, is essentially empirical in nature. One
therefore has to establish whether the effective patterns of Italian
export and import flows (or, if you prefer, the elasticities of these
flows with respect to domestic and foreign demand and the real
exchange rate) have been such in the recent past as to imply
substantial adjustment problems in the near future. With this in mind,
Part II of this paper will be dedicated to an empirical check that sets
out to estimate a series of functions relating to the balance of
payments flows between our country and the rest of the world, the
United States, and Germany.
II. - Models for Analyzing the Effects
of the Exchange Rate Agreements:
the Case of Italy Vis-a-Vis Germany,
the USA and the Rest of the World
1. - The problem that is making itself felt ever more strongly
within the ERM is, as noted above,that of reconciling the different real
growth rates of the member state economies and their different

EMS Membership Under etc. 405
inflation rates within the ambit of a mechanism that aims at a
substantial fixity of the nominal exchange rates. The problem springs
from the fact that two goals with different time profiles are being
pursued as part of the unification process. The search for greater
convergence in the growth of the monetary aggregates and the
maintenance of substantially fixed exchange rates are seen as the
prerequisites of greater Community integration, though the ultimate
objective is that of realizing the kind of development that will make it
possible to bring the economies of the member countries closer to
each other than they are at present.
The different time horizons associated with the two goals may
lead to a divergence between the adjustment mechanism implicit in
the exchange rate agreements and economic performance in keeping
with the attainment of the long-term objective. Adding to this, at the
Community level there is a tendency to view as “good” the countries
that realize the short and medium-term goal with ease and in a
comparatively short time; it practically follows that the countries
more directly involved in a catching-up process or in regional policy
aimed at reducing historical situations of territorial dualism, are
included in the other category.
The catching up process requires the economies of the more
recently industrialized countries, as also those of countries with
substantial regional disporities, to grow at a faster rate than the
economies of the other countries, a condition that may imply a faster
growth of internal demand. The substantial fixity of the nominal
exchange rates in a context characterized by different inflation rates
implies gradual changes in the real exchange rates. Thus the problem
arises of evaluating the effects that changes in the real exchange rate
and the domestic demand of the individual countries exert on interna-
tional trade flows, not least with a view to assessing whether pursuit
of the short and medium-term objective is compatible with the
long-term goal. The emphasis placed on these two variables justifies
the examination of models that consider them to be the principal
causes of changes in import-export flows.
1.1 The limits of the analysis inevitably make tentative any
assessment of the sustainability of possible trade imbalances among

406 Raul de Luzenberger - Cesare Imbriani
the ERM countries. The system of transfers constructed on the basis
of the Basle-Nyborg agreements and the possibility of capital flows of
such a nature as to make it less necessary for deficit countries to seek
adjustments in the short term could well render these imbalances
more sustainable. Nevertheless, there are reasons to believe that the
stability of the system is not compatible with the structural imbalances
induced by the catching up process or implicit in the adjustment
process bound up with the exchange rate agreements. Miller and
Williamson [17] argue that the effects of a real exchange rate
appreciation may be substantial and imply high costs in terms of
production and national income over the medium term. If this is true,
the costs of the ERM for the countries with higher inflation rates are
bound to grow in the course of time.
2. - Models that relate demand and real exchange rate patterns
to imports and exports have, for various reason, attracted a certain
amount of interest in the United States in recent years. Krugman and
Baldwin [13], for example, analyzed the causes that could have been
responsible for the substantial deficit of the trade balance of the
United States in the course of the eighties. They reached the con-
clusion that the traditional explanations offered by theory seem to be
sufficient to understand even the most recent developments. In
particular, the trend of home demand and the real exchange rate, as
well as the dynamic effects that these variables exert on the import
and export flows of manufactured goods, are deemed capable of
explaining the pattern of the US trade deficit.
But the conclusions reached by Krugman and Baldwin are not
unanimously accepted in literature. For example, Dornbusch [7]
argues that the events that characterized the international economy in|
the eighties can hardly be explained on the basis of the traditional
models for determining the exchange rate. The author analyzed the
“explanatory performance” of the three principal models for
determining the exchange rate or the current account balance,
namely the macroeconomic model (or Mundell-Fleming approach),
the monetarist model, and the equilibrium model of New Classical
Macroeconomics. Dornbusch argues that none of these models can
explain — without additional ad hoc assumptions — either the pattern

EMS Membership Under etc. 407
or the magnitude of the changes in the real-term exchange rates in the
eighties and, consequently, the behaviour of the trade balances.
More recently, Mundell [15] and McKinnon and Ohno [16] have
argued that the real exchange rate plays no part in determining the
trade balance, which — according to these authors — is determined
solely by the difference between the gross domestic product and
aggregate expenditure, that is to say, by the difference between
savings and investments (plus, where appropriate, the public budget
deficit). As has already been noted (and we shall subsequently illus-
trate this in greater detail), Krugman [12] argues that domestic
demand may be substantially irrelevant for determining trade balance.
In the last resort, however, the relevance of the real exchange rate
and of aggregate demand as determinants of the international trade
flows, as also the relative importance of these two factors, is a
question that can be settled on an empirical ground.
3. - Ignoring the dynamic aspects, Krugman and Baldwin’s
model consists essentially of two equations: in one exports are
function of foreign demand and the real exchange rate, demand and
the real exchange in the other imports are function of domestic rate.
The authors justify this structure on the basis of various theoretical
considerations such as the J curve model, the extended form of the
absorption approach model (which takes also into account changes in
the real exchange rate and multiperiodal contracts that yields a lags
structure), and also on partial equilibrium models with variously
determined lag structures.
Krugman [12] used this model to analyze the relationship be-
tween the real growth rate of the economy (and the rate of expansion
of domestic demand with respect to foreign demand), the real import
and export flows, and the real exchange rate. The model is similar to
the one used by Krugman and Baldwin; all its variables are expressed
in logarithmic form and the place of the rate of growth of real demand
is taken by the growth rate of real income (which is often used as a
proxy for demand growth). The model is therefore given by:

Krugman  argues  that this relationship  is satisfied  in practice  and
that the elasticities  of import  and export  with respect  to real income
behave in such a way as to compensate  the differentials  in the growth
rates,  thus  ensuring  that  the long-term  impact  on  the real  exchange
rate will be practically  zero  (11); i.e. the so-called  45-degree  rule.
It is difficult to give an interpretation of Krugman’s results and of
the constancy of the real exchange rate that he is able to infer from his
data.  More  specifically,  it  is  not  clear  what  might  be  the  causal
relationship between  the variables  under  consideration.  For example,  -
it is undoubtedly  possible  that,  in a group  of countries  among  which
competitive  devaluations  cannot  be  readily  accomplished  without
provoking  reactions,  those  countries  enjoying  a  favourable:  combin-
ation  of import  and  export  elasticities  can  have  higher  growth  rates
then  other  countries.  But  the order  of causality  and the implications
for economic  policy that may be deduced  therefrom  could well be the

| III.  -  | Some Consequential  |             |     | Considerations  |     |     |     |
The European Monetary  System may be considered  as one of the
greatest results of the process of European integration and, at one and
the  same  time,  as  the  instrument  for  achieving  an  even
greater
integration  in  future.  However,  it has  been  observed  that  if this
integration
is really  to come  true,  «the  fight against  inflation  can  no
| longer    | be  the     | unifying     | goal  |          |             |                 |       |
| --------- | ----------- | ------------ | ----- | -------- | ----------- | --------------- | ----- |
|           |             |              |       | in  the  | management  | of the  EMS,    | even  |
| though    | this  goal  | is becoming  |       | ever     | more        | widely          |       |
|           |             |              |       |          |             | shared  by all  | the   |
| members»  | (19).       |              |       |          |             |                 |       |
Some  concerns  are  coming to the fore,  especially  as regards  the
| compatibility  | of the adjustment  |        |             |                 |                           |              |          |
| -------------- | ------------------ | ------ | ----------- | --------------- | ------------------------- | ------------ | -------- |
|                |                    |        |             | process         | implicit in the exchange  |              | rate     |
| agreements     | with               | other  | objectives  | of the process  |                           |              |          |
|                |                    |        |             |                 |                           | of European  | integr-  |
ation,  and this both as regards the trend that seems  to turn the trade
imbalances  within  the Community  into structural  imbalances,  and as
| regards          | the  consequences  |                   |     |             |      |                           |     |
| ---------------- | ------------------ | ----------------- | --- | ----------- | ---- | ------------------------- | --- |
|                  |                    |                   |     | that  this  | may  | have  on  the  hoped-for  |     |
| (19) SARCINELLI  |                    | M.  [22], p. 71.  |     |             |      |                           |     |

EMS Membership Under etc. 417
convergence of the economies of the member countries. The catching-
up process clearly requires the less rich countries as also the countries
that have to deal with regional disparities, to have a higher long-term
growth rate. The consequent faster demand expansion may cause
imports to grow at a greater pace than exports. If this process is to be
compatible with the maintenance of equilibrium in the trade balance
and a constant real exchange rate, it is essential that in the faster
growing country the import elasticity with respect to home demand
should be sufficiently smaller than the elasticity of exports with
respect to foreign demand.
In the presence of inflation rate differentials, however, the con-
stancy of the nominal exchange rates implies an appreciation of the
real-term exchange rates that, in the countries that have had a growth
rate in excess of the German one, has gone hand in hand with the
coming to the fore of growing trade imbalances within the Com-
munity, especially vis-a-vis Germany. This is happening in a context in
which there is a tendency at the Community level to consider the
countries that succeed in realizing both rapidly and efficiently the
short and medium-term goal implicit in the ERM as “good and
virtuous”, so that a number of countries, generally the countries
interested in catching up process or dealing with wide regional
disparities, are almost automatically assigned to the other group.
Tendentially, therefore, the adjustment mechanism implicit in the
ERM has effects that are in contrast with the attainment of the
long-term goal of reducing the differences among the economies of
the member countries. It may well be that these tendencies, even
though they have been making themselves felt gradually but steadily
over a number of years, had an important panacea in the part played
by the growth of the US economy in the Eighties, together with the
steep appreciation of the dollar vis-a-vis the other currencies — in
both nominal and real terms — within the period.
In the last resort, however, the problem of a possible contrast
between the ERM and the objective of lesser disparities within the
Community, as also between the adjustment processes implicit in
these two goals, is also bound up with the elasticities of imports and
exports with respect to demand (domestic and foreign) and with
respect to the real exchange rate. Examination of the relationships

418 Raul de Luzenberger - Cesare Imbriani
between price and quantity elasticities allows a first assessment of the
extent to which the ERM is the source of trade imbalances that are
not compatible with the desired convergence of the real economies.
An evaluation of these effects — if it is not to be a mere opinion —
must ultimately be based on empirical research. The present paper,
which set out to make a contribution to a more detailed understand-
ing of the problem, adopted this approach: the analysis here per-
formed, which is limited to Italian trade with the rest of the world and
as also with Germany and the United States, during the period
1974-1988 seems to confirm the expected effects that an appreciation
in the real exchange rate and a growth of domestic demand exert on
import and export flows. More particularly, considering the rela-
tionship between the import and export elasticities with respect to
demand, Italy would seem to be a high-risk subject as regards the
manifestation of trade imbalances.
At this point we do not attempt at going into the basic
compatibility between participation in the present Community logic,
territorial balancing within our country, necessary stabilization of the
public finances and maintenance of a satisfactory growth rate, prefer-
ring to leave the matter open for the time being. The difficulty of
reconciling such an extensive set of problems must not, however, give
rise to a trend in favour of Community disengagement, which is
neither conceivable nor desirable.

Washington  DC,  1987,  Institute  for International  Economics,  1987.

422 Stephen Marris
the major industrial countries have proved to be more elastic and
farther away than seemed likely from earlier experience.
Nevertheless, I shall argue below that the main reason for the
“perverse” nature of events in the foreign exchange markets over the
last eighteen months arises from the fact that both governments and
the markets are in the middle of a learning process with a new and
untested exchange-rate regime, with some unexpected and unwel-
come results.
The first Section reviews events since the Louvre Agreement as
seen from the markets. The second section attempts to interpret what
has been happening in terms of what we already know about the
operation of a “stable but adjustable” exchange-rate system, notably
from the experience of the EMS. The last Section discusses the policy
issues.
The conclusion reached is that either we shall move to a more
rigorous stable but adjustable currency regime, or that this will be
regarded as involving too great a loss of economic sovereignty. In the
latter case, we are likely to see a continuation of the cycles of
misalignment that have characterised exchange rates since the
breakdown of the Bretton Woods system. With luck, such cycles
might be of shorter duration and lesser magnitude than during the
1980s, but they would also be likely to involve chronic overvaluation
of the vehicle currency, the US dollar.
1. - Events as Seen from the Markets
At the Louvre, on 22nd February 1987. The G-7 (actually the G-6)
inaugurated a “reference range” exchange-rate system. We know this
to be true because we have Yoichi Funabashi’s authoritative account
of what went on (3). We also know, however, from the same source,
that the agreement reached was fuzzy, pragmatic and short term, and
that both then and subsequently the participants had different inter-
pretations of what they had agreed upon. It thus is all the more
(3) See VoIcHI FUNABASHI: Managing the Dollar: from the Plaza to the Louvre,
Washington DC, Institute for international Economics, 1988.

Deficits and Surpluses Forever? 423
remarkable that within two years foreign exchange dealers had come
to interpret what was happening in the markets almost exclusively in
terms of their understanding of the central banks’ intentions with
regard to keeping the yen and the dollar within quite specific quan-
tified ranges vis-a-vis the dollar.
Initially, however, the dealers were singularly unimpressed. The
“markets know best” philosophy still prevailed, and conventional
wisdom had it that central banks had far too little ammunition to have
more than a temporary influence on markets where hundreds of
billions of dollars were changing hands daily. Thus in the weeks
following the Louvre meeting there was a severe dollar crisis. US
interest rates rose sharply, but the dollar plunged, and (as emerged
subsequently) there was a substantial net outflow of private capital
from the United States (4). By the end of the first week of May,
however, the first battle of the dollar had been won. And, although
not obvious at the time, we were in a new ball park.
The dollar began to rise, and by July the markets were trying to
find the upper limit of the reference range. Toward the end of the
month the central banks moved in quite strongly to cap the dollar’s
rise. In the meanwhile, however, the Bundesbank had taken advan-
tage of the dollar’s recovery to bring German interest rates up more in
line with what it considered appropriate on domestic grounds. This
led to a general escalation of interest rates, and an unseemly public
row between Mr. Baker and the German authorities. The dollar
started to slide and the stage was set for Black Monday.
For a short time after the crash the dollar was left in the doldrums
in the worldwide scramble to get out of equities. Subsequently it
appeared to the markets that Mr. Baker’s overwhelming concern was
no longer to defend the dollar but to avoid a recession by pumping
liquidity into the economy. In the last days of December the dollar
seemed to be in a free fall. The fact the G-7 had failed to meet and had
merely produced a stereotyped “telephone” communique was widely
interpreted as sounding the death knell of the Louvre Agreement.
The first days of January 1988, however, witnessed what was

In 1985  and  1986 things were  relatively straightforward.  The

Deficits and Surpluses Forever? 425
dollar was going down and the only question was at what price and
how far ahead to hedge. But since the Louvre things have been
different. The “fundamentalists” have tended to remain short in
dollars at considerable expense and no profit. Even the more specula-
tive short term operators have found it hard to get timing of the ups
and downs of the dollar right.
Indeed, after a while, some adventurous operators decided that
there were other better ways to make money. Since governments
were now managing exchange rates, this greatly reduced the
downside exchange-rate risk on otherwise suspect currencies; and
since countries with such currencies generally had high interest rates,
there was money to be made out of a “high coupon” strategy. Thus it
was that investments in such currencies as the Australian dollar, the
lira and the peseta became increasingly popular. But the biggest
attraction was the pound sterling — so attractive that the markets
were able to force Mr. Lawson to remove the 3 DM cap on sterling,
thus giving the investors both high interest rates and a handsome
profit on the exchange rate.
Foreign exchange dealers are no fools. They are perfectly well
aware that high interest rates normally reflect high inflation, a weak
external position, and in time the likelihood of currency depreciation.
But in this age of instant communications they feel confident in their
ability to move fast and hedge or sell their positions in these suspect
currencies as soon as (or just before?) the going gets rough. Thus they
held on to their sterling positions through 1988 even as the United
Kingdom’s fundamentals turned disastrously for the worse (a rip
roaring domestic boom, the unexpectedly rapid rate of inflation than
in virtually any other industrial county). The lesson seemed to be that
with the present exchange-rate regime one could safely ignore the
fundamentals for quite a while, making money both from high
interest rates and with luck also from currency appreciation. In the
UK case the first cracks only came in February and again in May
1989. But when they did come the pound dropped so swiftly that few
people managed to get out in time, as was perhaps to be expected. So
far, however, the fall in the pound has been relatively limited so that it
was only the latecomers who lost money.
This brings us back to the dollar. By early 1989 the markets felt

were  in the middle  of the range,  then  the odds  of making  exchange-

Deficits and Surpluses Forever? 427
True, two bouts of fairly heavy coordinated intervention (in
which the Bundesbank participated) had, by the end of the first week
of June, driven the dollar back below 2 DM. It was symptomatic,
however, that Mr Pél was quoted as saying on 7th June that although
the current exchange rate pattern «is not helpful for the adjustment
process ... I have no judgement if the dollar is too high or too low, that
is for the markets to decide» (6). This was a remarkably agnostic
statement coming, as it did, from the President of the central bank of
a country whose currency had depreciated against the dollar by 15
percent over the previous six months, and where inflation has picked
up to what is, by German standards, a high level.
Given all this it would be hardly surprising if the markets have
begun to wonder if they need take the G-3 seriously any more. If not,
perhaps the dollar could rise a lot further. True, US fundamentals are
not in good shape — but they are a lot better than in the United
Kingdom, and look how long that bandwagon lasted. Maybe this is
the moment to forget the fundamentals and listen to the chartists (7).
Stripped of the mumbo jumbo, chartists are in the business of
extrapolating short and longer run cycles from the past into the
future. Thus, since the dollar rose for just over four years to February
1985 and has now been falling for just over four years, it is hardly
surprising that they have been bullish on the dollar for some time.
Equally, experienced portfolio managers no doubt remember that
in the last cycle the dollar rose by over 50% against the DM in the
twelve months from October 1980. Indeed it rose so fast that within
six months dealers were forecasting that it would fall by about 10
percent over the next twelve months, and held — quite incorrectly —
to this view for the following three years (8). Recently the dollar has
been rising in the face of a declining interest-rate differential, helped
by political instability in several parts of the world. Could this mean
that we are on the eve of a replay of the dollar bandwagon of the early

2. - A Comparison with the EMS
In trying to interpret this unfinished story of markets versus the
authorities under the Louvre Agreement, I find it helpful to go back to
earlier experience with the EMS. Admittedly there are important
differences between the two regimes. In the EMS the bands are much
narrower and the outer limits are known to the markets; there is a
formal commitment to defend these limits; and a there is an estab-
lished collective decision-making process for changing the central
rates. But although the modalities are different, the basic obiective is
the same: to keep exchange rates “stable” in a range around a
mid-point which is considered to be consistent with the “funda-
mentals”, while being prepared to’ move the range in line with
changes in the fundamentals (9).
A first lesson comes from the early days of the EMS. Although
often now forgotten, it initially proved far from easy to eastablish the
credibility of even the short-term commitment to defend the margins.
It soon became apparent that sterilized intervention was insufficient,
and in the face of strong speculative attacks participants were forced
to make drastic use of monetary policy, especially short-term interest
rate policy, to defend the margins. At the time this experience tended
to confirm the view of the many sceptics that the system would break
down because it involved too great a subjugation of domestic mon-
etary policy to exchange rate objectives.
In time, however, as the monetary authorities gained credibility,
and as the rules of the game regarding realignments became estab-
lished, it proved possible to maintain the margins with only quite
moderate intervention and quite modest and short lived deviations of
(9) Quite possibly some G-5 participants would reject or heavily qualify this
definition of the objective. De facto, however, the G-5 decided (and said) at the Plaza
that the dollar was out of line with the fundamentals and should go down, and at the
Louvre that it was roughly in line with the fundamentals and should neither fall nor rise
(this was said later) by much from its current level.

Deficits and Surpluses Forever? 429
monetary policy from domestic objectives. Thus, as the EMS
matured, it generally proved possible to maintain stable exchange
rates while at the same time allowing monetary policy to be directed
primarily to domestic objectives dictated by inflation, employment
and budgetary considerations.
There were, of course, exceptions. The most important came in
March 1983, when the French Socialist government made a. miajor
shift to a more «Germanic» economic policy largely as a result of its
decision to stay in the RMS. But although this episode was crucial to
the subsequent evolution of the EMS, it was also untypical. Between
1981 and 1983 the French government had indulged in fiscal expan-
sion during a major world recession, embarked on a large scale
programme of nationalization, and imposed a wealth tax. It is very
doubtful whether, in today’s world, it could have got away with this
even if it had left the EMS (which could well have made things worse).
Looking at experience with the EMS more generally, the surprising
thing is to what extent it has proved possible to reconcile reasonable
exchange-rate stability with substantial differences between the par-
ticipants in inflation, growth and budget deficits (e.g. Italy!) (10).
Thus early German fears that the commitment to defend fixed
margins would be inflationary soon proved unfounded. For quite a
while the converse fear that the Bundesbank would impose excessive
deflation on the rest of Europe seemed more legitimate. There is a
considerable and rather inconclusive literature on this subject. My
own view is that while up to about 1986 a plausible case could be
made, it is now much less convincing. The record shows that dom-
estic demand has grown much faster in the rest of Europe during the
1980s than in Germany, and that it has proved possible for the EMS
countries to live with significant (but narrowing) inflation and nominal
interest-rate differentials vis-a-vis Germany.
There is a second lesson from the EMS which is particularly
relevant to recent experience with the Louvre regime. As the
credibility of the system became established it became quite normal
for the “weak” currencies with high interest rates to trade above

First,  because  the  bands  are  narrow,  the  attraction  of high  interest

speculation that has helped to prevent the sort of perverse exchange-

3. - Policy Implications
To sum up at this point, a comparison of the EMS with the
Louvre regime suggests the following: 1) establishing the credibility of
the margins in the EMS initially involved far more strenuous use of
monetary policy — in particolar, short-term interest rate policy —
than the participants in the Louvre Agreement appear prepared to
undertake. While this reluctance may be understandable, especially in
the case of the United States, it may also be shortsighted, since EMS
experience suggests that once credibility has been established the
deviations in monetary policy from domestic objectives needed to
defend the margins could well become quite modest and short lived;
2) contrary to a widely held view, it may be easier to operate a stable
but adjustable exchange-rate regime with narrow margins rather than
a wide and elastic band. Narrow margins both reduce the incentive
for “perverse” capital movements seeking short-term exchange-rate
profits, and ensure that exchange rates cannot be pushed far in the
wrong direction with regard for the need to correct external imbal-
ances and to offset differences in national inflation rates; 3) most
important, for a stable but adjustable exchange rate regime to operate
successfully, the markets have to be convinced that when central rates

to be justified by a remarkable convergence in national unit labour costs movements
over the last three years. But this has not prevented the emergence of a very large
German current. account surplus, notably vis-a-vis other European countries. For the
time being this has not proved troublesome because for so long as the United States is
running a very large deficit the deficits of the other EMS participants have remained
relatively small. But if and when the US deficit comes down sharply, correction of the
major payments imbalance within Europe could well involve an upward realignment of
the DM of a magnitude which could seriously undermine the hard won credibility of the

are  changed the changes will be in the right direction  with respect  to
the  fundamentals.  It  is in  this  respect  that  current  events,  in  the
currency  markets  are  of such  importance.  If, in the  face  of current
bullish  market  sentiment  in favour  of the dollar,  the authorities  give

that  the  Louvre  experiment  will  be  in deep  trouble  —  although  as
EMS  also  shows,  there  could  later  be opportunities  to  recoup  from
past  errors.
It should  be stressed  that  I am  not  suggesting  that  the  Louvre
experiment  could  only  be  made  to  work  by adopting  all  the  more
rigorous  features  of  the  EMS,  including  narrow  and  publicly  an-
nounced  margins.  From  my  fairly  lengthy  experience  in this  area  I
have  been  impressed  how  much  influence  governments  can  have  on
exchange rates simply through the demonstration
of political commit-

there
can be a vicious  circle between the behaviour of the foreign exchange

poor  fundamentals,  thus as a general  rule making it easier  to finance

deficits
prove  easy  to  finance  often  leads  governments  to  persuade

(12) Viz.  the  recent  statement  by Michael  Boskin,  Chairman  of the
Council  of

in  US
economic  policies.

Deficits and Surpluses Forever? 433
In turn, this complacency may well infect the currency markets,
making it even easier to finance the deficit. And so on.
In my view this kind of perverse interaction between govern-
ments and markets played a major role in the mismanagement and
eventual breakdown of the Bretton Woods regime — which was, after
all, meant to be an adjustable — peg system. Regrettably, there are
signs that the same fate may befall the Louvre experiment.
This brings us to the central issue of to what extent a given
exchange-rate regime does or does not provide incentives to govern-
ments to follow sensible policies. It can be argued, for example, that
the current strength of the dollar is entirely consistent with the
(wrong) fundamentals. The US economy is fully employed and do-
mestic demand has been rising as fast as potential output. There is
thus no room for a further improvement in the trade balance. The
rising dollar, by choking off the improvement in the trade balance, is
simply the price mechanism’s response to the fact that US savings are
insufficient to finance both US investment and a large budget deficit.
Analytically this is correct. But it is also true that in terms of
policy-making the strength of the dollar is counterproductive, since,
together with the associated bullish sentiment in the markets, it
provides little incentive to the administration to do something about
the budget deficit, rather the contrary.
This question of the incentives to good policy-making inherent in
different exchange-rate regimes is still hotly disputed among econo-
mists. My own view is that experience — particularly with the EMS —
has shown that the obligation to defend a fairly explicit exchange-rate
target provides, on balance, the most effective incentives. In the
current case of the United States, for example, if the dollar had been
held down to the lower half on the band, continuing improvement in
the trade balance would have led to serious overheating in the
economy. The administration would then have been forced to face up
to a choice between cutting back consumption by cutting the budget
deficit, or leaving the job to the Fed, which given that consumption is
relatively insensitive to interest rates, would have meant cutting back
investment and provoking a recession. As it is, by allowing the dollar
to rise, the need to do something about the inadequacy of US savings
has once again been put off into the future.

434 Stephen Marris
In conclusion, I believe that unless the Louvre regime is tightened
up it will probably break down. This does not mean that the only
alternative is a fully-fledged EMS type regime, although it does
probably mean that over time the width of the bands should be
somewhat reduced and the agreed limits publicly announced.
As of now, however, the governments concerned seem more
inclined to move to a looser regime. In this case I believe that we are
likely to see a continuation of the cycles of misalignment that have
characterised the exchange rates since the breakdow of the Bretton
Woods system. With luck, the cycles might be of shorter duration and
lesser magnitude than during the 1980s. On average, however, they
are likely to involve chronic overvaluation of the vehicle currency, the
US dollar — the same fate that befell its predecessor, the pound
sterling.

Mario Baldassarri is Professor of
= Economics at the University of Rome, ‘La
Sapienza’, Italy. He is editor of Italy’s most
prestigious economics journal, Rivista di
Politica Economica, and was formerly
economic adviser to the Italian government.
Luigi Paganetto is Professor of Economics
and Dean of the Faculty of Economics and
Business Administration at the University of
Rome, ‘Tor Vergata’, Italy.
Edmund S. Phelps is McVickar Professor
of Political Economy at Columbia Univer-
sity, New York.
